Over the past ten of years, machine learning researchers have rigorously studied neural networks, yielding valuable insights for the field. Building upon our earlier work that showed convergence rates for two-layer neural networks in Euclidean space, this paper extends these findings to a hypercube setting. We present statistical analysis that reveals how a neural network's generalization performance is influenced by its architecture and data sampling technique. Our mathematical framework allows us to measure the accuracy of a neural network's approximation of a function, as well as its ability to generalize from training data to unseen scenarios. Our analysis shows that neural networks trained on adversarial samples exhibit better generalization than those trained on randomly drawn data. We leverage our mathematical framework to establish a lower bound on the dimensionality of neural networks and neural ensembles with adversarial training, revealing a phase transition near a particular dimensionality threshold. This method employs a modified version of the influential PAC-Bayes bound, offering an alternative perspective that can be applied to two-layer neural networks. Furthermore, our results, which are applicable to a wide range of data distributions, align with empirical observations on the effectiveness of adversarial training. To showcase the applicability of our findings, we examine a binary classification task involving noisy data that spans a hypercube, observing a significant improvement in classification accuracy with adversarial training. We also apply our mathematical framework to a binary classification task involving data that follows a Gaussian distribution within a high-dimensional space. Here, our analysis identifies a balance between neural network complexity and dimensionality that yields optimal generalization performance, revealing that neural ensembles can achieve better generalization than standalone neural networks of comparable complexity. Our mathematical framework's predictions are verified through numerical simulations, demonstrating a similar trend between neural network generalization performance and the predicted bounds we've established. Our research offers a theoretical understanding of neural networks, adversarial training, and the impact of data structure on generalization performance. We anticipate that our method for establishing bounds on neural network generalization performance could be applied to a broad range of neural network architectures and datasets. Theoretical research into planetary properties within tight multi-body systems revolves heavily around orbital resonances. To investigate this, we introduce a novel computational framework that evaluates planetary configurations at arbitrary stages within a given resonance. Our method computes key orbital resonances of Saturn's Moon, Galilean moons, and other planetary systems by employing the multiple-scale theory. Furthermore, it's also applicable to compact systems containing a central star and multiple planets displaying resonant behavior. Using the framework, we develop a numerical algorithm to solve and compare orbital phases and angular momentum derivatives at various levels of approximation. To assess the algorithm's performance, we conduct an analysis of orbital phases and angular momentum to confirm its reliability. Our findings support that the algorithm yields consistent results across varying orders of approximation and reveals discrepancies between first-order and higher-order computations that decrease significantly upon enhancement. Finally, we demonstrate the algorithm's capability in analyzing the orbital dynamics of the Galilean moons and compare its outcomes with existing theoretical models and observational data. Our results suggest that higher-order computations often lead to better agreement with experimental data and theoretical models. The developed algorithm remains modular, facilitating effortless integration with other planetary dynamics projects. As such, we anticipate its potential contribution to various compact system investigations. Our methodology extends to narrow asteroid systems by providing a framework to analyze orbital phases and the eccentricities of narrow asteroids. Furthermore, through the comparison of first-order and higher-order computational results, the potential benefits of incorporating higher-order calculations into the MESA Jupiter Moon Circulation In Depth (MACiD) model into the study of Jupiter's rocky moons are unveiled. Overall, the software package comprising our computational framework is made available for community use at https://github.com/CESM2-RP/ORbit, with the research paper itself located at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14666. Lastly, a companion paper explores the incorporation of the orbital resonances framework into the MACiD project, highlighting the advantages of employing the developed software to investigate orbital phases and the eccentricities of Jupiter's rocky moons. The SiD Detector is one of the six proposed Vertex Detector Simulators for the ILC. It's a compact, solenoid-based detector with an advanced silicon vertex detector and precise calorimeter system designed for precise jet energy measurement. The calorimeter's integration with a high-luminosity, polarized beam allows it to achieve accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range with a single detector component. The joint HL-LHC and ILC beam test demonstrated the detector concept's effectiveness and showed its ability to measure jets and electrons/positrons efficiently. This paper details the jet and electron/positron reconstruction methods used in the beam test, focusing on jet energy measurement, and provides an update on the detector's performance. Energy spectra of jets and electrons/positrons were generated based on simulated data, and measured data was corrected for detector efficiency. The correction was applied using a linear or quadratic function, followed by a Gaussian fit to obtain energy distributions. The jet energy resolution was calculated by comparing simulated data and measured distributions, and similar calculations were done for electron/positron reconstruction. The detector's performance was found to be in line with designed precision for jet and electron/positron reconstruction. This precision is sufficient for precise calorimeter-based jet energy measurement across a wide energy range with a single detector component. The joint HL-LHC and ILC beam test demonstrated the proposed SiD Detector concept's effectiveness, and the results are expected to influence the future detector design. This paper details the jet and electron/positron reconstruction methods used during the beam test, providing an update on the detector's performance. The jet energy resolution was found to be 2% and 10% (rel.) across an energy range from 50 to 200 GeV, and electron/positron reconstruction precision was found to be 2.3% and 20% (rel.). These precision levels are significantly higher than the proposed detector design precision, indicating the significance of the beam test results. The results are expected to influence the future detector design. Reconstructing jets and electrons/positrons requires efficient electron/positron identification and separation, particularly important for jet measurement, as electron/positron contamination can adversely affect jet energy resolution. This paper details the joint HL-LLC and ILC beam test methodology for electron/positron identification and separation methods used in the beam test. Electron/positron discrimination was carried out using various variables such as scintillator-based timing, electromagnetic shower patterns, and collimation, and accuracy was assessed in various regions of the detector.

This study developed a new experimental protocol to acquire high-quality 1D and 2D NMR spectra of amorphous ices samples at various temperatures and pressures, utilizing a probe designed specifically for use under pressure. The spectral quality attained allows for the creation of a hydrogen-bond network model which describes the structure of low-density amorphous ice and its phase transition to higher-density amorphous ice. The model also provides a quantitative understanding of the structure of specific types of hydrogen bonds, indicating their presence in specific proportions. The protocol demonstrated the ability to detect specific types of terminations and the changes occurring in the hydrogen-bond network over a range of temperatures and pressures. The study also provides recommendations for optimizing NMR acquisition parameters and suggests that solid-state NMR has the potential to provide detailed information regarding the structure and properties of ices under various conditions of temperature and pressure. The data presented has been made publicly available in support of future studies to develop quantitative models describing the structure of ices, however, it is essential to implement improvements in probe design that will allow for pressure optimization, leveraging recent advancements in the field. This study categorizes different materials that serve as ideal conductors and semiconductors to explain the principle of Scanning Tunneling Microscopy. The experiment involves analyzing the Local Density of States of gold, graphite, and silicon wafers using an STM scanner. The results show that silicon exhibits the highest Local Density of States compared to gold and graphite. The current versus voltage characteristic of the three materials displays a linear non-contact mode in the range of low tunneling distances. The findings are compared with existing research on various materials, thereby validating the applicability of the proposed principle. The researchers also identified a maximum range of linear variation in the tunneling distance for gold, graphite, and silicon of 0.75 nm, 1.0 nm, and 1.5 nm, respectively. The research provides a clear understanding of the material characterization required for the non-contact mode of STM operations. The study ultimately concludes in favor of using silicon as the optimal sample material for STM applications due to its highest Local Density of States and extended linear range of tunneling distances. The proposed principle and characterization method can be further utilized to develop application manuals for different materials and scanning probe tips to facilitate precise and efficient scanning tunneling microscopes. To facilitate searching, a scalable algorithm is proposed, reducing computational effort by leveraging FOP's architectural features and enabling users to identify the closest relationship between arbitrary given elements. Additionally, an evaluation of the impact of architectural improvements is presented, showing FOP's performance in response to different user queries before and after optimization. General guidelines are provided to facilitate the development of suitable search algorithms and architectural designs for FOP. The method successfully determines the relevant counterterms that allow these solutions to be conformally coupled to AdS spacetime. The Graph Programming language GP is utilized for specifying distributed network processes and their concurrent behavior. GP is interpreted as a collection of graph transformations operating on a network's state, where new features include temporarily locking shared resources to avoid race conditions. A two-stage semantics for GP has been previously established, comprising a blocking semantics ensuring race-free execution and a more efficient, blocking semantics-related trajectory. Here, a new trajectory semantics is proposed that bypasses the blocking mechanism by instead incorporating blocking points within program expressions. We demonstrate that this novel trajectory semantics accurately represents the blocking trajectory semantics and detail a strategy for reducing GP programs into their equivalent, point-blocking forms. As a result, GP's semantics no longer gives rise to nondeterminism. Key benefits include a significant reduction in the complexity of program semantics analysis, as well as simplified evaluations. A thorough comparison with the standard semantics-cloning technique is also provided. Trajectory semantics allows for the development of new optimization techniques, like inlining, to further enhance GP's efficiency. A supporting implementation is available online at https://github.com/GraphProgramming/GP-trajectory-semantics. Using a generalized kinetic approach, we derive a comprehensive conductive Hall module for various systems, including normal and multi-electron systems, where the latter's conductive Hall module is influenced by the complex combination of individual and pairwise electron velocities. The calculation of the multi-electron velocity in an ordinary metal reveals a significant nonlinear change in velocity in response to a magnetic field at zero charge accumulation, underscoring the importance of the electron-electron interaction in explaining the geometric Hall effect. Conversely, for multi-band materials, the electron velocity in the perturbative regime is primarily determined by the highest energy band, leading to a geometric Hall effect. By extending the kinetic approach to multi-band materials, we verify that the geometric Hall effect holds across different band configurations. Furthermore, we apply the kinetic approach to superconductors and find that the geometric Hall effect does not arise due to the complex relationship between the superconducting gap and the electron velocity. Lastly, the effect of temperature on the geometric Hall effect is investigated, revealing that the effect's magnitude decreases as temperature increases in an ordinary metal. The unique characteristics of the geometric Hall effect in multi-electron, normal, and superconducting systems are distinguished from those in single-electron systems. Notably, while single-electron systems are often subject to Thomas-Fermi approximation, the derived conductive Hall modules for multi-electron systems cannot be reduced to the Thomas-Fermi approximation, underscoring qualitative differences between single-electron and multi-electron systems. Overall, the derived modules indicate that the geometric Hall effect is unlikely to be experimentally detectable due to its relatively low magnitude compared to ordinary Hall effect, except possibly at extremely high magnetic field intensities. As an example of potential experimental detection, we analyze the geometric Hall effect in phosphorus, a material known to be subject to significant spin-orbit coupling, revealing that the effect's magnitude is comparable to its ordinary Hall effect but reversed in terms of charge accumulation. The Zel'dovich--Sunyaev (ZS) solution is a continuous differential equation that describes how the radiation temperature changes as it interacts with hot gas in the universe's vicinity. This paper explores a discretized ZN (Zel'dovich--Sunyaev) algorithm that efficiently solves the ZS equation through a recursive relationship. Unlike conventional numerical methods for ordinary differential equations that look back in time, the ZN algorithm forecasts the radiation temperature at future points, allowing for easy computation of related quantities like the Compton Y-parameter. The ZN algorithm is suitable for various physical conditions, including when the radiation four-momentum vector has a negligible magnitude in relation to the gas's velocity, a scenario commonly applicable to Earth-based observations. This approach's exceptional accuracy for simulating real-world observations on a local scale is shown. The underlying mechanisms of how light is processed and perceived in the retina remain complex and not fully understood. Researchers have been exploring the existence of two distinct light response pathways, one centered on light sources and another reacting to surrounding light, to better comprehend this phenomenon. Studying the European cricket frog's retina, researchers discovered that these organisms' light response can be modeled using a complex interaction of these two pathways, one being excitation and the other being inhibition, with the latter primarily located at the edges of the retina. When stimulated, the central pathway initiates a light response faster than the surrounding pathway, while the latter slows it down with increased intensity, leading to the dark adaptation of the retina. By combining and regulating these pathways, the human visual experience can be accurately replicated using a computer model that mimics the response of frog photoreceptors, suggesting a similar dual light processing system in humans and other mammals. This discovery could lead to a better understanding of how retinal disorders and visual defects interact with light intensity. The interplay of these light response pathways may also reveal insights into the accuracy of digital simulations of eye movements and vision processing. The unit commitment problem's operational constraint analysis is crucial but computationally expensive. This challenge is addressed through the application of machine learning models, specifically an ensemble of learned reduction methods. By leveraging these models, the screening time is dramatically minimized, enabling a separate, more time-efficient verification process for detailed models. Trail data derived from detailed models is utilized to train the machine learning models, enhancing their accuracy and robustness. Implementation of these models on actual power grid systems significantly reduces solution times for various detailed models. For both modified security problems and comprehensive pre-dispatch problems, the machine learning models yield a 2.6-fold performance improvement, paving the way for their broader adoption in the energy sector. Furthermore, the ensemble of machine learning models exhibits enhanced robustness, illustrating the benefits of combining models trained on detailed models. This research demonstrates the significant potential of machine learning models, not only in streamlining the process but also enabling the development of accurate and robust models. As a result, the machine learning models yield a 1.3% error relative to detailed models, whereas prior methods exhibit errors of 16.7% and 33.7%. Evaluation of the models reveals that the level of accuracy depends on the type of detailed model used during training. By leveraging this knowledge, the machine learning models can be applied to a diverse array of detailed models, producing high-quality unit commitment solutions. Importantly, the models do not learn critical information, such as power system topology, thereby ensuring security and privacy. Example cases illustrating the effectiveness of the machine learning models on actual power grid systems are presented in Appendix D of the publication. The Synthetic Control Method, widely employed for program evaluation, relies on a weighted average of pre-intervention time series from a treated entity's past. Typically, estimating these weights necessitates access to the treated entity's pre-intervention data. However, this is often unfeasible due to data restrictions, leading some to utilize "black box" methods such as principal component analysis. This paper addresses this challenge by developing an adaptive procedure using multiple unsupervised learning methods from the field of matrix factorization to create synthetic control units from a model's self-learning capabilities. Key innovations include an adaptive selection of relevant control units, a novel weighted average process using a temporal kernel weighted by past performance, and a novel cross-validation procedure leveraging ensemble forecasting. Synthetic control estimators are assembled by combining the weighted averages of multiple unsupervised methods with additional human input. A simulation study demonstrates that these new estimators outperform "black box" methods like principal component analysis in building Synthetic Control weights. Moreover, they possess additional benefits, such as the ability to incorporate subject-matter knowledge and use control units with missing data, as well as produce a variety of candidate estimates with corresponding confidence intervals. The Synthetic Control Model's implementation also accommodates treatment periods in addition to pre-intervention periods. A practical demonstration of these new methods is provided using pre-intervention data from 15 Swiss cities to create a Synthetic Control weight for Munich, with additional resources made accessible online. Finally, this paper empirically compares these new estimates with traditional PCA on real-world cases, highlighting their relative performance. The new method's code has been made available at the address https://github.com/Ernest-DataSCI/synthetic-control-unsupervised-learning. In many graph-based applications such as link prediction, authors address a key challenge of preserving privacy while learning on graphs that contain sensitive information. To achieve this, the method incorporates local differential privacy using the optimally perturbed sketch algorithm. This algorithm first applies noise to the graph in an 'upstream' step that is optimised for minimal loss of predictive accuracy, before the noisy graph is observed by the learner. This approach distinguishes itself from traditional differential privacy mechanisms which add noise after observation, with resulting loss in accuracy. When combined with a downstream machine learning model, the method utilises the noisy counts from the upstream step as input. Notably, the method allows the creation of models that simultaneously meet both upstream and downstream privacy and accuracy requirements. By analysing the trade-offs, the method incorporates a tunable hyperparameter that balances the level of upstream perturbation and the resulting downstream accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the method's ability to yield models that predict well with link data while maintaining robust upstream perturbation. This research further shows the method's potential for use on more complex problems such as heterophilious graph, and outlines open questions including the development of downstream privacy mechanisms. The relationship between the renormalization constants for the scalar densities created from the tensor product of two fermion fields and the anomalous dimensions in QCD is still a topic of debate in the literature. However, using an analytical approach based on the method of differential recurrence, it can be demonstrated that this relationship holds exactly in accordance with the standard QCD evolution equation. This level of accuracy is only achievable if the renormalization constants for the $F \widetilde{F}$ and $F^3$ operators are equal to the anomalous dimensions, and both are associated with the same beta function, specifically $\beta(\alpha_s) = b\alpha_s -...$. Consequently, this implies that the relationship between the anomalous dimensions and the renormalization constants for the $F \widetilde{F}$ and $F^3$ operators is governed by the standard product rule, thereby validating a recent theoretical prediction. Furthermore, this analysis also reveals that using an approach based on the method of differential recurrence is equivalent to combining mass subtraction schemes, and both approaches are mutually consistent. This is also reflected in the MRST '93 NNLO parton distribution functions, where the evolution of the renormalization constants is consistent with our findings, and in the QCD evolution equation, which holds up to order $(\alpha_s)^3$. However, our analysis deviates from the QCD evolution equation at order $(\alpha_s)^4$, where the relationship between the renormalization constants and the anomalous dimensions begins to exhibit discrepancies. This level of divergence is only resolved when higher-order corrections are accounted for, which includes corrections from color-enhanced loop diagrams, specifically the six-loop corrections. This analysis also underscores the significance of the standard renormalization group equation and the equality between the renormalization constants and the anomalous dimensions, which may have far-reaching implications for various problems under investigation. For instance, this analysis also exposes inconsistencies in an approach to higher-order QCD calculations by Caprini, Nesterenko, and Robbesyan, which may have unintended consequences for our understanding of nucleon structure and function. To summarize, our analysis offers an analytically sound method for mass subtraction in QCD evolution equations, which is designed to facilitate widespread use, and provides a clear framework for resolving long-standing debates in the field. Existing colorization techniques often struggle with recognizing and preserving fine-grained object classifications and spatial information. This paper proposes an innovative method that integrates optical flow techniques to facilitate colorization, allowing source images and target images to be correlated through frame differences. When the classification label of a target image matches the source image's classification label, the optical flow field is utilized to align the two domains, and our method estimates the correspondence between pixel positions in the two domains. This enables our method to perform colorization while preserving the target image's texture and the source image's explicit features. Evaluation of our method reveals significant improvements in preserving the target image's texture and the source image's explicit features compared to existing colorization techniques. Additionally, our method's ability to leverage pre-trained semantic segmentation models allows it to match the performance of state-of-the-art semantic segmentation techniques. Code and model implementations can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Lee-lene/FlowColorizationNet. Our method's efficacy is demonstrated through qualitative and quantitative assessments in multiple colorization datasets as well as real-world applications in self-driving cars. The research shows that even small changes in a system current operator through a defect can significantly alter its non-invertible nature, thereby allowing for the creation of defects with lower topological complexity. We investigate how to utilize the classification uncertainty provided by the Bayesian Neural Network in making decisions that reduce gravitational-wave detection time. By leveraging the predicted probability distribution, which considers both the likelihood of data and potential measurement errors, we identify various decision criteria for determining optimal event analysis methods. Evaluation of these methods on known data from the LIGO-Virgo Observatories reveals they are capable of decreasing detection times by approximately 10-20%. The optimal strategy depends on varying levels of data quality but generally involves combining most or all of the available methods unless there is a high confidence in the detection or significant systematic uncertainty involved. In the latter case, more aggressive candidate trimming is recommended. Current implementations face technical limitations due to varying data amounts among events, making it necessary to refine the processing of data across events. Moreover, integrating the proposed method fully demands an enhanced evaluation to gauge its impact on detection rates. To facilitate widespread adoption, we strongly advise utilizing a global optimal selection threshold derived from considering all available information, including potential measurement errors. Lastly, we found that employing a Bayesian Neural Network directly for event analysis is not as effective as using it to make a preliminary classification, after which the most promising candidates can be selected using other analysis methods. However, it is crucial to further refine the network's training to achieve better results before utilizing it directly. In recent years, the vehicle routing problem with multiple dimensions has received significant research attention due to its practical applications and associated challenging optimization tasks. This paper focuses on the two-dimensional vehicle routing problem with multiple constraints, specifically the stochastic undirected single-capacity multi-vehicle problem (SUKP) and the binary multi-vehicle problem (BMCP). To efficiently solve these related problems, we employ a dual algorithm to yield high-quality solutions for single-capacity instances that are comparable to their binary counterparts. Furthermore, to improve computational efficiency, we develop an enhanced local search engine (E2LS) with two distinct iterations, including edge and path modifications. This algorithm is thoroughly evaluated through experiments with various randomly generated instances of different sizes, under two different settings: deterministic and stochastic. To stimulate future research, we also provide high-quality solution samples of SUCP and BMCP with differing capacity levels. These sample solutions can serve as benchmarks for similar optimization problems with multiple dimensions. Churn prevention has emerged as a critical concern for the retail sector, prompting the use of machine learning models to forecast and predict customer behavior. The practical application of machine learning models for churn prevention involves using a time-series analysis of customer data to estimate future behavior and identify high-risk customers before they discontinue service. This research delves into the relationship between the length of customer history used for training and the quality of predictions generated by machine learning models. To investigate this, a dataset of 2 million customers from a real retail environment was used, spanning a period of 2 years with daily data points. The results from 22 neural networks, including multi-layer perceptrers, recurrent neural networks, and long short-term memory models, reveal a significant negative correlation between history and prediction quality, as well as substantial variability in model performance with regards to history. The paper also examines the relative importance of recent customer data, finding that models trained using full customer history significantly overestimate recurrence compared to models trained using limited recent data. To address these issues and improve prediction quality, the concept of recentization is introduced, aiming to incorporate both recent and full customer history into models for churn prevention through weighted calculation. The results demonstrate the efficacy of recentization in enhancing prediction quality, increasing model confidence, and reducing overestimation, as evidenced by cases with multi-year and recent-only customer history. The proposed recentization approach subsequently yields significant improvements in model performance, both in terms of loss and AUC metrics, across multiple neural network models with varying architectures. The paper showcases recentization's effectiveness using a multi-layer perceptron, recurrent neural network, and long short-term memory model on real-world data, achieving 0.855 AUC without recentization and 0.860 without recentization. Recentization's potential and applicability are discussed in the retail industry, as well as suggestions for future research directions. The code and dataset used for this research have been made publicly available at a specified repository, enabling other researchers to access the data and replicate the experiments. The dataset contains artificial cases with both recent and full customer history to facilitate future research. The repository's address is provided below: https://github.com/aman7314 recentization. Ising Field Theory is an effective 2-dimensional quantum field theory used to describe systems near Ising critical points and is known for being integrable. We intentionally disrupt this integrability by incorporating an irrelevant operator $L_{-4} \bar L_{-4} \eta$, and we are manually calculating the associated self-energy in terms of energy-momentum tensor's two-point correlation function. In heavy-ion collisions, the joint electromagnetic and strong interactions influence charged-particle dispersal equally, primarily due to homogeneity in electric and magnetic potentials across space. However, when collisions involve ions with non-zero total charge, an additional potential creates uneven distributions of electrons and positrons. Although this effect is typically negligible for collisions between light nuclei due to the negligible mass of electrons, it may become significant for collisions involving heavy ions. Since the creation of electron-positron pairs is typically a rare occurrence, the uneven electron distribution typically doesn't impact the production of charged particles. Nevertheless, in collisions where the charge of the participating ions is considerable and the density of produced charged particles is high enough (such as at high energies), the uneven electron distribution can impact positron production, resulting in discrepancies between expected and actual production rates. In this response, calculations are provided to estimate these discrepancies and collision factors that could lead to notable effects. Cycle tracking technology holds great potential for enhancing cycling safety due to the dense distribution of users in urban areas. By analyzing collective cycling patterns, we can pinpoint high-risk zones where accidents are more likely to occur. Our method for generating a cycling danger map relies on a random forest model to predict event likelihood based on geographical location. This map serves as an invaluable resource for municipal officials and transportation specialists, enabling them to identify areas where supplemental safety measures are most urgently required. In our case study, we demonstrate that this cycle risk map surpasses a more traditional approach based on population density. Furthermore, we also explore the effect of data compression using the Principal Component Analysis method from the statistical field. Our results show that the quality of the danger map is maintained even when data is reduced to 10% of its original size, indicating that the risk map concept is highly robust. Ultimately, this research highlights the immense potential of cycle tracking data to improve pedestrian and cyclist safety on a large scale. To facilitate the adoption of this technology, we have developed a web-based visualization tool that facilitates the comparison between population and cycle risk maps in real-time. This tool, which is accessible via any web browser, can be tailored to meet the needs of geographic regions of varying scales, from a neighborhood to an entire city. The tool's open-source code is available for immediate use. This research aims to unlock the full potential of intelligent transportation systems, minimize traffic hazards, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions by leveraging the unique insights offered by modern navigation and cycle tracking technology. Additionally, we have conducted a discussion with experts in public health and transportation on the practical implications of this research, yielding valuable feedback that has prompted further development. This paper presents a path planning method tailored for robust robotic navigation, capable of incorporating various model uncertainties. Several studies have been conducted to generate collision-free paths, but the influence of uncertainty in robotic models has been largely overlooked. In order to robustly establish a robotic motion strategy, we propose a method that formulates a constrained optimization problem in the framework of a moving frame of reference on the robotic arm itself. Using the concept of differential motion planning, the trajectory of the robot is optimized while considering uncertainty factors, taking into account the necessity of correcting the robotic arm's position. Several case studies have been conducted to validate the efficiency of the proposed algorithm, demonstrating its ability to robustly plan the path of robotic arms with various types of actuators. Furthermore, we have analyzed and compared the performance of the proposed method against traditional planning techniques that do not account for uncertainty, demonstrating the immense benefits of utilizing robust planning methods to robustly control multi-link robotic arms. The proposed algorithm was implemented using the OpenRobotics Toolkit, allowing it to be easily integrated into Gazebo simulations and real-world ROS applications. The associated code can be accessed at: https://github.com/JCFlora/Robotic_Motion_Planning/tree/main/uncertainty_nlp. We explore the behavior of nonlinear diffusion equations derived from entropic regularization of conservation laws, specifically with nonlocal convolution kernels. The nonequilibrium entropy dynamics displays two distinct behaviors, characterized by the kernel's convexity and the nature of its convexity at its origin. For kernels with convex origins, the solutions' profiles converge exponentially to entropy-admissible solutions. Conversely, if the origin convexity is absent, the solution's dynamics undergoes a phase transition, during which its gradient increases without bound. The nonequilibrium entropy dynamics then converges to a steady state, which differs from the entropy-admissible solution in this scenario. The nonequilibrium profiles and the associated dissipative structures are further analyzed. The study highlights fundamental differences between locally convex kernels and nonlocal ones, and it emphasizes the need to reconsider established notions of entropy-admissible solutions in the context of nonlocal kernels. The numerical approximation of the nonlinear diffusion equation is investigated using an upwind method, and we demonstrate that the rate of convergence depends on the spatial discretization. The work concludes with a brief discussion on the generalization of the nonequilibrium entropy dynamics to multidimensional space. The study provides a framework for extending well-established concepts of entropy-admissible solutions to nonlocal frameworks, and it paves the way for the exploration of fundamental aspects of nonequilibrium dynamics. The work is supplemented by computational results illustrating the behavior of nonlinear diffusion equations derived from nonlocal kernels in one- and two-dimensional spaces. The paper may be considered a foundational work in the field, and it raises crucial questions and hypotheses that require future investigation. We consider a hyperbolic surface \textit{F} within the unit disk, defined as a quotient of the Poincaré disk under a lattice of isometric transformations, to study its hyperbolic closed geodesics. Given that the surface meets a specific requirement, which ensures that the boundary of a particular region does not coincide with itself, we derive two key results: Firstly, the direction of all the hyperbolic closed geodesics, regardless of their period, collectively form all possible directions around the unit circle with the sole exception of a singular direction determined by a certain unique feature. Furthermore, the total length of the hyperbolic closed geodesics, when categorized based on their periods, exhibits a tendency towards an infinite summation, which indicates a diverging value. In a contrasting scenario, when the surface meets an alternate requirement, which necessitates that the boundary of a particular region overlaps with itself, we establish the existence of a non-empty set of directions, corresponding to the hyperbolic closed geodesics, which does not contribute towards the total length, using techniques from Teichmüller space, resulting in a converging hyperbolic closed geodesics total length, when paired with a lower bound. Consequently, this allows us to differentiate between two types of hyperbolic surfaces, which share certain similarities, by identifying the distinct characteristics, which include direction density and length convergence, respectively, to distinguish them as an arithmetic hyperbolic surface or otherwise. Additionally, we present an alternate characterization of arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces by identifying key features, including unique features, periods, and lengths, that contribute towards the total length, which diverges, while ruling out other contributing factors, including the lambda direction, Lyapunov exponents, and Schottky groups. This research introduces a network analytics framework known as NeuroCORE, which leverages total correlation for analyzing complex systems in neuroscience applications. By applying this method to functional MRI data, it identifies connectivity patterns within brain functions and reveals distinct network structures. These structures can either enhance our understanding of neuroscientific processes or serve as diagnostic indicators for brain disorders and damages. Utilizing a dataset with traumatic brain injury, the study reveals underlying network alterations. Moreover, the research demonstrates the potential therapeutic effects of parametric modulation on total correlation networks. Interestingly, the proposed approach also shows promise in revealing the functional links associated with visual stimulation. Our analysis points out limitations of current network analytics, while validating the accuracy and practicality of the proposed method. The article provides a comprehensive review of core network analytics techniques, highlighting their advantages and disadvantages. It further discusses the significant contributions of each method, along with potential applications, and outlines various tools and datasets that our community can leverage for further research. We explore the relationship between Gaussian process (GP) posteriors and the empirical process, a more efficiently sampleable form, through a process of conditioning. To achieve this efficiently, we rely on a data-driven technique to approximate the GP conditional mean, both for the purpose of improved posterior sampling and to facilitate the propagation of uncertainties in forward simulations. By leveraging these approximations, we develop a high-order quasi-Monte Carlo method for computing GP-based surrogates and uncertainties. Our approach effectively counteracts pathwise variance inflation while taking advantage of GP antithetic variates, resulting in enhanced convergence rates. Furthermore, we also investigate the effectiveness of this method in the context of targeted Expectation of Maximization algorithms, finding that it reduces computational expenses associated with probabilistic inference in models involving GP observations. Our approach is applied to two complex real-world problems, the prediction of GP-based hydrology and the uncertainty quantification of a NACA 0012 airfoil, with promising results in terms of both convergence rates and computational efficiency. Our research, along with additional tools and resources, can be accessed at https://github.com/jmjames/gp-pathwise. Our study demonstrates that pathwise conditioning, when efficiently sampled, can effectively support a broad range of applications involving GP algorithms. Our approach provides an innovative general-purpose sampling technique for GP posteriors, applicable to a wide range of modeling challenges, which in turn facilitates uncertainty propagation at significantly reduced computational costs. Our technique enables high-performance computing for uncertainty quantification, allowing the field to leverage more computationally efficient GP methods while maintaining computational efficiency at the inference stage. Our approach essentially transforms the problem of efficiently sampling GP posteriors and inducing uncertainties into a combinatorial problem, which can be efficiently addressed through data-driven techniques, along with analytical and numerical transformations. Our technique effectively reduces variance in GP-based QMC methods by leveraging pathwise conditioning, along with antithetic variates, to achieve enhanced convergence rates. Our approach effectively addresses several significant issues in GP-based uncertainty quantification, including pathwise variance inflation and the efficient propagation of uncertainties. Our technique effectively supports the induction of uncertainties in GP-based surrogates and uncertainty quantification, along with GP-based inference, by addressing the problem of efficiently sampling GP posteriors and avoiding pathwise variance inflation. This research explores the deployment of massive Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) as flying base stations to provide continuous connectivity to a widespread network of ground sensors on the Earth's surface. Due to UAVs' highly dynamic movement, predicting the received signal power between a UAV and a ground sensor is complex. To address this challenge, our study proposes an innovative probabilistic approach based on the Two-Ray model for a UAV-ground sensor link. This model takes into account both direct and reflected signal paths, considering that ground sensors are scattered randomly. By utilizing the Two-Ray model's probability density function, our method effectively caters to various locations, heights, and densities of ground sensors. For practical implementation, our approach is evaluated in two scenarios: first, without accounting for UAV movement, where signal power is treated as a random variable; second, with full consideration of UAV trajectory data, where signal power is treated as a constant. This study assesses the performance of our probabilistic approach using absolute and relative error metrics. To demonstrate its efficiency, the proposed method is validated with actual flight data of a UAV moving at various altitudes across a field. By utilizing real flight paths, our study determines that our probability density function's error in predicting received signal power is less sensitive to UAV height. This reveals that deploying a UAV at higher altitudes offers improved connectivity to a wider range of ground sensors, as indicated by the relative error's decrease. The Large Underground Neutrino Detector (DUNE) is designed to be a sophisticated experiment that not only studies neutrinos but also has the capability to detect rare signals such as the proton decay at a distant point, due to its thick liquid-argon target. The primary purpose of this study is to assess the potential of DUNE far-detector in detecting the proton decay within the context of various models like the Grand Unified Theories, taking into account the current constraints on the decay time based on the Megascopica experiment. The outcomes show that DUNE has a unique opportunity to discover evidence for the Grand Unified Theories, given a proton lifetime of at least 10 seconds, at 90% confidence level. The results also demonstrate that DUNE can differentiate between these models, based on differences in their predicted proton decay lifetimes. Consequently, the outcome highlights DUNE as a versatile experiment that goes beyond its neutrino research, enabling the investigation of fundamental aspects of the Standard Model of Particle Physics. The study also emphasizes the broader physics landscape within which the Deep Underground Neutrino Detector operates. One technique for interpreting decision trees called SHAP enables the quantification and visualization of feature importance within an interpretable framework, which can then be utilized to measure performance across diverse datasets. In this research, a comprehensive analysis of the ShapTree data generation framework was undertaken. A novel method for generating ShapTree data specifically tailored for regression tasks was introduced. Additionally, a detailed examination of the ShapTree architecture was conducted, including the development of a new inference technique and the refinement of ShapTree learning methods. The results further introduced novel metrics for evaluating feature importance and provided insights into the ShapTree data generation process through both theoretical and experimental analysis. Lastly, a comparison was made between the proposed ShapTree approach and the partial dependence plot to highlight ShapTree's advantages. The findings were further demonstrated through the public deployment of the ShapTree data on the Kaggle ShapTree competition platform. A widely used technique for estimating policy gradients in reinforcement learning may have limitations due to underperforming exploration. Building upon this idea, a new approach called variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) has been developed to enhance policy gradient estimation and improve the convergence rate of related algorithms. By utilizing a novel replay strategy, VRER enables the creation of a fictional transition model via statistical inference and is capable of being incorporated into existing algorithms without requiring further modifications. When integrated with a maximum entropy policy gradient algorithm, VRER yields an optimized variant that achieves better convergence rates and provides more flexible options for exploring policies. Through theoretical analysis and simulation experiments, the efficacy of VRER has been demonstrated in various scenarios, showcasing its potential to improve the performance and efficiency of reinforcement learning algorithms. Furthermore, VRER may have far-reaching implications, such as enhancing the performance of exponential family policy gradient methods and contributing to the development of scalable reinforcement learning frameworks. As a future research direction, the application of VRER in reinforcement learning settings, including Markov decision processes, Markov chains, and semi-Markov processes, presents an avenue for further investigation. When tailored to specific applications, VRER may leverage its replay and variance reduction capabilities to yield improved convergence rates and scalability. By leveraging these techniques, VRER may achieve better results when applied to real-world reinforcement learning problems. The simulated results show that the VRER method has better convergence properties compared to traditional techniques, providing a solid foundation for its application in reinforcement learning settings. The optimal parameters obtained via simulation experiments provide useful guidelines for selecting suitable settings for the VRER method. As an example of its practical applications, the VRER method has been used to optimize commodity pricing, yielding a maximum surplus of 131.05, in comparison to a baseline value of 118.64, thus verifying its efficacy and applicability. The incorporation of the VRER method may also enhance the performance of exponential family policy gradient methods, providing valuable insights for their optimization. The optimality gap of the maximum entropy policy gradient algorithm utilising the VRER method shows an exponential relationship with the experience requirements, in contrast to a polynomial relationship for existing algorithms, thus illustrating its potential to yield scalable reinforcement learning frameworks. We introduce the Detail Context Block (DCB) to enhance the capture of detailed contexts in Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs). Our self-attention based DCB module facilitates the capture of detailed patterns and relationships beyond the limitations of grid-based constraints. The results demonstrate that DCB significantly enhances the predictive capabilities of ODEs on a range of spatiotemporal learning tasks, by the effective capture of detailed contexts facilitated by the use of a learned mask in the DCB module. We also propose a simple yet robust method for automatically selecting the most suitable mask for the DCB, by leveraging the predictive performance on a validation set as the objective. The code for the DCB has been made available at https://github.com/Pol Evan/Detailed-Context-Block. Our experiments show the DCB's superiority over the multi-scale context block on various benchmarks for spatiotemporal learning, and its efficiency in terms of computational cost. A type system ensures memory safety in programs written in imperative languages by verifying the types of expressions and statements and preventing type-related errors. By using memory locations as data types, it can also manage memory safely. However, when memory is not treated as a separate entity, the type system's full potential is not realized. In order to fully leverage the memory safety features, programmers must manually coordinate the life span of memory locations. This research proposes a novel, curried memory management system to safely use dynamic memory in languages like ML, enabling the type system to verify the correctness of memory dealings and eliminating the risk of memory leaks, incorrect free operations, and double frees. The design relies on a custom memory data type that enforces specific type class constraints, thus guaranteeing the correct usage of memory. The type system of ML can accurately verify the correctness of memory dealings and automatically prevent the most common memory safety errors, also supporting various memory management strategies. The implementation of the system only requires minimal extensions to existing compilers like Cminor and UMC, and we verified that the generated code can be safely compiled to C. The type system's efficacy was further demonstrated by converting common memory management errors into errors caught by the system. The development of the system can serve as an evaluation of advanced programming concepts, like curried memory management, to ensure memory safety in programming languages. A heavy neutral lepton, forming part of the standard model, can contribute to neutrino oscillation data through four-fermion interactions. These interactions can also indicate lepton number violation, which has significant implications for various processes such as $\mu \to e \gamma$, and can play a role in the decay of supersymmetric particles that produce neutralinos. We examine the production of neutralinos at a linear $e^+ e^-$ collider in a scenario of lepton number violation, focusing on final states involving single $W$ bosons and charged leptons. Our analysis shows that differential crossings provide crucial insight into identifying heavy neutral leptons, a finding with important consequences for supersymmetric searches. A major outcome of our study is the establishment of optimal search regions for $\mu \to e \gamma$ decay, tailored for the International Linear Collider. These search regions are highly sensitive to heavy neutral leptons, a consideration particularly essential for the ILC given beam polarisation, which is not the case for other experiments. We have also investigated the optimal mass split between neutralinos that would make their detection possible, a finding with important implications for the high-luminosity ShuShu phase II programme. Our analysis shows that heavy neutral leptons, with masses up to 40 GeV, can be detected at the ShuShu collider, which is essential for completing the theoretical landscape of lepton number violation and demonstrating the capabilities of the HL-LHC and ILC in this sector. We have also examined the potential of other searches such as $R_{\mu \tau}$ and $\mu \to e$E for identifying heavy neutral leptons, which may offer more sensitive lepton flavor violation searches with the development of MUSUBIX for the LHC. We intend to extend our analysis to include other final states and study the HL-LLC phase III period. We intend to present the results at the ILUC 2022 conference. The broader scientific community has been growing interested in DrizzlePacked, a combined image formation technique that encompasses both linear and non-linear processes. To address this, a critical assessment is provided of both linear and non-linear algorithms used in the drizzled images, focusing on their respective outcomes. It is observed that non-linear combinations like median and a clipped-mean do not maintain a consistent image profile for stars across all pixel values. In contrast, the profile is only preserved for intermediate pixel values. Furthermore, it is suggested that the image distortion caused by the non-linear combinations is a result of biased sampling of the point spread function. In addition, a quantitative framework for evaluating image information is presented, enabling a comparison of the information retained by the median and Voronoi binned algorithms. It is found that the Voronoi binned algorithm generally retains more information than the median algorithm but is also more susceptible to stars with low signal-to-noise ratios. Key findings are subsequently used to inform the development of optimal image combination algorithms for the next generation of wide-field infraspace telescopes. It is argued that the optimal combination algorithm is one that maintains a consistent image profile for stars across all pixel values. We propose the median algorithm with additional high and low pixel value corrections to achieve this. Notably, this corrected median algorithm performs similarly to the Voronoi binned algorithm in terms of information retention but avoids the limitations associated with low signal-to-noise ratio stars. Importantly, the corrections required by the corrected median algorithm are independent of the specific image reduction pipeline used, unlike the Voronoi binned algorithm. In addition to informational comparisons, the corrected median algorithm is also found to effectively handle halo suppression, showing comparable results to the Voronoi binned algorithm. Therefore, the proposed corrected median algorithm is recommended for use in future large infraspace telescope projects. Ultimately, the scientific implications of using various image combination algorithms on the final astrophysical results are an area for potential exploration in future research. It is noted that the decision to use a combination algorithm that maintains a consistent image profile for stars may minimize the potential for scientific impacts. In contrast, the use of biased image combination algorithms may result in similar astrophysical outcomes, but one that is dependent on specific signal-to-noise ratio thresholds. As a final point, the next generation of wide-field astronomical facilities may also benefit from the development of more sophisticated and optimized image combination algorithms and techniques. This integration, based on the Wilkins model, simplifies the failure process to a critical threshold problem along a predetermined fracture path. To address the tendency for stress accumulations to concentrate at the notch tip, an unstable instability mechanism 'flattens' the notch tip in two stages: an initial stage that is linearly related to the notch's initial sharpness and a subsequent stage that is exponentially related. This mechanistic understanding and resulting nonlinear transformation of notch sharpness offers a general solution for addressing initial stress concentrations, thus providing an alternative to more traditional failure predictions based on Linear Fracture Mechanics. To demonstrate its applicability, we've employed the failure transformation to expand the Linear Fracture Energy release rate 'parabola' into a new 'notepad'. Notably, the resulting failure predictions at the notch tip exhibit a greater level of consistency with observed fracture patterns when compared to Linear Fracture predictions, thereby facilitating the evaluation of the influence of 'notch' shape and material 'notch sensitivity' on material 'toughness'. Ultimately, the failure transformations and resulting 'notepad' failure predictions can easily integrate the effects of critical thresholds beyond fracture stress, such as grain size in metals, to expand the failure theory boundaries. This approach effectively unifies fracture failure predictions across a broad spectrum of materials systems. To facilitate the widespread adoption of failure predictions based on the Linear Fracture and Phase-Field fracture laws, we've developed the failure transformation to a 'notchpad' app, thereby making the new predictive framework accessible through an intuitive user interface. As a result, we derive local estimates for the solution's derivatives, showing that the maximum norm of the solution's derivatives is controlled by the maximum norm of the initial data, within a specific spatial and temporal context. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a continuous dependence relationship between the solution and initial data, measured in the maximum norm. This method can also be applied to the incompressible Smith-type transport equation, a simplified model derived from the Navier-Stokes equations, to obtain similar results. Unlike classical estimates that rely on global properties, our findings imply that the sum of local errors vanishes as the time step is refined. Consequently, we can significantly decrease the number of time steps required to achieve a specified accuracy without affecting the overall computational complexity, a property we refer to as local $\mathcal{F}$-coarse-grinding. Additionally, we extend this approach to higher-dimensional systems and include simulations from related research. These simulations demonstrate the applicability of our theoretical framework and showcase the computational benefits of our novel method. This study further sheds light on the well-posedness of the Navier-Stokes equations by providing explicit, local regularity estimates for the solution. This approach can be applied to the incompressible Smith-type transport equation, a simplified model derived from the Navier-Stokes equations, to obtain similar results. This method is reminiscent of the classical method proposed by Kreiss in the 1950s but has the additional benefit of allowing the number of time steps to be reduced without affecting the overall computational complexity. A prominent blockchain application is providing integrity and trust for cyber physical systems such as supply chains. The integrity and trust come from the consensus protocol, specifically consensus algorithms like PBFT. Past research, such as LC4IoT, has developed a lightweight consensus protocol suitable for constrained devices in the IoT. The consensus algorithm relies on a tree structure, where the generation of the tree is random, and the lightfoot node is chosen, resulting in a more centralised yet efficient consensus protocol. The tree structure, however, introduces centralization, overhang, and potential crashes. This research proposes an improved consensus protocol, LC4IoT+, to address the drawbacks of LC4IoT. The new protocol starts by creating a d-dimensional grid instead of a tree, where each device is assigned a grid node based on its unique ID. The protocol then defines and applies the centralisation, overhang and crash metrics to the grid nodes, leading to a more resilient consensus protocol with fewer crashes, less overhang and a more dynamic consensus tree substitution. The improved protocol, LC4IoT+, achieves higher uptime, higher throughput, higher packet delivery ratio, lower energy consumption, higher average user bits, higher average user bits in LC4IoT+ compared to LC4IoT. The improved protocol, LC4IoT+, also maintains the same average depth during the user data transmission process, thus enabling higher average user bits for parallel user data transmission. The protocol, LC4IoT+, preserves the key properties of the parent tree structure in LC4IoT in terms of reduced energy consumption, parallel user data transmission and scalability, and it overcomes the main drawbacks of LC4IoT, namely centralisation, overhang and crash susceptibility in a dynamic environment, thereby making LC4IoT+ more suitable for IoT applications requiring parallel user data transmission in a dynamic consensus tree structure with low cost. The protocol, LC4IoT+, shows how the improved user bits transmission in the improved grid structure affects the overall performance of LC4IoT+. The results of the prototype implementation demonstrate that LC4IoT+ outperforms LC4IoT in terms of higher uptime, more packet delivery ratio, less energy consumption, and less crash rate. The comparison between LC4IoT+ and other consensus algorithms, such as RAND PA and LSP, in terms of overhead shows that LC4IoT+ achieves the lowest crash rate, lower energy consumption, lower overhead and more packet delivery ratio, thus making it the best consensus protocol among the ones considered. As a fundamental unit of life, cells are vital to understanding and discovering basic biological processes and functions, which is why designing and synthesizing cell shapes could help bridge the gaps in current biomedical image analysis knowledge. By producing an enormous library of synthetic cells, deep generative models can enhance the accuracy and reliability of image analysis tasks, such as cell tracking and segmentation. In the context of granulosa cells, researchers have obtained over 10,000 real cell images from public databases and used them to train an U-Net-based autoencoder, converting it into a generative model by combining the encoder with a Gaussian noise vector. With sufficient training, this model successfully synthesizes 1,000 new cells, exhibiting significant similarity in shape and size to the original cells. Additionally, combining multiple synthesized cells through layering increases the accuracy of segmentation results for a cytoflow image analysis task compared to the use of a single real cell. However, cell tracking precision using synthesized cells is not consistently improved and is sometimes equivalent to, or even inferior to, using real cells due to limitations arising from the limited duration of cell tracking. Consequently, it is essential to leverage the synthesized cells primarily for the segmentation of cell shapes at a given time point, and for tasks requiring cell tracking over extended periods of time, it may be more beneficial to utilize the synthesized cells as a source of diverse cell motion phantom data. Furthermore, considering the significant synthesis capacity of deep generative models, it is recommended that at least 1,000 or more synthetic cells be utilized for optimal analysis outcomes. Researchers created a theoretical framework for examining the swimming mechanics of a centipede-like swimmer by accounting for both fluid-driven drag and the force generated by accelerating limbs as they pull water towards their origin. By modeling this complex motion through geometric constraints and the energy function, scientists could demonstrate that this multi-scale approach's outcomes could outperform an model that uses inertia for achieving optimal velocities, potentially even matching or surpassing the performance of highly efficient swimmers like the undulating eel. To verify these results, researchers numerically solved the system's dynamics and found that its non-linear, phase-locked behavior closely aligns with the theoretical predictions for high swimming speeds. Conventional methods of fitting elastic scattering data are hampered by limitations in their analytical models. For instance, the Sarrao-Love atomic form factor doesn't account for non-drude behavior observed at lower energy, whereas the sum-rules method is only applicable for high energy, above the resonance region. Our work presents a new function that effectively combines the love and sum-rules approaches, making it suitable across various energy ranges. This new function also enables an accurate description of non-drude behavior at lower energy, allowing for a separation of intra and inter atomic contributions. By employing this new function in fits of various measurements, we're able to determine relatively tight constraints on the density of charge excitations in gold, including their density near the Fermi level. These results are compared with density functional theory predictions and theoretical models of the dipole oscillations of a metal body. Moreover, we're able to identify a significant short-range peak in the density of charge excitation, which isn't anticipated by established many-body theories. Our work on the dipole strength function reveals increased strength on the low energy side of the $J^{tot}=2$ resonance, which could be related to the observed heavy quasiparticle peak and the density of states near the Fermi level. This low energy enhancement of the strength is also visible in the comparison of the calculated $\frac{D_2.sparkling}{E_f}$ with PE spectroscopy data on copper. To further validate the love and sum-rubers based method, we applied it for calculating longitudinal dielectric function and compare it with PE spectroscopy, we got almost similar results in both methods. In summary, we're able to introduce a new function which is capable of describing scattering data and spectroscopy across various energy ranges, offering a highly accurate description of the density of charge excitations in gold, identifying a significant short-range peak and compared with theoretical models and simulations. The new function also enables comparison with spectroscopy techniques like PE spectroscopy, allowing for a good agreement with experimental observations. This method can be further applied for calculating longitudinal dielectric function and compare it with PE spectroscopy, offering a good agreement with experimental observations. Functional connectivity networks (FCNs) generated through correlation analysis are widely utilized for distinguishing individuals and detecting group differences. Nevertheless, recent research indicates that inter-site signal effects, comprising shared signal phases across brain regions, can significantly impact the accuracy of these assessments. This study aims to evaluate how inter-site effects influence FCN similarity metrics and render them less reliable for distinguishing individuals and group differences. We introduce a novel approach for evaluating inter-site effects by treating FCNs as representations of random vector fields. We then apply this method to a large dataset comprising 1,148 participants from the Human Connectome Project, finding extensive evidence of inter-site effects in resting-state brain networks. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that measures incorporating inter-site effects are less reliable for distinguishing individuals and group differences compared to those that do not account for inter-site effects. Lastly, our findings suggest that a substantial portion of inter-regional inter-site effects is attributable to shared signal variations resulting from vascular factors, as evidenced by a significant correlation between inter-site effects and blood oxygen level-dependent signals derived from conduction delays. This study emphasizes the importance of considering inter-site effects in neuroimaging research focusing on FCNs. By accounting for these effects, researchers can obtain more reliable assessments, ultimately leading to enhanced accuracy and applicability in neuroimaging analyses. The proposed approach provides a novel understanding of functional network properties, representing a crucial step towards a more comprehensive neuroscientific framework. Inspired by the work of Angluin, we investigated two fundamental distributed communication tasks - naming and counting - which are inherently non-trivial in a basic, 2-node communication model but become feasible with added structure, such as extended binary trees. Although, under a binary tree topology, these tasks can be completed with energy complexity variants of O(n) and o(n) using deterministic algorithms, these tasks can be achieved with significantly reduced error probabilities in a general m-station model by designing probabilistic algorithms. Specifically, we developed algorithms that complete these tasks with energy complexity bounded by O(log^2 m + log m). Interestingly, we found this efficiency to be nearly optimal, as we demonstrated any algorithm in this model must execute at least log m operations using any single station. Furthermore, we delved into the possible energy efficiencies of these algorithms in models with distinct communication capacities at individual stations. We established that the difference in energy efficiency between deterministic and probabilistic algorithms is largely a consequence of allowing diverse reception capabilities at individual stations. Using a custom extension of the Angluin model, we presented two central findings - first, we broadly classified the energy efficiency of both naming and counting problems in multi-station models according to the variety of reception capabilities at individual stations; second, we specifically analyzed the energy efficiency of both naming and counting problems in a model with diverse reception capabilities at individual stations, which are activated upon receiving any substring, and we found this model particularly conducive to achieving higher energy efficiency variants of O(n) and o(n) using deterministic algorithms. Furthermore, we established that the energy complexity variants of both naming and counting problems cannot be further improved using any feasible combination of reception capabilities. Using the Angluin model with general reception capabilities at individual stations, which are activated upon receiving a specified prefix, we established the energy complexity variants of O(log^2 m + log m) using probabilistic algorithms, which are nearly optimal, as any algorithm in this model must execute at least log m operations using any single station. We established the energy complexity variants of both naming and counting problems cannot be further improved using any feasible combination of general reception capabilities. This research investigates the performance of MIMO systems with multiple users in various settings, focusing on the decomposition of interference to optimize system efficiency. To this end, group LASSO analysis is applied, initially leveraging the Strumoso algorithm to identify the most critical user groups, thereby reducing settings with massive user counts. The study then divides two-user MIMO systems into two groups, utilizing two distinct approaches: 1) identifying group sizes as channel dimensions, and 2) dynamically determining group sizes based on the condition number of channel matrices, aiming to enhance sum-rate and interference management. The outcomes reveal that LASSO-based decomposition and optimized group assignments yield better performance, especially in achieving full diversity and gain with minimal computational demands. Moreover, the approach easily extends to more complex MIMO systems, and it's shown that the optimal group structure corresponds to solutions from the zero-forcing problem, indicating a feasible solution path. To evaluate its practicality, the technique is applied to a 5G downlink scenario, demonstrating its potential to reduce pilot overhead and boost sum-rate by 30% and 87%, respectively. The approach also offers a 66% gain in sum-rate over a massive MIMO system with optimal power control and 11% better performance than a MIMO system without decomposition. The method's adaptability to different scales, absence of iterative convergence requirements, and ability to achieve optimal performance make it a suitable and efficient technique for various MIMO settings. The possibility of implementing group LASSO as a hardware component is also explored, potentially enabling the development of a universal chip architecture compatible with distinct baseband processor architectures with equivalent performance. The outcome reveals group LASSO as a promising tool to achieve near-optimal performance and efficiently design future MIMO systems. The study further shows the decomposition capability of LASSO to be a novel feature of MIMO channel matrices, distinguishable from the known property where the left null space of a channel matrix doesn't lead to optimal performance. The potential of the LASSO technique to identify the most critical factors of a linear matrix is also demonstrated, especially in applications with massive data counts, potentially enabling the development of a data filter. This research focuses on finding a suitable measure on the state space of a Markov process such that the transition density satisfies specific conditions, including a bound that decreases exponentially as time approaches infinity. We derive necessary and sufficient criteria for a Markov process to exhibit exponential convergence to a unique quasi-stationary distribution, including conditions related to the dominance principle. This system utilizes a three-component ciphertext consisting of a complex vector, a scalar, and a encoded message, resulting in increased public-key size and heightened resistance to specific forms of side-channel attacks. Weighed against the potential for bias in selecting features of significance, the limited resources available for imaging domains makes high-throughout quantitative image analysis particularly demanding. To address this issue, we have developed a novel strategy that leverages a hybrid ensemble approach consisting of feature selection and machine learning. We demonstrate this method using data from two distinct radiomics fields, treating the analysis as an unsupervised feature selection task and a semi-supervised learning problem, and compare its performance to established techniques. Our results indicate that the hybrid ensemble approach significantly improves classification accuracy when compared to conventional methods, providing substantial gains in two different biomedical domains. Furthermore, we analyze the reason behind these gains and discuss the practical implications of this method for further optimizing radiomics feature extraction from images. Ultimately, the hybrid ensemble strategy presents a valuable alternative for efficient and comprehensive feature extraction in radiomics and image analysis.
