A novel cosmological model, the deceleration-acceleration transition driven by inflationary quintessence, is examined through a cosmographic analysis based on higher-order derivatives of Hubble's law. This model has previously been proposed as a potential solution to unify dark energy and dark matter. By using up to fourth-order Hubble parameters, the model's dynamics can be represented in a parameter space defined by three dimensionless coefficients. These coefficients represent the deceleration parameter, a parameter characterizing the change in deceleration, and a parameter describing the deceleration-acceleration transition. A mathematical system governing the model's evolution and an invariant measure for its phase space are formulated. This approach enables a comprehensive understanding of the model's evolution and allows for the recovery of widely used cosmological scenarios, including the λ-φ model and quintessence models featuring an inverse power-law and a logarithmic coupling. Furthermore, the model's ability to replicate the present-day acceleration of the universe's expansion is investigated, as well as its predicted spectral features, including a monochromatic distribution of gravitational waves, a consistency relation similar to Harrison-Zeldovich, and constraints on the model's parameters aimed at reproducing the observed deceleration parameter value. Ultimately, the model's ability to explain the universe's evolution from the inflationary stage to its present-day state is discussed. A future outlook is provided, including the potential for further model refinement to reduce parameter space and make inferences without relying on auxiliary parameters. Lastly, the cosmological model's compatibility with current observational data, including Baryon Acoustic Oscillations, Supernovae, Hubble parameters, and the Cosmic Microwave Background, is investigated using the confidence level framework. A thorough examination of the model's ability to match the data is provided through the use of contour maps displaying the confidence levels for its parameters, and a comparison with the ΛCDM model is performed using the figure of merit. This model has been found to be compatible with the data, including with the Hubble parameter measurements at 1σ confidence, and possesses the potential to explain the universe's expansion history up to its present-day state. In conclusion, the model's unification of dark energy and dark matter has been successfully demonstrated using the confidence level method. A final conclusion is provided, stating that the model represents a promising candidate for modern cosmology.

We've developed a Gaussian model for course preferences that uses a low-dimensional variable to explain which courses students take, considering that some courses are mutually exclusive. By assuming certain properties about the Gaussian distribution, we've created an efficient learning method. Our approach has a simplified structure that makes it easier to identify key parameters, including the number of dimensions, certain covariance properties, and a measure of student diversity, or homogeneity. Through synthetic data experiments, we've demonstrated that our model can be effectively learned, even under different and independent enrollments, and we've validated its real-world applicability by applying it to Princeton University's course data, exploring factors that influence student diversity in course selection. The insights we've gained offer a new perspective on understanding student course enrollment patterns. The implementation details of our model, along with the code, can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/yixiangguo/GaussianCourseEnrollmentModel. The actual Princeton University course data can be accessed through Oracle's Princeton University Course Database. 

Keywords: Gaussian distribution, latent variable, course enrollment, preference learning.

This study employs deep learning techniques, specifically autoencoding CGAN, to devise a dynamic portfolio allocation strategy that optimizes returns and minimizes risk. By adapting the Markowitz framework's traditional portfolio allocation approach, which selects securities with lowest variance, to one that selects securities with lowest reward relative to risk, we investigate the potential for improved performance. As CGAN learns the Markowitz framework's underlying distribution, we introduce a loss function incorporating portfolio theory to guide the learning process and assess portfolio efficiency. Using data from the S\&P 500 index from 1990 to 2019, we compare portfolio returns and volatility with those of the Markowitz framework and observe notable enhancements in certain quarters over the twenty years examined. Furthermore, we find that this ACGAN-based strategy outperforms the Markowitz framework across multiple risk metrics in about 57.5% of instances, while experiencing no instances of portfolio failure, as evidenced by a zero occurrence rate of all assets. By diversifying into a minimum number of stocks, the ACGAN-based strategy also exhibits robustness. Ultimately, the ACGAN-based strategy consistently produces superior outcomes, albeit with occasional underperformance when chosen by the algorithmic strategy, which can be attributed to the shortcoming of a single algorithmic strategy. Future work could focus on leveraging multi-objective deep learning to tackle this issue, which involves balancing returns and risk in the portfolio allocation decision. The proposed framework also offers potential applications in other portfolio allocation contexts. A standalone code repository is available for further examination at \url{https://github.com/fintechAsia/DeepPortfo}. Deep neural networks can effectively classify data, but they often struggle with limited or irregular data. In such situations, incorporating a Bayesian perspective helps limit the impact of arbitrary initializations and adapts better to out-of-distribution instances. By combining these aspects, Bayesian neural networks exhibit superior performance across various tasks. This paper investigates the challenges of applying Bayesian neural networks due to the inaccessibility of their posterior distributions. To address this, we develop a approximation technique that enables learning with Bayesian neural networks on real-world tasks, including misclassified and irregular data from a leading medical diagnostic system. We also analyze the consequences of our approximation and compare the results to non-Bayesian alternatives. Our analysis confirms the superiority of Bayesian neural networks in producing accurate predictions, reliable uncertainty estimates, and valuable insights. By applying our techniques to a real-world medical diagnostic task, we significantly improve the prediction accuracy and provide valid measurements of data uncertainty. This improved model, along with its uncertainty estimates, has the potential to decrease the overall cost of medical diagnosis. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/harvard-asthma/lbnn. This research was supported by a grant from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, Number 1R01AI139182.

This enables \LBNN to attain a high level of approximation (less than 1% error) while being efficient in terms of computation costs, specifically in classification problems. We evaluated the effectiveness of \LBNN by applying it to a leading medical diagnostic system which has faced significant challenges in achieving accurate and robust results due to its limited and irregular data. Specifically, this system was developed using data from asthma patients and had been found to be prone to overfitting. We demonstrated that \LBNN is capable of successfully addressing this issue by providing accurate and reliable predictions as well as valuable insights into data uncertainty. By utilizing a real-world transfer learning scenario, where the model is trained on data from asthma patients and then applied to related but distinct test data from other geographic regions and patient groups, we verified the robust nature of \LBNN. This \LBNN model is now publicly accessible at https://github.com/harvard-asthma/lbnn.

To facilitate research using user-generated content, we have developed a customized framework for multiple Facebook Group APIs, allowing for streamlined data collection. Our early-mover strategy is grounded in our long-term Facebook App Developer partnership, which enables novel, unencumbered access to rich user-generated content, including posts and comments. Our API prototype successfully demonstrated the ease of collecting and processing large datasets of 1,000 users and 10,000 groups, equivalent to approximately 12GB and 3GB of generated content, respectively. We introduce an exterior algebra system over algebra systems based on the concept of $ext{F}_1^{\pm}$, which also encompasses determinantal algebraic matroids. This creation of an exterior algebra system allows us to define an exterior cohomology system, which provides a dual perspective to the cohomology theory developed by Berline and Vergne for complex matroids. Our work builds upon their groundbreaking results. Moreover, determining the cohomology classes in the top degree of the exterior system holds significant importance, as these classes are directly linked to the Kapranov cohomology classes of the matroid. This relationship offers an alternative, complementary approach to a recent result obtained by Adiprasito, Huh, and Katz, published in 2021. The theory outlined in this paper also extends determinantal matroids to include linear iterated matroids as a special case, where the exterior system can be represented as the exterior algebra of a combinatorial nature, analogous to the free and signed loop algebras. In addition, we have successfully removed dependencies on complex numbers and Berline-Vergne cohomology from Huh's recent result on the exterior cohomology of complex matroids. The theory developed here also provides an extension of the recent result obtained by M. Matsumoto on the Kapranov cohomology of the signless exterior algebra of a matrix over the reals. We explore the application of attention mechanisms to enhance the modeling of dialogue state tracking. By using a confusion network encoder with attention capabilities, our system learns to prioritize specific spans of dialogue history when determining the current state. The proposed attentional model enhances the capability of the base model to identify relevant sections of the dialogue history, leading to improved performance. Furthermore, the model's ability to disambiguate key information in dialogue history is demonstrated through automatic evaluation. We also present variants of the attentional model that leverage external knowledge, including a graph attention network, to further improve the model's accuracy. Experiment results show that the attentional model, combined with graph attention, achieves a high DSC of 0.908, outperforming current state-of-the-art models. The benefits of the attentional model are also assessed in terms of computation cost, with significant speedup observed on a GPU. The proposed model's ability to focus on crucial information in dialogue history while disregarding insignificant segments is an invaluable guide for future development of dialogue state tracking models. The performance of the attentional model, along with its potential for application in multi-domain settings, is also showcased in the latest official evaluation dataset. The paper's main contributions include the application of attention mechanisms to the modeling of dialogue state tracking, enhancement of the base model's performance through attention, integration of graph attention to improve the model's accuracy and speedup, and release of the source code at https://github.com/ChaubeyVivek/ATTN-GraphDST. The paper additionally presents analysis of the model's performance and shortcomings, along with directions for future enhancement. In entangled systems, decoherence arises from diverse noise patterns, and our main objective is to identify these patterns using available data from local measurements. Applying the principles of parameter estimation, we compare the precision in estimating different noise models in an entangled qubit. By leveraging optimal estimators, we find that several specific noise models can be determined with the highest possible level of accuracy, specifically, the (a) noise strength, rotation angle, and mode coupling, and, separately, the phase shift, rotation rate, and decorrelation time. Moreover, we analyze how the noise-decoherence trade-off affects the precision in estimating coherence times and demonstrate that optimal estimates for certain noise models are achieved when correlations between noise parameters are minimized. Ultimately, our findings indicate that optimal estimates for the noise-decoherence balance are reached when the ratio of coherence-destroying to coherence-inducing processes is directly proportional to the square root of the noise strength. By establishing this proportionality, our results improve the existing understanding of the noise-decoherence balance and verify Johnson-Nistz rules under optimal estimation conditions. The methods employed in this work are versatile and can be easily extended to analyze the effects of other noise patterns in entangled qubits. Moreover, our framework holds great promise for addressing real-world challenges in the development of quantum processing units for multi-qubit systems. As an example, we investigate how the optimal estimates of parameter values, precision, and correlations change when the noise-decoherence balance is shifted from coherence destruction to creation. The findings reveal that optimal estimates for the latter case correspond to specific noise models, and their analysis allows us to derive general conditions under which quantum processing unit technologies can be safely coupled to other systems without losing their quantum properties. By establishing these conditions, we aim to contribute to the development of error-robust quantum strategies for sharing and for the secure key exchange, and show that optimal estimates improve the existing bounds on the key exchange rate by up to three orders of magnitude, and, potentially, eliminate previously existing drawbacks. Regression defects in object-oriented programming continue to pose significant challenges to software maintenance. Despite decades of research, the task of transforming human-written repairs into applicable patches in object-oriented code remains understudied. Previous studies primarily focused on the technical aspects of repair tasks, resulting in little overlap with existing transformation research. To bridge this gap, our work presents novel evaluations that compare multiple human-written repairs for each issue and multiple automated repair techniques. We utilised these comparisons to enhance existing repair techniques and conducted comprehensive testing, encompassing over 1,600 defects drawn from eight software maintenance repositories. Our findings from over 13,000 preliminary comparisons and 5,370 comparative evaluations revealed that approximately 33% of defects had patches identical to human-written repairs and around 10% of comparisons had identical patches across multiple automated tools. We conducted six distinct comparative studies, including five that compared various tool-based repairs and one that compared multiple comparative approaches. Notably, our research highlights that integrating contrasts from multiple comparative techniques can substantially enhance the quality of generated patches. We observed that combining the comparative techniques of Cross-Field Move and Similarity Guided Move results in nearly 50% of generated patches matching human-written repairs, indicating significant room for improvement. We also conducted a pilot study to further explore the potential of integrating these comparative techniques and the words expressed in code. The findings from over 1,300 comparisons revealed that the methods of Cross-Field Move and Similarity Guided Move (but not code words) helped reduce the space of possible transformations and resulted in improved patches. However, integrating code words did not yield the expected outcome in our evaluation and occasionally made patches worse. We hypothesise that this code word effect stems from conflicting meanings and grammatical nuances. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for transforming human-written repairs, contributes new insights to the field, and opens up fresh topics in comparative research. Teacher-student knowledge transfer has emerged as a vital component in knowledge distillation, facilitating the transfer of valuable information from a larger teacher model to a smaller student model.  However, the process of knowledge transfer is significantly hindered by the significant parameter reduction brought about by channel pruning, with various prior methods experiencing difficulties in effectively tackling this issue.  To address this problem, we have developed Layer-wise Distillation Pruning (LDP), a novel, layer-based strategy that integrates channel pruning and student model training in a simultaneous and interactive framework.  The key insights that inform LDP involve recognizing that various layers within a network demonstrate distinct characteristics and varying capacities for learning, with parameters essential for capturing key data features being most prominent.  To reflect these differences, we have established two distinct parameter groups, utilizing LDP to simultaneously prune channels, adjust weights, and guide the training of the student model using the structure and knowledge from the teacher model.  The efficacy of LDP has been demonstrated through its application in multiple benchmark datasets, with notable gains in accuracy of up to 8.6% and a parameter reduction of approximately 87%.  Computational experiments have shown LDP to be approximately 2-3 times faster than traditional distillation methods when run on a GPU and 10 times faster when run on a CPU.  LDP has been used to develop Distilled EfficientNet, a family of lightweight, high-accuracy neural networks based on the recently introduced EfficientNet theory.  The Distilled EfficientNet family includes 14 members, with parameter and computation costs varying from approximately 0.5 million to 40 million, and includes models with varying accuracy levels, including a member of the family, dubbed distilled-l0, which exhibits a top-1 error rate of 20.97% on the ImageNet dataset. Grazing ecosystems, like many natural systems, exhibit abrupt, irreversible shifts due to increasing aridity, which can lead to critical threshold crossings. Past research has shown that grazing ecosystems tend to be more resistant to abrupt collapse when considering the spatial influence of grazing dynamics. However, the underlying mechanisms for this resistance are still unclear. In this study, we used a simple grazing model with spatially extended effects to explore how this extended model compares to its simplified, local counterpart. Our analysis revealed that the extended model exhibits a prolonged delay in the onset of collapse and reduced frequency of catastrophic transitions to chaos. The delay in the onset of collapse has been quantified and expressed in terms of the system's dimensionless parameters, providing valuable insights for evaluating the effects of spatial grazing dynamics on ecosystem stability. Additionally, this work lays the groundwork for further research into the influence of spatial extension on complex ecosystem behaviors. Furthermore, it enables quantification of spatial non-locality's influence on the ecosystem's critical properties and offers a simple means of detecting and tracking spatial non-locality's effects over time. Lastly, it suggests potential avenues for investigating the effects of spatial extension on ecosystems and discovering other complex, ecosystem-related phenomena. We introduce a novel selling mechanism that guarantees buyers tell the truth in an $n$-player game, unaffected by the nature of demand functions. This mechanism's operational basis, rooted in the fundamental concept of dividing an unitary object, relies solely on a noninteractive procedure determining shares among buyers, distributing the item to those with highest allocated portions. Mechanisms of this kind work by employing a "threshold" value $t$, used to determine the portion allocated to each buyer, $\frac{i}{n}+b$, with buyer $i$ receiving the sum of these two quantities. A given demand function's intensity is reflected in the value of $b$, while the threshold $t$ influences the distribution of goods. We show that any feasible allocation can be achieved through a suitable choice of $t$ and $b$, demonstrating that mechanisms based on dividing an unitary object of currency are powerful multi-object commodification tools. This study also explores an extension, enabling the mechanism to accommodate multiple commodities. However, addressing the problem in this more general context proves to be more challenging, and we present an alternative, non-combinatorial solution for the case of three commodities. Finally, we show the mechanism's efficacy in handling utility functions with negative affine components. This approach finds applications in scenarios where buyer utilities cannot be determined from their bids, an issue present in various contexts and the main motivator for this work. This paradigm is fundamentally distinct from existing approaches, differing primarily in their failure to generalize beyond single commodities as well as their reliance on non-affine utility functions. Unlike prior work, our study focuses on the axiomatic approach, and a novel framework is developed to decompose an unitary object of currency based on the principles of proportionality and fairness. We begin by establishing the core axioms and leveraging them to establish the central result - showing that any feasible allocation can be achieved through a suitable choice of $t$ and $b$. This result is then leveraged to establish the central claim, presenting a universal mechanism addressing the original problem. This result is further leveraged to present two novel extensions addressing additional problems. A significant issue in abstractive summarization is the lack of control over inaccuracies. In this work, we develop a new approach to mitigate inaccuracies by preserving the structure of the source text. We propose the concept of "entity chains", which enable exact control over inconsistencies. Additionally, we introduce the approach of "structurally minimizing errors", contrasting with prior methods that aim to minimize errors in summarization by relying on pre-trained language models. Our findings indicate that our technique outperforms existing methods in minimizing errors, while maintaining summary fluency. Notably, our approach is the first to successfully replicate the structure of source texts in summarization. It has also been demonstrated that its unique objective can be utilized in conjunction with fluency objectives in other types of language models. Overall, our work signifies a significant step towards enhancing the reliability of abstractive summarization by preserving the structure of the source text. The code and model will be made available upon acceptance. Additionally, we have deployed a live summarization system, which allows users to provide a source document, ground truth summary, and settings for entity chains, with the system generating a summary based on these specifications, at https://sumie-air.iihe.be/. The following study presents a necessary and sufficient condition for a function 
$F:\mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}$ to be differentiable in relation to the 
differentiability of a related $(n-1)$-variable function $f$, where $F$ 
depends on $x_n$ through $f$. This reveals an indirect link between the 
differentiability of a multi-variable function and its lower-dimensional 
counterpart. Similar results are provided for the continuity of $F$, as well 
as an analysis of various special cases of the theorem. Furthermore, this 
research opens up the possibility of developing a induction-based framework 
for proving differentiability. Ultimately, this is achieved by proving that 
the function $F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ can be expressed as a product of functions 
$x_1^{m_1},\ldots,x_n^{m_n}$, where the differentiability of $F(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})$ 
guarantees the differentiability of $F(x_1,\ldots,x_n$. In addition, this 
result is extended to functions with polar monomial forms and symmetries, as well 
as those defined in a free topological vector space. The study also provides 
original applications and generalizations of the theorems, including a result 
for functions that can be expressed as the sum of powers of variables. 
Finally, illustrative examples are presented to demonstrate the validity 
of these findings. The research further provides an extension to a recent 
paper titled "Some results on differentiable and continuous multi-variable 
functions" by A. Ali, A. Khan, and S. Jafarian. The analysis is concluded 
with a future research perspective, where the issue of whether the theorem 
holds when the function $f$ has a closed domain is raised. All the study's 
code and figures can be found at https://github.com/sadafja/Multi-variable-functions. 

This work is a part of the Ph.D thesis of the corresponding author at 
Hitit University, Turkey under the supervision of Dr. A. Khan.

This study investigates the potential for using vocal entrainment as an indicator of conversational engagement in people with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Entrainment, a phenomenon where two individuals synchronize their physical or psychological patterns, can be measured in the form of autoregressive coefficients or spectral density. Our research involves analyzing the speech patterns of 44 individuals with ASD and 28 neurotypical individuals during conversational exercises with a trained interviewer. In contrast, the process of estimating three-dimensional scene geometry can provide a more stable foundation for pre-training, as it results in a relatively small set of plausible configurations. This realisation prompted the development of Tsuki, a pre-training method that leverages scene geometry by applying unsupervised stereo matching and 3D reconstruction before fine-tuning a neural renderer to generate geometric images that match real images. By training this approach on vast datasets like ImageNet, the research demonstrates that Tsuki maintains its ability to adapt to novel images and tasks, outperforming previous top approaches by a significant margin while avoiding over-specialization with a more robust view on image and 3D vision. Further analysis shows that the latent 3D geometry learned by Tsuki contributes substantially to its capabilities. Tsuki's code has been made available. Tsuki's website hosts a user interface for exploring its 3D latent spaces as well as demo videos that illustrate its ability to generate geometric 3D models. As an alternative, we're also introducing a straightforward solution that utilizes $O(N^2)$ time. To compute this metric, we're comparing two datasets, using one as the base and varying the other, then calculating the maximum Maclaren's U-coefficient and minimizing it through a series of rotations, while leveraging the Divide-and-Conquer approach to streamline computations. Our results from experimental testing reveal that when dealing with large datasets, the efficient algorithm exhibits significantly superior performance compared to the straightforward method and other competing approaches such as the Korol and Sharpe or Belbin algorithms. The code for our implementation has been made publicly accessible on the GitHub platform. A persistent homology theory is applicable to multi-variable topological data analysis, yet some complex datasets are beyond its reach due to difficulty in partitioning them. One method to circumvent this challenge involves using coverings without a priori restrictions on them, but this leads to inconsistent results. In an attempt to resolve this issue, we make use of a detailed analysis of the Euler characteristic for computing the persistent homology of a filtered complex, and we demonstrate that it is possible to define one-way persistent homology for a filtered space without reference to a partitioning. This allows the application of persistent homology to a broader class of inputs. We provide examples to illustrate the fact that one-way persistent homology of certain spaces is not determinable by multi-variable homology with respect to arbitrary coverings, and finally, we investigate the relationship between one-way persistent homology and the more extensively studied type, such as one-dimensional homology. Specifically, under certain conditions, we verify that it is possible to exactly replicate one-way persistent homology using one-dimensional homology. Biological population dynamics models that incorporate time-varying and spatial variables are increasingly being investigated. In this study, we explore a two-species model that accounts for spatial dependence and intraspecies competition, which exhibits various bifurcations, such as Hopf and saddle-node bifurcations. These bifurcations significantly impact a population's stability and allow for the existence of multiple stable solutions, including periodic and stationary patterns. Using an advanced computational technique, we identify and analyze the spatial patterns emerging across the bifurcation curve. Our research also reveals the presence of mixed patterns, comprising one species exhibiting spatial patterns while the other does not. Furthermore, we have developed an early warning system for potential outbreaks in the species A by analyzing the variability of their spatial profiles across the bifurcation curve. This warning system is based on an instability measure that forecasts an increase in the species A's spatial profile before the onset of an outbreak. These findings align with theoretical predictions and observed patterns in scientific literature, and are confirmed through numerical simulations and analytical calculations. The relationship between the variability of spatial profiles and an upcoming outbreak in the species A is investigated further in this study. Through systematic analysis, we have identified a connection between the variability of the species A's spatial profile and an upcoming outbreak through a critical time, which can be determined from the species A's spatial profile. This relationship holds for distinct bifurcation parameters, including the Hopf and saddle-node bifurcations. In order to confirm that the variability of spatial profiles is an early warning system for an upcoming outbreak in the species A, we have carried out an across-bifurcation analysis, which shows a consistent increase in the species A's spatial profile in both Hopf and saddle-node bifurcations. In addition, we have investigated the relationship between the variability of spatial profiles and an upcoming outbreak in the species B and discovered a similar trend across both bifurcations. This study presents novel insights into the variability of spatial profiles as an early warning system for an upcoming outbreak in both species A and B. These findings are confirmed across different spatial configurations and bifurcation types. In contrast to existing literature, which focuses on single-species models and a single type of bifurcation, this study explores two-species models that account for spatial dependence and bifurcations of Hopf and saddle-node types. Linear programming is a fundamental tool that has significant implications across various disciplines. Due to its versatility, high-speed solutions, and widespread applications in procedures like convex optimization and subgradient methods are highly sought after. Although the interior-point method, developed by Boyd, Mohri, and Heng, provides fast solutions, it's not feasible for some procedures. The proposed facet pivot method presented in this paper offers a refinement of the vertex pivot algorithm previously utilized. The enhanced algorithm includes features like automatic choice of basic variables, the application of Frobenius' inequality, and the implementation of a cyclic ordering technique, which can be transferred with minimal modifications from the LP-solver program written in C, currently available on GitHub. The efficacy of the facet pivot method was demonstrated in numerical tests, where it successfully solved problems within a timeframe of seconds, with its performance comparable to the interior-point method. The method proved particularly effective in scenarios involving small to medium-scale problems, with its future potential to extend to more complex high-dimensional cases. The paper also showcases the applicability of the facet pivot method to solve convex minimization problems via subgradient methods. As an example, it illustrates how the method can provide an $\varepsilon$-exact solution to the binary quadratic binfit problem, widely employed in the study of phase transitions in statistical mechanics and the self-assembly of nanostructures. Binfit problem solutions, accurate to a predetermined margin, can be attained within a timeframe of seconds, with its vertex count capped at millions. The paper further suggests that the facet pivot method may also yield positive outcomes for other optimization challenges involving combinatorial functions. The method's potential applications extend to percolation, contact processes, and the study of systems comprising few degrees of freedom, which is currently under initial investigation. The numerical results illustrate how the method can provide accurate solutions, transfer to different problem domains, and yield insights into statistical mechanics, while offering significant computational advantages. The numerical tests show that the method's computational requirements are negligible even when dealing with large high-dimensional problems featuring millions of vertices, with its time complexity displaying a logarithmic dependence on the problem dimension. The method's potential was also extended to the task of convex optimization, with its application to binary quadratic binfit problems providing the main case in point. The method's efficacy was demonstrated through its application to various problem variants, including those involving small, medium-scale, and large high-dimensional problems, with results comparable to the interior-point method and the standard convex approach. When examining differential distributions for top quark phenomena, a commonly applied technique, narrow width approximation, may lead to inaccurate outcomes, especially in situations where gamma distributions intersect. This inaccuracy tends to be minimal when analyzing clumps with relatively high statistical significance but becomes critical when analyzing low-Stat signals where numerous partial contributions are involved. To resolve this, a novel method is proposed for creating an all-statistics range NMA and, through comparison, assessing the impact of NMA on a particular result. By applying this new test, research has revealed that NMA introduces noticeable distortions of around 1-3% in the top quark pT and b-flavor fraction analysis but has a much greater influence, up to 20%, when considering the top quark b-flavor fraction in NMA. Furthermore, it has been found that NMA yields results compatible within two standard deviations. To correct these discrepancies, the CT10 NNLO QCD parton shower matched at NLO QFT is employed, and predictions are provided for the t-channel single top quark production. We suggest that alongside parton distribution function uncertainties, the NMA method should also be considered when reporting results for the t-channel single top quark production to remain compatible with state-of-the-art results. We believe this approach can be used in the majority of cases where NMA has been found to introduce noticeable distortions in the top quark physics phase space. This research investigates the effectiveness of learning transferable knowledge from fake pulse and pulse-related signals for anti-spoofing in facial recognition systems. As facial motion data is challenging to collect and label, we propose using normal pulse signals from users via a peripheral imaging technique called photoplethysmography. Furthermore, recent advancements in the Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture, which facilitates the transfer of knowledge across domains and modalities more efficiently than CNN-based methods, make it an attractive choice for this task. We present novel methods for processing low-dimensional pulse signal data and integrate them with magnitude and spatial features from ViT models to train discriminative fake pulse detection classifiers. Our experiments, conducted across three different ViT models, demonstrate improved AUC values when using the combined pulse signal and magnitude and spatial features, yielding first-rate performance with a high AUC of 99.54% on the Bounded Variation Input Transform (BVI-T) benchmark. Moreover, we evaluate the robustness of our approach against varying temperature and illumination conditions and find that it exhibits resistance to adverse environmental impacts. This study provides an innovative framework for ViT-based pulse signal transfer learning in anti-spoofing facial recognition systems. With its simple yet efficient design, it can be readily adapted to other related applications such as human authentication and pulse signal analysis for various purposes. Autonomous driving systems are beginning to emerge as a highly developed technology, designed to navigate diverse environments and achieve various objectives. The majority of research has been dedicated to analyzing the driver's intentions and predicting their actions, based on the observed scene and a database of driving manuals. However, a significant challenge arises when the system is unable to perceive the driver's goals, due to obstacles in the scene or a lack of relevant experience. To address this issue, a novel approach is presented, leveraging Recurrent Neural Networks and Temporal Convolutional Networks to create an autonomous driving system that learns to navigate uncertain environments and estimate the driver's objectives, utilizing only contextual clues from the scene. The proposed system demonstrates exceptional performance in simulating real-world driving scenarios, where it successfully predicts the driver's actions and autonomously navigates the route. The method's capabilities are further evaluated through various experiments, highlighting its advantages and applications. The research data, source code, and trained models are available for download on the GitHub repository. 

Keywords: Autonomous driving systems, Temporal Convolutional Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks, Temporal Evolutionary Deep Graph, contextual scene analysis.

The new version retains the method's primary objectives and is complemented by additional experimental findings. In parallel evolutionary algorithms, the way in which the fittest individuals are chosen to form the new generation significantly influences the search process.  A novel selection technique is presented, which prioritizes the most eligible offspring based on their proximity to the fittest individuals within their respective populations. This new method aims to enhance search progress in the overall population.  To test its effectiveness, a study was conducted on simple one-way migration parallel evolutionary algorithms, which includes experiments combining NSGA-II, GSE, and our proposed selection method, all within a single search environment.  To compare performance, the inverse distance sum ranking and inverse distance selection methods were used to analyze results on a high-dimensional uniform problem and a high-dimensional problem with a known optimal solution.  Results indicate our method, inverse distance selection, consistently outperforms inverse distance sum ranking in a high-dimensional uniform problem and yields comparable results with NSGA-II, GSE, and our method, inverse distance selection, on a high-dimensional problem with a known optimal solution.  Results also show our method, inverse distance selection, consistently outperforms NSGA-II, GSE, and our method, inverse distance sum ranking, on a high-dimensional problem with a known optimal solution.  It was also observed that populations with our method, inverse distance selection, demonstrate reduced speciation compared to NSGA-II, GSE, and our method, inverse distance sum ranking. Contributions of this research include an innovative search technique, inverse distance selection, and a unified theoretical framework for studying parallel evolutionary algorithms and their impact on search progress in the overall population.  It is hoped that our new method, inverse distance selection, will facilitate the development of search orientation algorithms and enhance our understanding of selection from a population perspective, facilitating the design of better parallel evolutionary algorithms with improved search progress in the overall population.  In addition, our study provides novel insights into the search process in high-dimensional problems and aids the avoidance of undesired features such as premature convergence and speciation in the search process in the overall population. Moreover, our analysis highlights that, under moderate to strong coupling conditions, the Lilouville probe overestimates the environmental bath density of states, whereas, at low driving frequencies, the BTP probe underestimates it due to the influence of micromotion. Compared to CePdIn, where full hybridization leads to increased electronic conductivity and high-temperature magnetic clustering, substitution of Rh into CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ alters the materials' electronic structure. Furthermore, the measurements demonstrate increased magnetic cluster sizes with increasing Rh content and a significant slowdown in the development of the superconducting Ho layer in Eltonium. This research warrants domain adaptation in image classification, where an trained model, pre-trained using diverse images across the world, needs to be fine-tuned on a specific dataset with known labels, yet collected without regard to the training data's origin. We focus on three key domain adaptation methods: adversarial training, maximum mean discrepancy, and adversarial refining, and assess their effectiveness in the supervised unsupervised domain adaptation framework. We conduct comprehensive experiments, evaluating the trade-offs and performance of these techniques on three datasets: MNIST, CIFAR100, and Sylvatic. The code and results are publicly available on our GitHub repository. Furthermore, we develop two novel techniques: 1) a novel adversarial training method, integrated with generative adversarial networks, and 2) a simple yet efficient way to generate adversarial examples using a distillation gradient. These techniques can be applied to the domain adaptation context and may have additional applications. We observe that the recently proposed adversarial defence method no longer functions in this setting, offering one possible explanation for its ineffectiveness in the general context. In addition, our findings suggest that the distillation gradient is more efficient than traditional methods based on projected gradient descent to obtain adversarial examples. A simple model of migration's impact on language evolution is investigated through simulations and analytical analysis. The model distinguishes between migrant and native groups and accounts for factors such as migration rates, language distribution, and group dynamics. By examining the long-term language convergence and the rate at which one language supplants another, the model sheds light on how migration influences linguistic patterns and processes. Three essential conditions must be met to determine the magnitude of migration's effect: the ratio of migration rates between groups, the relative sizes of the migrant and native groups, and the duration of language usage within each group. These conditions enable a qualitative understanding of migration's impact, but a fourth factor, language characteristics, is also revealed to have a significant role. Ultimately, the model indicates that the effect of migration is typically marked by gradual, long-term language convergence rather than rapid replacement. This approach is applied to two specific scenarios: the replacement of Latin by French in Gaul and the supplanting of Native American languages by English. Both scenarios are examined using a simple model that highlights the model's strengths and limitations. Furthermore, the model's validity is verified through additional case studies of the Roman Empire, the Anglo-Saxon conquest of England, the Inca Empire, and the colonization of the Americas. These comparative analyses demonstrate that the model's focus on four key factors provides a comprehensive framework for investigating the complex relationships between migration and language change. However, the model's simplicity also stems from its omission of other crucial factors, such as cultural, social, economic, technological, historical, and linguistic disparities. These omitted factors are shown to have the potential to reverse the model's predictions and may ultimately lead to the model's applicability being restricted to a relatively small set of language convergence events. This limitation is, however, somewhat mitigated by the model's ability to capture the qualitative properties of a broad range of convergence scenarios through a limited set of quantitative properties. Consequently, the model is proposed as a starting point for the development of more intricate and sophisticated models of migration's impact on language evolution. By comparing the model's predictions with empirical data on language, the model's validity is evaluated and the future directions for further research are identified. This involves an examination of the interplay between migration and language change at a finer granularity than the group-level, a deeper exploration of the model's assumptions and parameters, and the integration of additional factors to enhance the model's applicability and predictive power. Ultimately, the model represents an important milestone in the ongoing quest to create realistic simulations of migration's impact on language evolution

By applying HARL to an established reinforcement learning method, we have successfully demonstrated its application on various tasks, achieving effective action and state extraction. A thorough analysis of dark matter interactions with lithium has been carried out by examining high-energy particle interactions with lithium-6 and lithium-7. Prior studies focused solely on lithium-7, whereas our investigation covers both isotopes and conducts a comprehensive review of dark matter liabilities. We assess liability for two significant dark matter particles, axions and charginos, and derive more restrictive liability for dark matter interacting with lithium-6 compared to previous studies. Furthermore, since lithium-7 liability is also constrained by existing measurements, our findings apply mainly to lithium-6, which serves as a superior dark matter detector for light dark matter particles. We suggest using lithium-6 dark matter detectors to verify a dark matter signal in future analyses. Finally, we outline a relevant experimental setup for a proposed experiment.

a semantic concept that necessitates a novel computational model to address. This 
paper outlines a foundational framework for defining theatures property and 
determining the applicable programs. It further explores extensions to handle more 
complex scenarios, including multiple programs and theabilities of theatures property in 
relation to program control flow. Additionally, the research describes practical 
applications of theatures property and presents a possible approach to 
automatically detecting violations of this property. This framework builds upon 
previous studies, ultimately aiming to facilitate a complete automation of 
natural-language program verification. It has been implemented in a tool called 
Agri-Assert, which enables natural-language program assertions to be automatically 
evaluated. This evaluation method employs theatures property and employs a computational 
model that uses trees to represent programs and their governing rules. Furthermore, 
the research describes practical applications of theatures property and presents a 
practical approach to identifying program property violations. We demonstrateAgri-Assert's 
utility through several case studies, showcasing its potential to automatically 
detect property violations in programs expressed through natural language.

Canopus is a widely-used abstract machine for developing efficient distributed key distribution protocols. However, a flaw exists in Canopus when a failure occurs on one device, causing the distribution protocol to halt and require restart from the beginning. Our RCanopus extension builds upon Canopus by introducing resilience against device failures, allowing the protocol to continue operating after a failure occurs. RCanopus achieves this through a proven linearity analysis and a new implementation that ensures the same operational effects as original Canopus. Furthermore, RCanopus adds new properties: (i) fault tolerance, where the protocol can withstand device failures, and (ii) partial fault tolerance, where the protocol can tolerate failures occurring in a specified subset of devices. Specifically, RCanopus demonstrates stability with failures affecting at most one device and offers partial fault tolerance, encompassing a diverse range of distributed key distribution protocols. By combining fault tolerance and partial fault tolerance, RCanopus adapts various distributed key distribution protocols. Our results showcase that RCanopus enhances the efficiency of Canopus, resulting in improved linear and non-linear storage overhead, which ranges from 0 to 50% depending on the specific Canopus protocol utilized. Ultimately, RCanopus extends the can of errors in existing distributed key distribution protocols, offering a range of fixes from simple reimplementation to comprehensive upgrades. By addressing the subtleties of abstract machine implementation, RCanopus facilitates the efficient operation of distributed key distribution protocols. Existing can errors affecting widely-used dist key dist protocols like RAcrypto and RDHQ have been corrected, resulting in significant improvements to storage efficiency. Our proposed framework supports automatic correction of similar can errors affecting other dist key dist protocols, thereby enhancing storage efficiency. As such, RCanopus constitutes a valuable tool for promoting the efficient operation and maintenance of distributed key distribution protocols. Additionally, our work highlights dist key dist protocol developers' need to monitor the performance of abstract machines to prevent inefficiencies and safeguard the integrity and resilience of distributed key distribution protocols. As the complexity and variability of distributed key distribution protocols grow, the emergence of modified can errors becomes increasingly likely, underscoring a pressing need to address potential inefficiencies. Our analysis further demonstrates the applicability of Canopus to a broader range of distributed key distribution protocols. As such, RCrypto and RDHQ serve as ideal case studies in the context of CRYSTAL, while RCrypto and RDHQ fail to satisfy the requirements of LRT and CRYSTAL. Transport experiments across lipid bilayers have shown that different properties of the bilayers, such as thickness and water permeability, are inconsistent.  In contrast, experiments measuring equilibrium properties of the bilayers report a single, uniform value for all investigated lipids.  This study employs molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the reason behind the apparent discrepancy, and it reveals that the problem arises from a particular artifice inherent in time-dependent transport methods that miscalculates the membrane's properties, resulting in incorrect perceptions of lipid structure.  m a system where the membrane is composed of two types of lipids, the simulations demonstrate that molecules of the two types randomly co-mix within the membrane, and this is reflected in uniform values of thickness and water permeability obtained from equilibrium experiments.  Notably, the simulations demonstrate that the membrane's properties in equilibrium are superior to those obtained from transport experiments.  In an effort to rectify the mismatch, modified versions of time-dependent transport methods that correctly estimate the membrane's properties are proposed, and the simulations show that the new methods accurately replicate the results from equilibrium experiments, thereby addressing the discrepancy between the two types of measurements of lipid structure. Ultimately, the simulations suggest that the time-dependent transport method's artefact has led researchers to incorrectly conclude that the membrane's structure is irregular, and this may have prompted modifications to the lipid's chemical structure in order to increase water permeability through the membrane, a change that is investigated in the simulations.  However, the modifications have been found to have undesirable effects on other membrane properties, such as thickness and elongation, as measured by the transport experiments, as the membrane's chemistry is altered to enhance its performance.  In contrast, changes in the membrane's chemistry based on equilibrium experiment recommendations have been found in the simulations to yield a superior performance profile for all measured properties. The simulations's findings suggest an opportunity for future research to rectify perceived irregularities in the membrane's structure by altering its chemistry based on equilibrium experiment results. The current work's novelty lies in the simulation of transport experiments across lipid bilayers, and the elucidation of the discrepancy between the two types of measurements of lipid structure. The study's accuracy is reinforced by the fact that its results from equilibrium experiments align with existing published studies, and the simulation's scope and applicability are thereby extended to existing research data. The simulations's results provide insights into the dynamics of transport across lipid bilayers, and the study's novel aspects serve to enlighten researchers working in this area. In this work, we present a novel approach, BayesOD, that leverages deep learning models, specifically employing a deep neural network trained with a likelihood-free method to estimate detection uncertainty. By integrating a spatial attention module and employing class-conditional Gaussian distributions for detection uncertainty modeling, BayesOD enhances its capability to narrow down detection regions and generate more precise uncertainty estimates compared to traditional frameworks. Experimental evaluations on the COCO dataset demonstrate BayesOD's capacity to generate highly accurate uncertainty estimates, outperforming current state-of-the-art models. Additional evaluations show that uncertainty calibration techniques can further enhance the accuracy of BayesOD's uncertainty estimates. However, the widespread focus on path control has left the characteristics of the traversal modes underexplored. We investigated these modes in a parallelized photonic chip interferometer by focusing on a specific sub-system, namely, a waveguide with two parallel supermodes. Using a combined analytical and experimental approach, we uncovered the distinct traversal characteristics of each supermode. Notably, we observed that the modes' individual interference patterns mirror the system's path-level interference patterns, considering a transversal degree of freedom inverse to the corresponding path degree of freedom. This reveals a deep connection between path and traversal degrees of freedom. Moreover, our research lays out a general strategy for determining the traversal characteristics of complex interferometers, a crucial method for describing interference patterns. By revealing the relationship between the superposition of traversal modes and path degrees of freedom, our work advances the understanding of how individual photon states are represented within multi-mode interferometers. Consequently, this advances the capability to describe interference patterns, enabling the analysis of interference-based correlations, including those related to topological properties. Notably, under certain conditions, the superposition of transversal modes does not alter the path degree of freedom, allowing the detection of the individual contribution of each mode. As a result, the sensitivity of the system to any single parameter is enhanced. We propose that this capability could be utilized to measure the Stark shift of individual IT factor modes, enabling the control and manipulation of the individual modes' phases. Ultimately, our research provides new insights into the general applicability of global interferometers with multiple degrees of freedom, facilitating the analysis of complex systems and their capabilities to generate topological states, exploit non-Hermitian symmetry, and enable exceptional point detection. As these secondary particles, mainly neutrons and gamma rays, travel, they are tracked by detectors such as the ORCA experiment at the South Pole. By analyzing this data, researchers validate the accuracy of high-energy hadronic interactions within the atmosphere by comparing observed data with various models in multiple energy ranges. Furthermore, they use neutrons generated by cosmic rays to optimize the parameter for energy loss of neutrons, which is essential for accurate neutrino reconstruction in neutrino experiments like IceCube. By comparing observed data with models on multiple observables, they evaluate the consistency of various atmospheric neutron models and identify areas for future improvement. We provide recommendations for how to utilize neutron tracking experiments to maximize the detection of the atmospheric neutron flux at the detector's location. We also outline a potential future project that we propose to establish, which is designed to measure the atmospheric neutron flux at the detector's location. The pyramidal skeleton, with its hierarchical properties similar to AlexNet, can expedite training of neural networks by reducing the number of required backward computations, achieving a time reduction of 2-3 folds in practice. This paper offers an algorithm to generate the pyramidal skeleton from a given directed acyclic graph, and proves that the pyramidal skeleton is optimal in terms of reducing the computational complexity. Additionally, we present an easy-to-implement method to further decrease the memory usage during the backward phase. Our experiments with various deep learning models show that the pyramidal skeleton can lead to a speed-up of 2.03 times and a decrease of 1.96 times in memory usage over traditional approaches. Moreover, we find that the pyramidal skeleton can help in linearly expanding a network without increasing the backward phase complexity, making it an efficient means to implement progressive learning and model parallelism. This research is now available online at arXiv:2103.12238. Our code has been shared on GitHub at https://github.com/lingcat/PyraGN. Additionally, training procedures using the pyramidal skeleton can be found on https://pygn.github.io/. We believe that the pyramidal skeleton provides an innovative solution to address the computational constraints in deep learning model training. We intend to explore its potential in facilitating learning on large-scale graphs in the future. Mechanisms like the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms offer such services but come with a significant computational overhead. A new mechanism, the proposed Huber mechanism, offers differential privacy and performs better than the existing mechanisms in terms of communication efficiency and computation speed. The Huber mechanism's privacy guarantee and query privacy preservation analysis reveal its performance advantages along with other notable features. The proposed Huber mechanism, being based on a truncated Gaussian noise, loses its differential privacy guarantee if the truncation point is too low, a property that is mathematically proven. To ensure this privacy vulnerability is avoided, a method to set the truncation point is developed along with a mechanism to derive from it a perfectly differential private Huber mechanism, thus preserving all the Huber mechanism's benefits while maintaining differential privacy. The performance comparison of the proposed Huber mechanism, Laplace mechanism, and Gaussian mechanism, based on mechanism's privacy guarantee and query privacy preservation analysis, reveals their respective mean error ratios, which shows the proposed mechanism's superiority. The proposed mechanism's superiority also manifests in its application to the privacy preservation of deep neural networks, where its performance surpasses both the applied machinery learning mechanism with a mechanism's privacy guarantee and the Laplace mechanism. The far-infrared polarization of dust, determined through observations of various interstellar dust, does not vary with frequency, leading to a common understanding that large dust grains are spherical in shape. This study, inspired by a different interpretation of the data that reveals a change in polarization angle near the frequency at which dust grains are expected to be aligned by magnetic forces, suggests an alternative explanation. By using a novel model of dust grain behavior, we demonstrate that our initial insight can be retained, along with the notion of spherical grains, by describing the far-infrared polarization as a combination of the model's predicted alignment and the large-scale magnetic field's effect. This model is consistent with its large-scale magnetic field parameters. Following the large-scale magnetic field removal, the circular polarization observed in the data, indicated by the angle parameter $\chi$, oscillates between positive and negative values at various frequencies. A detailed analysis of this parameter reveals that its sign change is influenced by the size of the analysis segments, with larger segments exhibiting a frequency-dependent $\chi$ for smaller values. Conversely, larger values of the segment size result in a frequency-independent $\chi$. Combining the criteria of the frequency independence of $\chi$ and a minimal shift in the angle parameter relative to the large-scale magnetic field, we identify an optimal value for the segment size. For our data interpretation, we utilize a dust model comprising two grain species with different sizes, to accurately reproduce the observed emission and polarization characteristics. This model takes into account the large-scale magnetic field, grain size variations, and the Rau et al. catalog data, while ensuring that the Rau et al. observed polarization matrix data is fitted at lower frequencies. Furthermore, the model fails to capture the observed depolarization at higher frequencies with any settings. To account for this depolarization, we consider an optical depth flag in the code for the polarization matrix calculations, with both the model including and excluding the polarization from the smallest grains being unable to replicate the observed polarization behavior. Consequently, the model includes the polarization from the smallest grains until a specific optical depth threshold, following the large-scale magnetic field description, to accurately reproduce the observed polarization. Utilizing the optical depth flag in the code for the polarization matrix calculations, we find the threshold to be approximately 0.1. With both the optical depth flag in the code for the polarization matrix calculations and the model describing the large-scale magnetic field, we find the model parameters and variables to be consistent with prior research, except for the Varilla et al. 2017 study.

This research explores the Most Clicks Problem (MCP) through a distinct perspective rooted in information theory. By examining MCP, we aim to determine which image is most frequently selected by users when presented with two images, one of which has been modified using different levels of compression. This study focuses on examining the effects of significant compression thresholds on the chosen image, utilizing an information-theoretic approach called nullity to measure the magnitude of compression. Our analysis begins with a lower-bound estimation on the amount of compression generated by the MCP algorithm, followed by an assessment of four popular image compression tools (ImageMagick, imghdr, Pillow, and Google's Compression tool), where the results indicate that three of these tools (Pillow, ImageMagick, and imghdr) do not exhibit consistent consistency. However, our MCP algorithm does demonstrate consistent consistency, and its "most click" parameter is directly related to a measure of nullity, where consistent consistency increases as nullity decreases. This relationship holds true for a wide-ranging set of images and compression tools. This study also delves into the variations in human behavior based on the dimensions of the grid used in the MCP, discovering that altering the grid's dimensions affects the "most click" image and the amount of compression but does not impact our information-theoretic lower bound. This research specifically highlights the MCP's inability to effectively choose an image when presented with specific pairs of uncompressed images compressed using the Pillow, ImageMagick, and imghdr tools, and reveals that all four compression tools can regenerate an image given sufficient samples, thereby recovering 95\% or more of an image's nullity in such cases. Conversely, our MCP algorithm is unable to recover an image from tools such as Google's Compression, which introduces additional noise that cannot be recovered even with an infinite number of "most click" images. In summary, this research leverages information theory to investigate the Most Clicks Problem's failure to consistently select an image compression algorithm choosing both original and modified images, and identifies a key connection between the amount of compression and our MCP's consistency, which grows as the amount of compression increases. Furthermore, our research shows that varying the grid size of the "most click" parameter affects the chosen image, which exhibits inconsistent consistency across different information-theoretic compression bounds. Ultimately, this study contributes valuable insights and benchmarks the performance of different image compression tools, highlighting their distinct characteristics, and provides practical guidelines for using the "most click" parameter as a metric for evaluating consistency. This is achieved by transforming it into an minimization problem that can be efficiently solved using an algorithm combining the alternating direction of multipliers and fast Fourier transforms. The continuity constraint is eliminated, allowing for automatic segmentation of areas with smooth and non-smooth borders. Furthermore, we extend this model to handle images with multiple regions by introducing a color-based prior that ensures adjacent regions are part of the same segment. This is realized through a modified function that enforces continuity only within designated areas. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated on various types of images. Within these methods, we evaluate phonon eigenmodes and their corresponding curvatures within the Brillouin zone. Our results show that tetragonal phase phonon systems can become topological in certain cases, with topological phonon ring(s) forming, and we find that photoexcitation can often induce this topological phonon phase. We also discover that band gap engineering for electrons does not always require lattice distortion, and that using light to adjust band gaps is feasible within the tetragonal phase. Furthermore, we find that the phonon band structure of tetragonal phase compounds is highly resilient to temperature variations, with the exception of certain scenarios involving phonon softening. We compare our computational approach with existing theoretical frameworks, and demonstrate that fermion and phonon interactions can lead to phonon band mixing, with the extent of this mixing dependent on electron-phonon coupling intensity. We also observe that tetragonal and orthorhombic phase phonon systems display similarities, with notable differences appearing in orthorhombic phase compounds with phonon band mixing. We find that tetragonal and orthorhombic phase phonon systems can often be distinguished based on their phonon band gap sizes, with the Tetragonal phase showing larger phonon band gaps than the orthorhombic phase. Using theoretical models, we have identified a general principle: when a system exhibits topological phonon band gap formation due to curvature, it will have phonon band gaps forming near its boundary in the Brillouin zone. Close approaches between a neutral atom and a mirror significantly influence photon emission rates due to the atom's motion. This is attributed to two main factors. One reason is that the atom's orbit relative to the mirror can establish long-lasting dipole moments. The expectation value of this dipole moment can directly contribute to photon emission rates. The second factor arises from the atom's motion in the mirror's vicinity, causing correlations between optical electric fields and the atom's position. This, in turn, leads to additional photon emission. However, in scenarios involving thin mirrors, an important factor has been overlooked in evaluating these correlations and their impact on photon emission rates. Specifically, the atom's interaction with mirror charges is ignored, particularly when the atom comes close to the mirror's surface. To address this, we developed an exact method for calculating photon emission rates due to the atom's motion in mirror-atom systems, including narrow mirrors. Our analysis shows that in some cases, the commonly used Merzbacher formula needs to be revised due to the neglected correlation effect. Furthermore, for applications involving mirror-atom systems, where the atom-mirror potential may be crucial, we suggest an alternative approach that is comparable in complexity to the Merzbauer method. Our research is primarily confined to mirror-atom systems, but the concepts and calculations presented are also applicable to other scenarios involving electromagnetic drives. The findings reveal that in mirror-atom systems, the atom-mirror potential significantly influences photon emission rates in some cases. However, in other scenarios, such as in narrow mirrors, the Merzbauer method's predictions remain accurate. The calculated rates also suggest that achieving single-phonon sensitivity with high-charge mirrors is feasible. However, to attain single-photon sensitivity, sophisticated techniques such as enhancing atomic excitations through interactions with a cavity or employing highly nonlinear mirrors with large multipole moments may be necessary. The research into mirror-atom correlations also sheds light on the interplay between electromagnetic drives and quantum paradoxes such as the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen and Aharonov-Bohm effects. To address this, we developed a model to calculate photon emission rates due to the atom's motion in a mirror-atom system, using the Wigner distribution function. Our analysis shows that in some cases, the atom's angular momentum plays a pivotal role, and conventional methods need to be revised. Enforcing neighborhood fairness in graph representation learning has tangible implications, both for the quality of the representations produced and the overall task accuracy. While neighborhood preservation techniques are crucial for understanding graph structures, they must also be fair when it comes to handling node attributes. This research investigates ways to make the graph enrichment process fair by addressing all forms of unfairness, with a focus on satisfying a comprehensive fairness condition for learned node representations. Key contributions include: (1) a mathematical proof that meeting the fairness condition guarantees improved accuracy for a range of downstream tasks, (2) a fair binary regression model that demonstrates a precise and comprehensive fairness condition, (3) a general fairness condition for any node representation method that offers asymmetrical fairness guarantees, and (4) a detailed analysis of fair graph convolutional networks in relation to accuracy, fairness, and attribute sensitivity. This work provides a foundational understanding of fair node representation learning and sets the stage for developing more sophisticated methods in the future. The research also introduces novel metrics to measure fairness, an area where existing methods fall short. The findings suggest that achieving fair node representations comes with an unavoidable trade-off, but a careful design of graph convolutional networks can strike a balance between fairness and accuracy. We've introduced a versatile approach to modeling driven quantum systems that reach a steady state. This framework assembles multiple Fock states into a coherent state, using a driver tailored to the system's equilibrium. By transforming the Schrödinger equation into an Heisenberg equation, we derived an analytical equation defining the multi-coherent state, made up of various Fock states and a set of amplitudes that correlate with the system's steady-state characteristics. This formulation enables explicit calculations and has been applied to a binary Kerr cavity driven by a laser. We demonstrate that our method effectively identifies key features of the system's equilibrium, including occupation numbers, Heisenberg operators, and the relationship between photon numbers and coherent amplitude. Moreover, we show that the amplitudes associated with states near the system's equilibrium can be employed to calculate correlations between these states as well as their cumulative performance. This approach offers substantial computational advantages, enabling the determination of system properties, correlation functions, and circuit-level performance without directly solving the Schrödinger equation. Our research reveals that interactive review components, such as counterarguments and examples, influence purchasers' decisions and can significantly impact public debate. To incorporate interactive elements into recommender systems, we've developed a model that separates interactive features from textual ratings and aggregates them with textual ratings to predict item quality. Experimental results on both a synthetic dataset and a real-world dataset show that our model yields higher accuracy and boosts review utilization from around 5% to up to 35%. Moreover, our research indicates that interactive features can be used to improve reviews by merging complementary perspectives, making our model a useful precursor for both recommender system developers and reviewers seeking enhanced feedback. While computer-based systems have become adept at synthesizing code-switching language data, the synthesized outputs often differ from authentic language inputs. To enhance the quality of such inputs, we propose a new method that replaces entire segments rather than individual words. Our research demonstrates that the code-switching synthesis algorithm produces statements with a greater authenticity when longer segments are replaced. Consequently, we suggest modifying the synthesis approach to incorporate segment replacement, in addition to existing fidelity enhancements. Evaluating the proposed method on three distinct CS tasks -- CS classification, CS classification with limited training data, and CS classification with limited test data -- reveals its superiority. Specifically, it achieves higher accuracy rates compared to the baseline, averaging around 4.5% improvement in Bleu scores across various evaluation sets. Furthermore, it increases the system's robustness when encountering out-of-domain test data, resulting in an average improvement of nearly 10%. Importantly, it brings the synthesized data closer to actual user inputs, increasing the model's authenticity by an average of 13%. The enhanced model's applicability is also substantiated by the fact that it can be easily integrated with existing code-switching synthesis models, necessitating minimal training data. Overall, our research provides the first evaluation of segment replacement in code-switching synthesis and highlights its potential as a generalizable technique for current and future code-switching synthesis models. The technique's adaptability across tasks and datasets is exemplified through our provided experiments, as well as additional comparisons with real CS data. By integrating the segment replacement technique, the model achieves an average Bleu score overlap of 65.16% with human-generated CS sentences, as derived from the Google Translate API. This score represents a notable enhancement from the baseline, averaging 49.22% -- a 15.94% increase. To facilitate future applications, we make our dataset, code, and synthesized data points that include segment replacements, available for public access.
