In computational literature, meshes are commonly referred to as the essential components of computational models that enable operators to solve partial differential equations efficiently. A mesh consists of discrete elements that facilitate the approximation of operators, with results demonstrating a linear dependency on mesh quality. Consequently, the accuracy of computational outcomes is greatly affected by the quality of each individual mesh element. Mesh high-quality determination is a complex task involving the balancing of multiple aspects, such as ensuring mesh domains cover the required space and the boundaries conform to geometric specifications. Furthermore, the connectivity of mesh elements needs to be consistent with underlying physical laws, with adjacent elements forming compatible shapes. Considering the significance of mesh quality for computational outcomes, considerable research has been invested in assessing mesh quality. Specifically, research has focused on defining and evaluating mesh quality through established criteria such as maximum element metrics. However, there is a lack of information regarding the incorporation of refractivity information into these criteria. This study proposes a novel method that modulates an adaptive mesh refinement process using refractivity information, with the objective of optimizing refractioned area mesh quality. An algorithm that modifies an adaptive mesh refinement process by incorporating refractivity information has been developed and tested on simulated data, including a simulated plane wave passing through a 10% refractive medium, demonstrating improved mesh quality through reduced interface element placement and minimal material interface element placement. Notably, the objective function modification allows for reduced interface element placement near material interfaces for all test cases. The proposed method has the potential to improve the accuracy of operator results by ensuring high-quality mesh formation. The method's performance can be further improved by implementing a comprehensive cost function that considers all material interface elements and incorporates secondary variables, with the potential for reduced operator approximation errors due to reduced element size. An optimized mesh refinement method has been demonstrated on all test cases, with significantly improved mesh quality, demonstrating its effectiveness and usability. An example of the method's effectiveness on a simulated data showing a 158.7% increase in I(t) has been illustrated. Knowledge graphs link prediction serves as a connection between relation extraction and knowledge graphs, where links representing relation instances are anticipated between already identified subject and object entities.  A major challenge in link prediction lies in its requirement for large-scale analysis of relation types, where each type is regarded as discrete and separate from others, despite many sharing similar characteristics. Traditional methods that tackle separate relation types independently, fail to recognize shared relations. However, a conventional link prediction model, Structural Similarity (SS), developed by Microsoft, Research, is capable of learning from numerous relation types and recognizing patterns common to many, acknowledging that all these relations share general structural characteristics. Currently, the widespread application of SS remains limited to a handful of large relation types, mainly due to issues related to scalability. Our study begins by analyzing the reasons for SS's limited scope and addresses these challenges one by two. Firstly, it's essential to decrease SS's computational complexity to process numerous relation types. Our second contribution involves leveraging SS-learned features across various tasks to transfer knowledge from prominent relation types to less prominent ones, effectively dealing with a large number of relation types on a smaller scale. Our study makes the following key contributions: We introduce an approach to decrease SS's computational complexity for link prediction, subsequently demonstrating the method's capability to process numerous relation types. Furthermore, we present an innovative transfer learning technique, applying knowledge from prominent relation types to less prominent ones, effectively utilizing knowledge on a larger scale. Our evaluation processes demonstrate that the techniques we proposed are capable of successfully addressing link prediction across numerous relation types with high accuracy. They have been integrated into the SS model, enabling the model to effectively apply learned features across various relation types, while reducing SS's computational complexity to handle a large number of relation types. Our study makes the SS code and features openly available for further analysis. Our study's findings indicate that SS features combined with the knowledge transfer method achieve an MRR score of 0.1633 on the FB15K-2 million benchmark. They even surpasses MRR scores of the top link prediction models on the FB15K-2 million benchmark by 0.0053 and 0.0112, respectively. Design centers utilizing Monte Carlo analyses rely on delay models that predict the timing of digital circuits. Traditional delay models, like those used in SPICE simulations, are often inaccurate due to the complexities of modern circuits. An emerging analytical delay model offers a reliable alternative, providing a straightforward equation for predicting signal delay in standard cells. We evaluate this new model, analyzing its performance across a diverse set of 65nm open-standard standard cells and finding it accurately reflects the behavior of more sophisticated SPICE simulations within 4% error. As such, it holds significant potential for enhancing the efficiency of digital circuit design. An open-source implementation of this model is available for free download at https://github.com/AdaptiveTechChip/newNMOSANADelayModel. We investigate the model's limitations and outline areas for future enhancement. The new analytical delay model offers a valuable resource for designers, offering a substantial 66x speed improvement over SPICE simulations while maintaining comparable accuracy. We anticipate this model to significantly aid low-power design centers, enabling the exploration of new design spaces and optimization techniques. An example case study detailing power optimization utilizing this model is featured in Section6. Further details on the model's implementation and the testbench used to evaluate its accuracy are provided in Appendix A and B, respectively. We also provide a brief overview of the underlying theory and a concise representation of the circuit topology in Appendix C and D, respectively. The new analytical delay model has the potential to alleviate many of the timing closure issues commonly encountered during circuit design. In the analysis presented here, we identify instances where the model may not accurately predict circuit timing, providing insight into areas for further refinement. We outline a multitude of potential applications for this new analytical model in Section8. The research is further enabled by the Adaptive Technology for Efficient Digital Circuits (ATEDC) facility, a cutting-edge research center focused on developing energy-efficient digital circuits. The findings presented here are also significant to the previously proposed analytical delay model, identifying areas for further enhancement and providing guidance for future developments. The research is open-access, facilitating seamless interaction with the research community. Machine learning advancements in complex continuous domains have been led by Deep Reinforcement Learning strategies, which have learned to play highly skilled video games and control intricate robotic arms. Yet, applying off-the-shelf reinforcement learning methods directly to multi-armed bandit problems with continuous actions results in overly exploratory behavior, leading to subpar performance in comparison to specialized techniques. This paper presents a novel approximation technique for estimating the posterior probability density of reward functions, which enables learning to predict optimal policies efficiently in high-dimensional spaces. We introduce a measure of function smoothness based on the stochastic gradient variance across a K-Nearest-Neighbors sample, which serves as a key component for updating the Gaussian process model. Utilizing Stochastic Gradient Descent, this method scales efficiently while yielding accurate posterior estimates. We evaluate the proposed method in a variety of scenarios, including learning to predict optimal policies and achieving state-of-the-art results in direct reinforcement learning settings, where available. We further provide online personal reward function learning results, demonstrating the potential for real-time adaptation to changing environments. We compare the proposed approach, named Smoothing, against existing Gaussian Process regression-based reward imputation techniques and find it effectively replicates the performance of state-of-the-art direct reinforcement learning methods, which learn to predict optimal policies and achieve relative improvements of up to 38% in comparison to the baseline. Furthermore, Smoothing retains the ability to adapt to changing environments in a real-time setting. Smoothing's source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/dmvgk/smooth_gaussian_process/tree/main/smoothing. We believe that Smoothing has the potential to enhance reinforcement learning and direct learning of optimal policies by providing an efficient approximation of the posterior reward density. Off-policy optimization experiments are currently in progress and will be added in a future update. Results from these off-policy optimization experiments will be shared once completed. We introduce a novel structure-preserving filter (SPF) that maintains the exact conservation properties of partial differential equations (PDEs) when applied to data obtained from higher-order polynomial approximations. Unlike previous approaches, our SPF is formulated as a constrained optimization problem with a cost function that minimizes discrepancies between the desired exact solution and the polynomial-based approximation. This results in a side-step of known issues related to polynomial-based simulations, such as incorrect mass or energy conservation due to integer rounding. Our SPF is represented as a large underdetermined linear system, whose solution yields a filtered array that conserves desired quantities exactly, with optional application to multiple fields. Furthermore, the SPF is compatible with a wide variety of conservative PDE systems, including linear and nonlinear equations, as well as systems with diadic or cross-diffusive terms. Notably, the SPF takes advantage of the exact conservation property of conservative discretization methods, leading to a straightforward formulation. We showcase the SPF's efficacy in non-overlapping domain boundary condition-based simulations, such as synthetic examples, bio-transport equations, and a thermalwave model involving multiple materials. These examples highlight that while polynomial-based simulations may incur errors due to numerical approximation, the SPF is capable of precisely maintaining desired quantities. Furthermore, the SPF's performance can be further optimized by incorporating data-driven techniques, such as machine learning algorithms. This enables the SPF to improve its performance at maintaining desired quantities during the approximation process, with substantial benefits expected in applications where exact conservation is essential. Additional details and SPF implementations are available at https://github.com/SoPAT-Research/StructurePreservingFiltering. Our detailed analysis of the broad frequency variability in the quiescent superior X-ray state of the black hole X-ray transient, GX 339-464, offers significant insights into the characteristics of the relativistic inflow cluster (RIC) in the hard-intermediate state of this object. Specifically, we identify distinct patterns of variability that coexist with the previously studied low-and intermediate-frequency variability in the soft state. Our observations reveal the coexistence of multiple variability components, each associated with different X-ray emission mechanisms. Notably, in the hard-intermediate state, the low-frequency variability exhibits an elevated amplitude that peaks at 7 Hz, alongside a type C quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) at 7.25 Hz, while an analysis of the Hubble shift of the power spectrum of soft variability in the soft state indicates a type C QPO at 0.7 Hz. Our findings suggest a continuous evolution of various variability components as the source transitions from the hard-intermediate to the soft state. By combining our variability measurements with the FIDO interferometry data, we define the dimensions of the accretion disk in the soft state and show that the broad variability observed in the soft state originates from different regions of the accretion disk. While the low-frequency variability in the soft state appears to originate from the outer accretion flow, the type C QPO in the soft state is likely generated by variability in the inner accretion flow, given its substantially higher frequency. Our analysis implies that the inner accretion flow in the soft state is a hot adiabatic flow with an inflow angle of approximately 45 degrees, which causes the emission from the accretion disk to be be blocked, thereby accounting for the negative correlation between the light curves of the variable component and the broad band, as observed in the soft state. Our findings also demonstrate that the frequency of the type C QPO in black hole X-ray transients is directly proportional to the mass of the compact object. Our analysis of the frequency of the type C QPO in GX 339-464 as a function of the mass of the compact object supports earlier studies indicating that the frequency of the type C QPO in black hole X-ray transients is a black hole mass-dependent phenomenon. Our findings also show that the frequency of the type C QPO in GX 339-464 is proportional to the mass of the black hole, which could provide a new method for estimating black hole masses using multi-transient observations. Focusing on the group average, we introduce the multi-agent maximum cumulative reward as a target for improved outcome evaluation, alongside a reinforcement learning mechanism that aims to maximize this metric. The proposed algorithm operates by incorporating a policy improvement technique based on the maximum cumulative reward, accompanied by a constraint that ensures policy consistency across related agents, thereby facilitating effective transfer learning between various scenarios. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and testing on a multi-agent grid-world, showcasing its ability to enhance empirical results and reduce variance. One recent application of deep neural networks for vibrational spectroscopy involves a transfer learning technique known as one-shot learning. This method trains a model to recognize vibrations from an unknown material simply by analyzing a single sample, typically in a complex environment, and then identifies its spectral pattern within a large database of other materials. In real-world scenarios, we develop customized one-shot learning models tailored to specific experimental conditions, such as using infrared radiation at various temperatures. Additionally, we demonstrate that such a model can easily generalize to diverse conditions, including when analyzing a sample excited by a different photon energy. In a more complex test, we find that the method remains effective even if the spectral analysis is performed on completely different vibrational modes, such as in a Raman experiment as opposed to an infrared one. Furthermore, we show that the model can successfully identify a sample excised from a tumor and analyzed in a Raman experiment, and reconstruct its original infrared spectrum by consulting the spectral patterns of intact tumor tissue and analyzable material. These findings and applications were motivated by a competition at the Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Medicine 2020, where we sought to develop a model for classifying Raman spectra into cancerous and normal materials, and subsequently expanded the scope of possible conditions, including the analysis of specific cancer subtypes, analytes excised but not from normal tissues, and assessed in diverse experimental conditions. In a related, more speculative application, we contemplate the analysis of a spectral pattern collected from an analyte excised but not from a human subject, and demonstrate its effectiveness in constituting a spectrum compatible with the analgesic Diclofenac, although such a scenario is highly unlikely in real-world scenarios. In the near future, we anticipate that neural networks paired with one-shot learning to be a valuable tool in assisting analysts as spectroscopists, analyzers, and clinicians in the analysis of vibrational spectra. In particular, we see a significant role for the method in helping clinicians diagnose rare, but not forgotten, cases, and ultimately pushing the boundaries of what is currently considered as the limit in the analysis of vibrational spectra. This paper introduces a cohomology framework for 2-algebras centered around Lie 2-algebras, extending the work of Boardman and Vogt on Lie algebra homotopy theory and not limited to Lie 2-algebras derived from homotopy groups. The text focuses on the higher cohomology spectrum and K-theory derived from this framework, including computations for the 2-algebras derived from the homotopy groups of spheres and a discussion on the theoretical implications. Additionally, it contains an appendix that outlines Lie 2-algebra representations and generalizations of the Maurer-Cartan equation, as well as a brief overview of key homotopy categories of Lie 2-algebras. Furthermore, it includes relevant comparisons with other similar cohomology frameworks for 2-algebras, such as those developed by Case, Nash, and Tsukamoto. The text concludes by outlining open questions and potential avenues for future research. The work is supplemented by a comprehensive reference list that includes contributions from the diverse research communities involved in the study of these structures. Given the relatively recent emergence of the field as a whole, it is anticipated that this review will play a significant role in shaping its future trajectory. The shape of an object's magnetic field is frequently distorted due to its composition, with fill fractions affecting the measurement of a magnetic field's strength. To rectify the discrepancy between detailed object structures and coarse-grained magnetic field models, we've integrated various scales of solar structures into a new formula for magnetic field strength. By applying this modification to data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager board on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we've found that considering changes in fill fraction across various scales reduces discrepancies in magnetic field strength, particularly during events associated with magnetic reconnection. As a result, our model further validates the role of shocks and arcades in magnetic field strength, providing insight into mechanisms governing magnetic field strength during events such as solar flares and quakes. Our analysis also reveals that adjusting for fill fraction in magnetic field strength helps to explain variations in strength, particularly during dim magnetic fields, matching observations of solar jets and loops. By applying the fill fraction formula to a model of a magnetic field in a small region, we've reproduced observations of a magnetic field in a small region, demonstrating the importance of object structure in magnetic field strength, particularly during events. Published observations indicate that magnetic field strength varies in proportion to area, but our data show that when magnetic field strength is measured per unit area, the relationship becomes more complex. Nonetheless, considering changes in fill fraction across scales in magnetic field strength helps to match observations of magnetic field strength during events, such as when magnetic field line shape changes. A novel model of an smart home's energy management interaction is examined, with multiple homes and the energy grid acting as players in an extensive game. Each home considers the cost of its own unit and other expenses when deciding on setpoints. A central unit, representing the community, is included to account for costs not specific to individual homes. With a central unit present, Nash equilibrium can only be achieved through specific grid offers, requiring new approaches for players to make strategic decisions. However, if the central unit is absent, a detailed algorithm allows computation of Nash equilibrium at grid distribution level. Yet, the problem becomes increasingly complex at lower grid distribution units due to computational complexity and lack of existing solutions. A novel methodology addresses this complexity by transforming the Nash problem into an extensive game with variable payoffs and multi-dimensional actions and strategies. This transformation enables application of reinforcement learning to teach agents how to cooperate and reach Nash equilibrium at various levels of the grid's power distribution structure. Numerical results demonstrate that our method successfully achieves Nash equilibrium in scenarios with and without a central unit. Furthermore, cooperation among consumers significantly lowers energy consumption and social welfare at equilibrium, especially in scenarios without a central unit. Finally, an analysis of cost structures and technology parameters indicates that natural outcomes vary greatly depending on specific conditions. Overall, our method provides valuable insights for extensive game theory applications in smart home energy management. Several factors influence an agent's cooperation; a central unit's presence impacts demand side decision making while grid structure affects an agent's decision to cooperate, leading to multiple possible scenarios. A comprehensive analysis based on these variables is presented to better understand different situations. A lower grid distribution level shows higher variances in social welfare and consumption while reaching Nash equilibrium, regardless of a central unit's presence. A detailed discussion of factors influencing consumption, cost structures, technology, cooperation, cooperation influence, and video analysis are provided in the paper. Diverse charged black string families result from this framework, featuring unique properties such as null energy density, causality violation, and a connection to Einstein's theory, among others. Stability analysis reveals how quantum gravity effects influence three types of charged black strings, primarily affecting the extremal case. Notably, quantum corrections strengthen the requirements for linear stability in non-extremal scenarios, but have the opposite effect in extremal cases. Moreover, continued radiation from the black strings leads to instability in extremal strings in the semi-classical sector, but this effect does not arise in non-extremal cases. All investigated black string types demonstrate similar behavior, with potential implications for their physical representations. Lastly, this research notes the absence of a decaying radiation mode in non-extremal cases, suggesting a non-trivial interpretation of the conserved quantities. Further investigation is necessary to determine the physical implications of these findings. Charging the black strings with both $Q$ and $Q'$ may offer insight into handling the complex theory, given that quantum corrections yield similar values of between $O(1)$ and $O(10)$. The rate of convergence in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for bounded linear operators on a Hilbert space depends on the sequence of time steps. When the spectral gap is present, the convergence rate is $1/t$. However, in its general application without a spectral gap, the convergence rate of past time averages is at best measured as an overestimate of $\log(t)/t$. This paper explores enhanced convergence rates for specific types of self-adjoint semigroups. For a broad class of discrete time Schrödinger operators on an infinite one-dimensional lattice, the convergence of averages is significantly improved, being at most an order of $t^{-1/2}$ in logarithmic terms. Similarly, we apply similar findings to a broadened class of uniformly elliptic diffusion operators defined on compact manifolds, including cases where the diffusion coefficient is zero. These diffusion operators cover the situations where the underlying manifold is an infinite one-dimensional loop or a compact surface with negative curvature. All of these improved convergence rates can be utilized as part of a strategy to introduce determinantal processes as limits of Gibbs measures, achieved through a generalized version of the BGK construction. This new method combines a transformation inspired by the BGK method with a conventional ergodic averaging, allowing for a control of the resulting errors that remains optimal in the case of zero diffusion. Furthermore, we show that our findings based on discrete-time Schrödinger operators apply directly to the half-space models for the KPZ equation. Consequently, the improved convergence rates for Schrödinger operators translate to the half-space models, yielding a significantly enhanced rate for time averages in the context of the KPZ equation. This new rate is at most an order of $t^{-1/2}$ in logarithmic terms. Similarly, we explore enhanced convergence rates for space-time averages, being at most an order of $t^{-1/2} \cdot (1 + t/T)$. For sufficiently large values of $T$, the order of $T$ can be substituted in place of the order of $t$. This new rate is at most an order of $T^{-1/2}$. Similarly, we apply similar findings to an improved version of Erdős-Schlein-Varadhan's transport estimate. This new estimate claims that for sufficiently large values of $T$, the rate of convergence for space-time averages of the work term in the Erdős-Schlein-Varadhan transport formula is an order of $T^{-1/2}$. We performed an investigation to determine whether active fire counts within various climate zones and countries had undergone any change over time. The analysis focused on five distinct fire seasons (the number of seasons varied by country): Australia during 2007-2008, Europe and Russia during 2010, North America during 2017, and South America during 2016. We utilized geostatistical analysis, specifically the Moran's I statistic, to analyze georeferenced active fire data from multiple countries. The results showed that the number of active fires had demonstrated an increase during certain fire seasons. Specifically, the southern regions of Australia experienced a significant rise in active fire counts. Conversely, the results showed a decline in active fire counts within Russia. Furthermore, the analysis revealed that the southern regions of Europe had previously exhibited a decrease in active fire counts but this trend had reversed in 2010, while the analysis of multi-seasonal data for North America and southern South America showed a positive correlation between consecutive fire seasons. The analysis yielded the following I values: Australia's southern region (0.73), Europe's southern region (0.0), Russia's northern region (-0.46), Russia's southern region (0.44), North America (0.22), and southern South America (0.29). The results suggested a mixed outlook for the countries in our study. The increases in active fire counts within Australia's southern regions and southern Europe could potentially be attributed to climate change, while the rise in active fire counts within Russia's southern region may be linked to past episodes of drought. By contrast, the declines in active fire counts within Russia's northern regions and Europe's southern regions were likely caused by rises in precipitation and reduced fire risks. The low I values for North America and southern South America indicated no correlation between consecutive fire seasons in these regions. In summary, the analysis provided valuable country-specific insights that went beyond general correlations between climate variables and active fire counts. Consequently, the proposed approach may be employed as an independent indicator in active fire forecasts. The increasing active fire counts within Australia's southern regions and southern Europe during high fire seasons served as a warning of potential ignition risks in these regions. By identifying regions with increased active fire counts, fire authorities may initiate early interventions to prevent devastating blazes. The decreases in active fire counts within Russia's northern regions and Europe's southern regions during high fire seasons served as a signal for fire authorities to relax restrictions. This research investigates the performance of reduced models for parametric partial differential equations, specifically focusing on sparse grids. We evaluate various observation operators for several benchmark problems and find that the efficacy of model reduction is heavily influenced by the choice of these operators. We examine several strategies for adapting the sparse grids method to accommodate non-periodic problems and combine it with the Bayesian inversion approach to generate informative grids for nonlinear problems. Essential insights into the limitations of sparse grids method and its future improvement are obtained. Furthermore, we assess the Bayesian inversion approach and identify its shortcomings, particularly the slow convergence and failure to reach convergence for nonlinear problems. We suggest merging Bayesian inversion with multi-fidelity techniques to create an auxiliary variable, thus facilitating the application of Bayesian inversion to nonlinear problems. We also introduce the sampling gradient method, a more efficient technique that employs multi-fidelity approaches to approximate unknown solutions. The sampling gradient method and its adaptation to multi-fidelity problems are evaluated, providing evidence of its superiority over Bayesian inversion for both linear and nonlinear problems and the significant influence of the observation operator on its performance. The computational efficiency and accuracy of the sampling gradient method and sparse grids are compared, highlighting their contrasting strengths and weaknesses. Ultimately, the sampling gradient method is shown to be a promising approach to accelerating multi-fidelity optimization problems. This research introduces the m-ar-K function as a modified approach to the well-known ar-K function, incorporating a specific parameter m. The m-ar-K function serves as a lower-dimensional counterpart to Riemannian distance and can be utilized for dimensionality reduction, similar to the ar-K function. However, the addition of parameter m enables the m-ar-K function to be tailored to maintain higher spectral elasticity compared to the ar-K function. As a result, the m-ar-K function can be designed to retain a higher proportion of the original distance information when transformed down to a lower dimensionality, making it well-suited for visualization purposes. Furthermore, the incorporation of the parameter m allows for the development of an inverse mapping that can reconstruct the original high-dimensional points with enhanced precision. To illustrate the m-ar-K function's capabilities, a dataset consisting of 1,579 3D mesh models of human lungs was utilized, with both visualization and inverse mapping results being successfully accomplished. The source code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/20220225ChienChen/m_ar_K. Non-Gaussianity is an essential property for various quantum technologies, yet a challenge in studying it involves identifying when its presence causes subsystems to exhibit negativity in Wigner functions. We address this by investigating how to link Wigner negativity in a subsystem to joint quantum correlations in two-party non-Gaussian states. We specifically focus on Glauber-Sudarshan representations and the specific form of non-Gaussian states describable by Fock expansion. We derive conditions confirming that all other forms of quantum correlations cannot cause Wigner negativity in a subsystem when shared as a non-Gaussian state, thus implying the significance of non-Gaussianity. We also illustrate the relevance of our findings to experiments using twin photons produced in spontaneous parametric down-conversion, which demonstrate that even though these correlations exhibit high negativity in Wigner functions, they lack mutual information due to lacking Gaussian quantum correlations. By leveraging these results, we outline how to improve the performance of estimators in phase estimation using non-Gaussian states drawn from Squeezed-Coherent ensembles, thereby enhancing sensitivity compared to similar states drawn from Standard-Coherent ensembles. Moreover, we show that all other states drawn from Standard ensembles have similar performance to those drawn from Squeezed-Coherent ensembles. We further explore how to exploit the non-Gaussianity of twin photons in down-conversion for improved robustness to noise while preserving the estimators' precision, thereby enabling more reliable simulations of Standard-Canonical distributions. We also derive an algorithm for producing Wigner negativity in a subsystem in parallel with preserving the lack of mutual information, thus allowing a reliable simulation of quantum evolution in systems with Gaussian environments. We name this the "Noise-Noise cancellation" algorithm. In addition, we show that noise cancellation happens optimally when the noise is added in the phase space and not in the physical Hilbert space, thereby validating an existing proposal with our theoretical framework. Lastly, we leverage our findings to identify key attributes necessary for a "quantum advantage" in the quantum information processing from non-Gaussian states, thereby establishing criteria for detecting quantum non-classicity based on Standard-Canonical distributions rather than Glauber-Sudarshan expansions, thereby significantly decreasing the required number of terms to detect it. We also show that the quantum non-classicity can be detected for any number of modes using the Wigner function, whereas the same cannot be said for the Standard distribution. The Bertrand curve is one of the constant curvature curves in 3-dimensional space. It's known that a Bertrand curve can be definitely identified in spaces with non-symmetric products of Lie groups or nilpotent Lie groups, and this research further expands that to more general symmetric spaces. By examining the differential characteristics of the Bertrand curve in Euclidean spaces, spherical three-dimensional spaces, and hyperbolic three-dimensional spaces, we establish a method to definitely identify Bertrand curves in these spaces. Additionally, we develop an algorithm using the Chern-Rund differential equations to identify the curve's higher derivatives from a given tangent vector in these spaces. By comparing the original curve and the derived tangent vector, we determine if the original is a Bertrand curve. If the original is a Bertrand curve, we continue to derive higher derivatives. This research further utilizes the obtained information to differentiate the Laplace operator, curvatures, and Ricci curvature in these spaces. This process is thought to have been influenced by the clusters' distinct locations and interactions with their surroundings during galactic mergers and interactions. A key issue at the moment lies in identifying the specific conditions and timing of these interactions and their impact on the formation and development of the clusters over their lifetime. This study aims to gain insight into these clusters' history and development by examining the variations in abundance ratios of key elements within 14 globular clusters. The analysis of the clusters' net and excess abundances not only confirms existing patterns but also reveals new and more nuanced trends, suggesting the clusters' formation and development were complex and varied. This complexity is thought to have resulted from different levels of dwarf galaxy involvement in galactic mergers and interactions, with clusters belonging to thicker clusters groups exhibiting more pronounced abundance variations. This could imply these clusters either merged with other galactic clusters at a later stage or were formed during separate episodes of star formation. The variations in the metal-line absorption within galactic bulge clusters also suggest the presence of two distinct populations of metal-rich and metal-poor stars. The former group's origins are thought to date back to 5-7 billion years, coinciding with galactic bulge formation, while the latter's origins are believed to date back to 7-12 billion years, during earlier phases of galactic formation and development. Furthermore, the study's analysis suggests the galactic formation and development were marked by the emergence of multiple supermassive stars, whose core collapse during the galactic dark ages influenced the galactic metal enrichment and the development of the galactic globular clusters. Previous experiments revealed a disparity between the expected and observed flux reduction, depending on the hydrogen pressure inside the cell. A particular correlation arose at a pressure of 0.79 Torr, where the measured reduction significantly diverged from the molecular model's predictions. In an attempt to explain this phenomenon, the cell's walls were coated with polycrystalline copper, introducing tiny copper atoms into the cell's pressure calibrating system. It is suggested that the imperfections in the cell's walls, such as holes and scratches, allow a small fraction of copper atoms to escape and mix with the main hydrogen gas, thereby explaining the observed disparity using a mixture of hydrogen and copper atoms rather than pure hydrogen. The rising availability of computing resources cannot resolve the main problem of distributed control systems, which is the excessive communication required to achieve stability. Recent advancements in wireless communication have made available a diverse array of transmission mediums with variable qualities that can be exploited to minimize communication costs. However, managing these tradeoffs necessitates a comprehensive evaluation of the system's performance and communication costs. To address this need, we establish a framework that establishes a lower limit on the overall system performance for a wide range of distributed control systems. This proof shows that even with unstable designs, the overall system can achieve a stable equilibrium. Furthermore, we investigate how to optimize the balance between communication costs and performance outcomes, and provide an analytical expression for determining achievable tradeoffs. This expression confirms that there exists a critical point representing the optimal tradeoff between communication costs and performance outcomes. Moreover, we show that designs which achieve this critical point are stable and optimal in a wide class of distributed control systems. This proof also validates these findings by showing that the Tico algorithm, which was previously thought to be the best available design, is capable of reaching the critical point. Finally, we illustrate how to incorporate additional constraints on video streams into the system design, which involves designing a network with a quality of service capability that matches the requirements of each video source. This investigation demonstrates that the resulting system is stable and capable of meeting all its quality of service goals. We also show that the desired level of separation between streams can be attained, and the desired levels of bandwidth and delay can be met for each stream. We demonstrate the additional requirements for each stream are characterized by a critical amount of separation between streams, a critical amount of separation between the video frames of each stream, a critical amount of separation between the decoding times of each stream, and a critical amount of separation between the encoding times of each stream, which are all dependent on the bandwidth of the transmission mediums. We also show that the desired level of separation between streams can be attained when the bandwidth is greater than a certain threshold. Conversely, when the bandwidth is less than the certain threshold, the separation between the decoding times of each stream is the most limiting factor in meeting the desired level of separation between streams. In order to provide practical implementations of these findings, we present two algorithms, which are the outcomes of extensive computational experiments designed to identify optimal designs. Our innovative solution for image copy detection employs an integrated approach combining both passive and active indexing techniques. This two-stage method enhances the resilience to image manipulation detected by passive indexing and elevates the overall detection rate. The proposed technique represents a versatile tool applicable across diverse scenarios characterized by varying degrees of image transformations and also extends to detection across multiple images. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using a large dataset of 1 million images harvested from the internet and compare its performance with existing state-of-the-art solutions. Results obtained on standard indices indicate that our technique matches or surpasses the detection rate of leading competitors while showcasing superior robustness against common image editing tools. Furthermore, we highlight the potential for further improvement by leveraging more advanced deep learning-based algorithms for enhanced performance. With proper tuning, our indexing technique can be optimized to accommodate a wide range of applications including multi-image and cross-domain detection. The proposed solution represents a scalable and efficient long-term viable alternative to existing image detection methods. The code and dataset used in this research are available at https://github.com/quant-vi/image-detection. Our study's findings are presented at the ACM Multimedia '22 conference. The research was partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 62172202). A grant from the CFI-JARI funded the creation of the benchmark dataset used in this research. Our innovative solution has real-world implications in diverse application areas such as image protection, news content verification, and video compression, among others. The technology has practical value in domains including social media, news, commerce, healthcare, and video production where image detection is a crucial requirement. The efficiency of our indexing technique allows it to process 1 million images in approximately 180 hours using 64 machines equipped with 64 GPUs. The innovative solution developed allows it to handle complex image transformations detected by passive indexing and also extends to detection across multiple images, thereby significantly enhancing the detection rate and robustness of existing solutions. The new technique represents an essential component of a complete image protection system addressing a wide range of challenges including image manipulation, multimedia search, and compression. The innovative solution allows it to detect images that have been manipulated using an image compression program as well as images copied multiple times. The new technique represents an essential tool for addressing a long list of critical issues including image piracy, multimedia search, news content fraud, and compression, among others. The innovative solution underscores the significance of addressing multimedia security in the context of across domain and multi-image detection as well as manipulating images that have been previously compressed. Automatic document summarization is the process of condensing lengthy documents into concise, bird's-eye versions via a computer algorithm. This framework employs a proprietary generator that utilizes a unique I-Structure to represent and organize sentence importance. This I-Structure is then refined via a context-aware allocator, which distributes, or allocates, sentences to maintain a well-structured summary. Notably, our approach diverges from the conventional method of using sentence extraction from original documents, thereby ensuring that only pertinent information is incorporated and redundant information is minimized, ultimately enhancing summary quality. The GAE-ISumm model outperformed prior models in several evaluating metrics, as demonstrated on standard document summarization datasets. Further visual analysis of the results revealed that, in contrast to prior models, the GAE-ISumm model effectively resolved key subtasks such as cohesion, structure, and sparsity in the generated summaries. Therefore, the GAE-ISumm model represents an innovative advancement in the field of automatic document summarization. A Variational Autoencoder (VAE) is a type of unsupervised learning model that
balances two key aspects: a Gaussian distribution for the latent space and
a specific distribution for the visible data. While the goal is to strike a
balance between these opposing desires, standard training methods typically
lack explicit rewards for doing so. Instead, we propose a new method,
Differentially Regularized Variational Autoencoder (DRVAE), that employs
different forms of regularization within the variational distribution.
This approach not only provides a more explicit incentive for maintaining the
desired distribution but also enables the incorporation of multiple,
diverse distributions for the latent space, resulting in more stable training.
Furthermore, we suggest employing a more sophisticated prior for the
latent space, one that is composed of multiple Gaussian distributions,
each with distinct means and covariances. This prior can be sampled from
in conjunction with the variational distribution, thereby allowing DRVAE
to model complex multimodal data while avoiding mode coverage problems.
As such, we provide explicit control over the sampling of priors and
demonstrate that our method can effectively tackle challenging tasks,
such as image creation and manipulation, including generating images of
different styles and creating images from scratch. Since DRVAE uses different
forms of regularization and employs a more sophisticated prior and sampler,
it exhibits better performance in terms of both learning and sampling. In
particular, it yields a more realistic representation of the data,
capturing its underlying structure and correlations in the process. Additionally,
our method offers the explicit control that is typically associated with
sampling from a prior, while also enabling the learning of complex data
that may exhibit multiple modes. We utilize a comprehensive suite of tests
to validate the DRVAE, including both qualitative and quantitative
evaluations, as well as adversarial testing in conjunction with Wasserstein
GANs (WGAN) and GAN-based adversarial testing. All of the source code for

A cost-effective and efficient technique known as RSSI-based trilateration is frequently employed in smart home systems for tracking objects or specific devices. Although this method is easily implemented and inexpensive, it requires analyzing the complexities of radio signal propagation to accurately calculate the tag's location. Our research reveals that RSSI values are significantly influenced by how radio signals are received, and different received signal strength is generated across varying data transmission rates. We explore the possibilities of using various data transmission rates in trilateration systems to enhance localization accuracy. Our experiment finds that enabling multiple data rates allows us to achieve more precise tagging without needing additional hardware. Our proposed method, which incorporates the average received signal strength across multiple frequencies, can achieve localization errors of around 4 square meters, making it suitable for applications like home automation. Our statistical analysis shows that using multiple frequencies is more effective in creating multiple possible tag locations than using a single frequency. Our simple hardware modification allows us to use any available data transmission rate, making our solution versatile. Our comparison of localization error using different approaches highlights the advantages of employing multiple frequencies in trilateration systems. Our simple framework, which combines multiple frequencies, can serve as a foundation for developing location-based services. Our research suggests that smart home localization systems utilizing RSSI-based trilateration should employ multiple frequencies to achieve accurate tagging, and our solution is versatile and compatible with various location-based services applications. Our work provides valuable insights into localizing objects or specific devices using RSSI-based trilateration in smart home systems. Our framework is transferable to other indoor localization systems, such as those based on sensor fusion or vision-based systems. Our research sheds light on the potential for using multiple frequencies to achieve accurate tagging or tracking. Our work is valuable to developers, architects, and engineers working on smart home localization services, providing practical information on trilateration system configuration and error analysis to inform design choices. Our research offers a foundation for investigating new techniques and developing new ideas related to location-based services in smart home systems. Our work could be extended to explore the potential of using multiple frequencies in trilateration systems, and our simple hardware modification can serve as a base for implementing different techniques. Our research provides practical information on error analysis, system configuration, and hardware modification that can inform designers' choices. Our work provides valuable insights into trilateration system configuration and can serve as a base for implementing location-based services in smart home systems. Our research explores new techniques for developing smart home localization services and highlights the importance of considering location-based service designs for different application requirements.

This paper introduces a new and efficient method of zeroth-order compression for remote service applications, where a parameterized model is updated on the fly after each interaction between the client and server. Known approaches for compressing the model involve iteratively refining subset versions, each with fewer parameters, until a quantized model is reached that accurately replicates the results of the original parameterized model. The key innovation of our approach is Suboptimal Basis Pursuit, a novel quantization technique that substitutes information about optimal quantization and suboptimal compression when available. We demonstrate that our Suboptimal Basis Pursuit, which incorporates a zeroth-order gradient scheme, yields results comparable to state-of-the-art methods like Maximum Mutual Information, whereas incorporating compression information significantly reduces computation time. We showcase the effectiveness of our Suboptimal Basis Pursuit in various applications such as remote sparse linear regression and a remote vectorized embedding device. When applied to remote sparse linear regression, our approach accelerates the compression process by 2.72 times while maintaining 99.4% accuracy, trained with 5% data. Using the compressed model on a 50 test sample dataset, our results reveal a 39.4% reduction in latency and an 81.6% decrease in server-side computation when compared to uncompressed models. Applying our approach to the remote vectorized embedding device, which requires 128 dimensions, resulted in a 98.6% accuracy and a 5.13 times speedup after just 10 iterations, exhibiting negligible latency and computation. To facilitate easier implementation, a Python library called PyCompress is provided, containing the proposed compression methods, along with a range of pre-existing models. Neural networks' resilience despite imperfect labeling arises from leveraging an ensemble of models, which can be interpreted as a voting system. However, calculating the posterior distribution in Bayesian neural networks proves challenging due to the lack of analytical solutions, prompting the use of numerical approximation techniques. A recent study employs Monte Carlo sampling and weight tying in convolutional and recurrent networks to derive posterior distribution classification probabilities. Building upon this, the authors improve existing approaches by proposing a novel posterior distribution classification probability formula, which is subsequently tested on simple neural networks and reveals an inherent benefit of ensemble modeling, where neural networks trained on multiple random labeling scenarios achieve higher accuracy than those dealt a single, certain label. The authors also extend this concept to variational autoencoders, where the posterior distribution classification probability is calculated by sampling latent codes and observing the resulting class distributions. An alternative formulation emerges, showing that neural networks trained on multiple random labeling scenarios are equivalent to a single neural network trained on the aggregated posterior distribution, further illustrating the benefits of ensemble modeling in deep neural networks. A Python implementation of these methods is also provided on the dedicated project website. The researchers' findings are seen through both synthetic experiments and an examination of the ResNet50 model, which is used for image classification but encounters labeling uncertainties during training due to the presence of mislabeled data. The synthetic experiments' results serve as a reminder of the significance of properly accounting for uncertainties in deep learning applications. The study concludes by applying the proposed techniques to the analysis of the ResNet50 model, which encounters uncertainties, leading to the derivation of a significant number of spurious mini-balance posterior distribution classes in the failure cases, as well as an estimation of the test accuracy based on the most frequently occurring class in the posterior distribution, which serves as an indicator of the inherent limitations of neural networks in handling uncertain data. Additionally, we establish a lower bound on the minimum number of required matrices. Given parameters n, m, and k, let B be the least common multiple of {1,...,m}, representing the uniformity constraint. We confirm this lower limit, while a higher bound is given by (n/m)(m/k)^(-k), demonstrating the tightness of the relationship. We investigate a simplified version of a strategic game known as the quantum game, specifically focusing on the CHSH task. When two players participate in the game, each having access to a limited quantity of copies of a bipartite state, their strategy selection is constrained. However, if they can replicate the state without restriction, each player's optimal strategic choice is unaffected, as determined by the state's density operator. When the quantum game's rules allow for the copying of shared bipartite states, the winning probabilities rise. Although methods like search or reinforcement learning have been highly successful in generating crash-inducing input for various bugs, these techniques tend to produce highly complex sequences that significantly exceed the actual triggering payload. Notably, previous studies have overlooked the fact that such techniques can struggle to reproduce previously seen crashes. In particular, our own reinforcement learning method was found to fail in reproducing around 27% of crashes it was trained on. In an effort to address this issue, we introduce a new method called DOMExplore that leverages tree-exploring expert designed using behavioural models. Our expert design approach enables DOMExplore to focus on the most critical parts of the program state and thus effectively reproduce previously seen crashes. In controlled experiments, we found that DOMExplore successfully reproduced around 98% of crashes, outperforming reinforcement learning in generating shorter input trajectories while also improving crash reproduction rates by a substantial 83.9% across a range of crashes. Moreover, our analysis suggests that DOMExplore may be able to take advantage of previously designed exploit patterns, leading to potentially more safe and effective techniques. Research into the anisotropic flow of light hadrons at high energy collisions has provided valuable insight into the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. Analyzing the ratio of second to third flow coefficients can distinguish between different scenarios, such as distinguishing between collision systems and the presence of back-to-back jet pairs. A study using data from the ALICE collaboration found this ratio to be comparable between different energy levels and collision systems, but showed significant variation with multiplicity, indicating a need for theoretical explanation. Moreover, when examining the variation with multiplicity, it was discovered that certain hadron mass segments display distinct patterns, with a notable phenomenon where pseudorapidity, hadron mass, and transverse momentum exhibit opposite trends with multiplicity, and a preliminary indication that this ratio might fluctuate with event configurations existed. Since this ratio is highly sensitive to the anisotropic flow, it offers potential for further exploration to gain knowledge about the quark-gluon plasma. In addition, when comparing to theoretical models such as AMPT and EPOS, it was discovered that EPOS failed to accurately replicate the observed multiplicity patterns, while there was not enough information to thoroughly assess the validity of AMPT. A more in-depth analysis by taking into account the event plane resolution and event centrality was then carried out, which revealed a notable fluctuation correlation between different centrality levels, indicating a need to consider these factors when analyzing the ratio in the future. In conclusion, studying the variation with multiplicity, particularly using this specific ratio, is highly rewarding as it provides valuable insight into the quark-gluon plasma, and further investigation by taking into account factors such as event plane resolution, hadron type, and different energy levels may uncover more detailed properties. Furthermore, a significant ongoing effort is necessary to thoroughly assess the theoretical models due to their significant variation in predicting this ratio. A future measurement using this specific ratio in lower energy levels, particularly with a focus on p-Pb and Pb-Pb collisions, is highly recommended as it has significant theoretical background and expectations that it can thoroughly explore the quark-gluon plasma. In the field of multi-site trial analysis, we aim to implement novel statistical tools to boost the power of identifying a general treatment effect while maintaining control over the false discovery rate. To achieve this, we will leverage existing techniques for combining p-values through a functional of random variables approach, followed by an estimation of false discovery rates using non-consecutive outcomes. Additionally, we will provide methods to calculate adjusted treatment effect estimates based on results from individual trial meta-analysis, as well as unweighted averages of trial-specific treatment effects. We use posterior sampling and Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms to generate sampling distributions for these estimators, allowing for the control of the false discovery rate using existing tools. Our methods' performance is evaluated using simulations of a hypothetical trial examining cognitive function in patients with Alzheimer's disease across 10 different areas. We also present case study results from the data-driven analysis of A011531 trial, examining the effectiveness of ivacaftor in patients with different types of cystic fibrosis genotypes. To facilitate the efficient implementation of these novel statistical tools, we have developed user-friendly R packages, currently available for public use: 'polyBAYES', 'bayesGMT', and 'bayesAND'. Using the existing Bayesian double robust approach, we have extended the 'bayesGMT' package to facilitate the control of the family-wise type I error rate in combination with the functional of random variables method, as well as the control of the false discovery rate in combination with the existing poly-TD method. Using the existing double robust estimation approach from Liu, Li, and Fu, we have extended the 'bayesAND' package to control the false discovery rate in combination with the existing maximum average partial correlation method. We have controlled the false discovery rate using the existing poly-TD correlation estimate, incorporating publicly available R code from the 'WGCNA' package to facilitate the efficient implementation of the existing poly-TD correlation estimate, as well as the estimated partial correlation at default prior settings. We have extended the existing Bayesian double robust approach from Andersson et al. to control the family-wise type I error rate in combination with the existing AND multiple testing method, resulting in the development of the 'polyBAYES' package. Our crowdsourcing study investigates whether concept location, the ability to identify primary sections of code, can be improved by integrating user perspectives. A recently developed metric, the Neural Entrainment Distance (NED), demonstrates strong potential in accurately identifying natural conversations and distinguishing them from artificially generated ones created through text augmentation. This finding presents a new, high-performance approach for evaluating convolutional methods in a completely automated manner, which could have important implications for preventing the spread of misinformation. By assessing conversation authenticity using NED scores, researchers can evaluate the effectiveness of convolutional techniques in creating natural and coherent conversations. This, in turn, can guide the development of improved optimization strategies, potentially leading to better performance in human-like conversation tasks. Building on this discovery, we use NED to compare the ability of various convolutional methods to produce natural and coherent conversations by applying it to two leading frameworks, the ROMPort and TWSSL models, while also testing its limits with a more challenging case involving randomly generated input sequences. The results show that an unsupervised version of the NED metric can accurately detect natural conversations produced by the TWSSL framework, which uses self-supervised learning, significantly outperforming other leading metrics such as the BLEU and SEM scores. Furthermore, when testing the full spectrum of natural and coherent conversations, including those produced by the ROMPort framework, which uses supervised learning, the NED metric demonstrates its ability to distinguish among different classes of conversations and successfully identifies artificially generated conversations produced by random input sequences. These findings demonstrate the superiority of the NED metric in evaluating convolutional methods and predicting the coherence of conversations. They also present new insights into the potential applications of the NED metric in automatically detecting and preventing misinformation. Based on these results, we propose a new framework that leverages the NED metric to develop an innovative convolutional strategy for optimizing natural and coherent conversation tasks across various domains. The framework combines principles from case-based reasoning, self-supervised learning, and semi-supervised optics, allowing it to handle limited labeled data and unsupervised scenarios. Using the TWSSL framework as an example, we demonstrate how our framework can strategically select and manipulate visual inputs to produce natural and coherent conversations by applying the NED metric, which can potentially be extended to other leading frameworks as well. The framework's ability to handle unsupervised and semi-supervised scenarios presents a crucial gap in the current research landscape, which we aim to address. yet its effectiveness relies on the quality of the galaxy spectra.

We explain our findings by acknowledging the limitations of the BPT diagram due to inherent noise,
thereby underscoring the importance of the quality of galaxy spectra in this classification process. 
This discovery has the potential to reduce the reliance on noisy data and employed methods in the future.

Current action parsing methods, which aim to segment and interpret action components, have proven effective, though their accuracy often hinges on the quality of provided video labels and annotated action sequences. To address this limitation, we've developed a Co-occurrence Action Parsing algorithm that uses co-occurring object information to determine context-based action features. Experimental results on a large dataset show significant improvements, with weights learned from an unsupervised co-occurrence network enhancing parsing performance. Additionally, our findings indicate that object-based features significantly contribute to the quality of parsed action components. Overall, our approach represents a promising direction for future work in this domain. We've made our source code available for public access. Testing is an essential skill for university students, particularly in the field of Computer Science. Research suggests that CompStat Labs' Unit Testing tool is effective in educating students, as indicated by preliminary evaluations. To further validate its educational value, a study compared the outcomes of two identical CS1 courses, differing in the way students were introduced to testing: using CompStat Labs' Unit Testing or a traditional method involving grading students' unit tests. By employing Seismic, a tool that analyzes code quality, the study assessed students' learning progress. Preliminary results reveal that, as expected, automated feedback led to better code coverage and enhanced performance. The experience also demonstrated that automated feedback can have a considerable impact on student performance when executed thoughtfully. The success of this approach prompted the development of a testing module for the popular CS education platform, GradeLab. The testing module enables automated feedback and assessment, as well as comprehensive testing of student-submitted code in multiple programming domains. By integrating testing and assessment tools, the development of GradeLab's testing module was accelerated. In some instances of domain adaptation, source data is unavailable or inaccessible, and thus cannot be employed for learning a transferable model. Although some traditional domain adaptation techniques are able to learn without source data by utilizing a target domain alone, such strategies prove ineffective in our proposed scenario of unsupervised single-carbon transfer learning, likely due to overfitting the target domain. In order to tackle this problem, we have developed a regularization-based approach. Our novel method requires training a target domain dataset multiple times, incorporating differentiable regularization terms designed to encumber model parameters that shroud target observations. The carboxylation protein subfamily, being smaller than the larger non-carboxylation subfamily, was chosen for this analysis. Our approach demonstrated notable improvements in performance, as model complexity was substantially diminished. Through ablation studies, it became evident that our proposed technique yields superior performance to related single-carbon and multi-carbon domain adaptation methods, while also significantly reducing model overfitting. The resulting models achieved accurate transformations from single-carbon to non-carboxylation and carboxylation domains, thereby facilitating the prediction of single-carbon information in the carboxylation and non-carboxylation domains. Our proposed method has potential applications in the single-carbon-based transformation of data from multiple subdomains. The source code is available online. To achieve optimal control, RNNs need to infer environment state beliefs from their hidden states. However, traditional RNNs lack a mechanism for expressing uncertainty or beliefs about hidden states. To address this, we introduce topological metrics on hidden states, utilizing geometric graphs to define a Laplace kernel as a transfer kernel. We then show that teaching RNNs with samples from this transfer kernel aids in optimizing hidden states to accurately reflect environment state beliefs. We propose a neural topology learning algorithm to simultaneously train RNN hidden states and their corresponding topological structures. The results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach for inferring environment state beliefs and achieving optimal control. Additionally, we present a novel neural architecture, the Laplace RNN, designed to implement the proposed topology and belief structure. Experimental evaluations validate the improved control performance of this new architecture. This study investigates the behavior of nuclear matter at zero temperature and without magnetic field effects using the relativistic quark-meson model. We analyze the properties of the energy density, the pressure, and spin polarization within the framework of the mean field approximation. Furthermore, we examine the stability of the system by considering its energy density, pressure, and pressure versus energy relationship. We also calculate the quark and meson condensates and assess the stability of the system by looking at the occurrence of spin polarization. We found that the nuclear matter phase diagram exhibits a transition similar to the Bag hadron gas at low densities, whereas at high densities it behaves like a free gas of quarks. Additionally, we discovered that spin polarization occurs in the presence of isospin asymmetric density and that the spin polarization density exhibits a positive value, showing Bag-like behavior at low densities and gas-like behavior at high densities. We also determined the spin polarization density's dependence on the isospin asymmetric ratio and found that it exhibits a linear relationship. We compare our computational methods with variational calculations and obtain comparable results. Finally, we explored the relationship between bag constant and quark condensates in order to assess the stability of the system. We found that the bag constant and quark condensates exhibit variations throughout the phase transition, whereas they resemble Bag properties at low densities and gas properties at high densities. We also found the bag constant and quark condensates to be proportional to each other. We compare our computational methods with existing data and obtain comparable results. Our computational findings are comparable to those obtained using the relativistic Brueckner Hartree-Fock approach. We also computed the phase transition pressure as a function of bag constant and found the former to be in agreement with experimental results. In summary, our computational study using the relativistic quark-meson model to investigate the properties of nuclear matter at zero temperature and without magnetic field effects provides insights into the nuclear phase transition, Bag properties, and gas-like behavior at high densities, as well as the relationship between bag constant and quark condensates. However, we found that the introduction of strange quarks into the model results in the observation of color superconducitivity in the presence of magnetic field effects. This observation highlights the ability of our computational model to capture the properties of a diverse range of particles. In conclusion, our computational study using the relativistic quark-meson model to investigate the properties of nuclear matter at zero temperature and without magnetic field effects provides insights into the complex behavior of this phenomenon

The widespread adoption of Federated Learning can be seen as a form of data compression, allowing for global model updates via aggregated client gradients rather than transferring the entirety of data. Recent studies have identified a connection between this compression technique and Differential Privacy (DP), with DP providing a mechanism to regulate the amount of information shared by participants. Building upon this relationship, we adapt the concept of DP to develop computationally efficient, privacy-preserving FL algorithms that don't require significant modifications to the existing framework. We establish a formal framework for this purpose, providing a comprehensive framework for its implementation as well as a thorough evaluation of its performance. Our findings encompass both theoretical proofs of the algorithm's effectiveness in maintaining data privacy and empirical evaluations of the algorithm's robustness in various scenarios. Our evaluation reveals that the algorithm achieves significant privacy gains while meeting the objectives of efficiency, consistency, and usability. Our analysis further shows that the algorithm's performance is comparable to that of models trained on a centralized dataset, with consistency and usability metrics rivaling those of the centralized approach in many scenarios. Our evaluation of the algorithm's performance across different parameter settings indicates that the algorithm achieves substantial privacy gains at relatively early stages of the training process. We observe that the trade-off between privacy and model accuracy is achievable without compromising accuracy when incorporating the DP mechanism from the beginning of the training process. Our evaluation of the algorithm's performance across different data sizes reveals that the incorporation of the DP mechanism results in minimal loss of accuracy for larger data sizes. Our findings show that the incorporation of the DP mechanism results in a tolerable accuracy loss for smaller data sizes, with the effect diminishing as data sizes increase. Our evaluation of the algorithm's performance across different DP levels reveals that the incorporation of the DP mechanism results in privacy gains across the entire range of privacy levels, with privacy records improving across all scenarios. Our findings show that the incorporation of the DP mechanism results in significantly improved privacy records for horizontal datasets, with significant privacy gains achieved for vertical datasets, while indicating that the incorporation of the DP mechanism results in better privacy records for both horizontal and vertical datasets when compared to previous approaches. Our analysis further reveals that the incorporation of the DP mechanism results in better privacy records for both horizontal and vertical data distribution settings when compared to a prior approach. To facilitate reproducibility, we have made the code used to evaluate the algorithm's performance available on a public repository at https://github.com/quantamediate/DPFL.
