A static filter using a compact in-memory table can effectively prevent false positives while maintaining high memory and speed efficiency. 

Consider a scenario where a stream of data includes a 64-bit address and a 32-bit value, and we want to create a filter that enforces a set of rules based on addresses. One simple way to achieve this is by assigning a 32-bit hash code to each address, and we can store unique hash codes in the filter. 

However, the problem with this approach is that we need to allow multiple hash codes for some addresses, and we want the number of hash codes to be as small as possible. 

Given a set of n positive integers, we want to split them into clusters such that for any i in the first k elements, the number of elements in the i'th cluster is at most bounded by a parameter C. If we can achieve this with a low value of k, we want to develop an algorithm that can efficiently determine the value of k for a given C. 

Using this problem as a building block, we want to develop a linear-time algorithm to determine the value of k for a given C when the input integers are already sorted. 

Furthermore, we can modify the above problem to a graph clustering scenario, and we want to develop an algorithm that can efficiently determine the value of k for a given C when the input graph is sparse. 

Based on this algorithm, we can develop a compact filter that can effectively prevent false positives. One possible application of this algorithm is the prevention of double spending attacks in payment systems, and we can demonstrate that the filter we developed has a high level of efficiency, specifically high memory and speed efficiency. 

To validate the efficacy of our filter, we conducted experiments to measure its memory and speed performance, and we observed that the filter we developed can effectively prevent double spending while maintaining a high level of efficiency, and the performance of the filter we developed is comparable to existing solutions. However, our solution has advantages over existing solutions in specific scenarios, and we observed that the filter we developed can significantly improve the false positive rate of existing solutions when the number of transactions per second is relatively low. 

One possible limitation of our solution is that the efficiency of the filter we developed may degrade over time, and we observed a linear relationship between the time efficiency and memory requirements. However, the filter we developed can achieve a high level of efficiency and memory requirements, and we observed that the filter we developed can achieve a high level of accuracy for a wide range of parameters.

Using an average-field approach based on the stochastic mean-field method, we study the pendulum model with atom-molecule conversion, which is analogous to a quantum system that experiences wetting transitions and loses stability. Our analysis combines analytical insights from the pendulum's classical dynamics with quantum fluctuations, allowing us to derive key parameters, such as the reduced Planck constant, from a cold atom experiment. This connection to classical dynamics facilitates a simplified interpretation of the quantum fluctuations' role in the system's behavior. Ultimately, our research provides a framework for understanding various aspects of quantum tunneling and the dynamics of complex quantum systems that exhibit extensive high-dimensionality. Furthermore, it is also applicable to other quantum tunneling phenomena, such as those observed in condensate fragmentation, as well as boson and fermion mixings. Pendulum models with atom-molecule conversion may also be emulated using optical Raman Hamiltonians, which could be investigated in ongoing experiments. The theoretical descriptions developed here are compared to experimental findings, and suggestions are provided for adjusting the model parameters. To facilitate further research, an experimental protocol is proposed that aims to measure the reduced Planck constant. The study concludes with considerations of future work aimed at extending the model to scenarios where three-body interactions play a prominent role. It is also explored how the model's effectiveness could be adapted to describe the dynamics of ultracold quarks, which lose energy through gluon emission. The connection to QCD, the quantum field theory that governs the behavior of quarks and gluons in nature, is made via a conformal mapping and a cold atom experiment where quarks and gluons are treated as pendulum oscillators. In the final section, we analyze the pendulum model's extensive high-dimensionality using the renormalization group, allowing us to understand how the model loses stability in the large quantum fluctuation regime, which is comparable to a quantum system that loses stability. A connection to the large-order perturbation theory's complexity is also made via the renormalization group, which is also applicable to other systems that lose stability. By implementing a version of the Distance Transformation Algorithm (DTA), the algorithm's convergence is expedited, resulting in a version dubbed QICI-DTA, in which each iteration's complexity is evaluated and compared to conventional approaches. Experimental results confirm that by leveraging quantum-inspired processes, problems amenable to clustering could enjoy accelerated solution times. The algorithm's implementation, including quantum-inspired source code, is made available online. The research suggests that certain clustering problems could now be solved more efficiently using strategies that predate quantum computing technology. The proposed approach also paves the way for hybrid computing applications where quantum and classical methods are seamlessly integrated, improving clustering performance. The hope is that this research will spark more innovative applications at the intersection of quantum and classical clustering algorithms. In the visual domain, objects are characterized by their distinct features and behaviors across multiple tasks, yet current methods often rely on task-specific representations, failing to capture a unified object presence across tasks. This study aims to identify spatiotemporal objects through self-supervised learning by designing an end-to-end framework. The proposal incorporates an adversarial loss to embed objects from different tasks into a unified space. Additionally, a contrastive loss is employed to isolate objects in spatiotemporal contexts, facilitating the development of an object-centric representation. As objects are characterized by their temporal attributes, a self-similarity auto-encoder captures the inherent object variability over time. The proposed framework's effectiveness is evaluated on various video benchmarks, including Marie, TSN, FlowPWC-19, and JHMDB, showcasing its ability to extract object-centric representations that are transferable and generalizable across different tasks. The approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods without task-specific designs and highlights the significance of object-centric representation in visual understanding. This research compares the predictive capabilities of various stochastic hierarchical models that describe how nitrogen soil levels impact tree growth. We evaluated six single-level models and four multi-level models, testing them on a specific dataset. The optimal single-model was the logistic regression, whereas the best multi-model was the linear mixed effects model. Across all models, the soil nitrogen concentration in nitrogen-fixing trees was found to be higher than in non-nitrogen-fixing trees, with this difference typically being statistically significant. Approximately 25% of the variability in tree sizes could be explained by the linear mixed effects model, likely due to the soil nitrogen concentration, with individual trees' characteristics resulting in an additional 10% explanation. By combining the linear models, an impressive 50% or more of the tree growth variability could be accounted for. Nonetheless, the models did not capture factors like foliage density, morphological variations, and specific ecological pressures on tree growth. We suggest that incorporating these factors into the hierarchy of the soil nitrogen concentration model could lead to an even better understanding of tree growth. Mafia is a popular party game or party-based hidden-trait social deduction mechanism, widely played globally. This study conducts the first-ever analytical examination of the game's dynamics using evolutionary dynamics. A four-role model, including detectives with two possible actions, innocent individuals, mafia members with two possible actions, and a prosecutor who can arrest a player, has been developed. The findings show that the mafia's likelihood of victory is determined by specific model parameters, such as the prosecutor's trust level, which can be linked to a threshold in the model. Further analysis reveals that the prosecutor's trust level is itself a function of two other parameters and identifies the critical role of these parameters in understanding the game dynamics. To model larger game scenarios, a two-role model, which includes a leader and follower, has been developed. The findings show that the leader's role can be interpreted as equivalent to the prosecutor in the initial model, enabling the generalization of the analytical results to this expanded model. Finally, a numerical simulation is employed to verify the findings from both models. The findings provide valuable insights for players to devise strategies and compensate for the leader's biased decision-making. The application of this methodology to other such games, such as Werewolf, is a potential avenue for future research. The existence of multiple giant planets, as seen in the past decade with exoplanet discoveries, poses difficulties for formation models based on single-planet scenarios. Our research uses a series of planetary-scale atmosphere models to simulate the growth of multiple Jupiter-mass planets accretionally bounded by gas disks. We examine three distinct scenarios: single-planets, double-planets, and triple-planets, with a focus on how disk mass and scale vary. Our findings show that multiple planets can coexist and evolve independently, with each planet developing a circumplanetary disk. As a planet masses, its circumplanetary disk expands, with the thermal emission from this disk contributing substantially to the planet's total brightness. By contrasting single-planet and multiple-planet thermal emission patterns, we show that differential therapy can explain the varied infrared light curves of planets like HAT-P-7b and UMP-CMIb, with multiple planets accreting from the same disk potentially resulting in equal light curve fits. Furthermore, our results indicate that multiple planets are more likely to be detectable at wavelengths of 10-50 $\mu$m due to their unique thermal emission patterns. With the aid of future dedicated space-based missions like LEVIT and PLATO, we anticipate that multiple planets will be commonly discovered. Ultimately, our goal is to develop models that accurately predict and match the light curves of multiple planets to their actual thermal emissions. With this approach, we aim to develop a standardized method to link observed light curves to planetary characteristics and disk properties. By achieving this connection, we will gain a deeper understanding of planetary development and disk structures, paving the way for future exoplanet and disk research. We investigate electron-phonon and photon-phonon interactions in armchair single-wall carbon nanotubes using the tight-binding model within the $4^{th}$ order perturbation theory. Calculations of the deformation potential for both electron-phonon and photon-phonon interactions are carried out, and the high temperature conductivity of an armchair single-wall carbon nanotube film is determined. By integrating the conductivity of individual tubes and considering the percolation theory, the conductivity of the nanotube film is expressed through the filling factor of the tube assembly. Furthermore, the influence of temperature, tube radius, and carrier concentration on conductivity is examined. Conductivity patterns are categorized into three regions: tube radius-dependent thermal or photon-dominated transport, tube radius-independent electrical transport, and tube radius-dependent transport. It is found that the photon mechanism significantly contributes to transport in larger tubes at high temperatures, as indicated by the photon factor. The photon factor is identified as nearly constant with respect to tube radius in the range of large tubes. Additionally, the photon factor's influence on conductivity is predominantly non-dispersive, and the impact of carrier concentration is minor. Consequently, the photon factor primarily dictates transport in the high temperature conductivity of an armchair single-wall carbon nanotube film. Based on this investigation, the photon factor can be utilized as a reference for identifying carbon nanotube systems. Furthermore, the photon mechanism significantly contributes to transport in both 2D and 3D carbon nanotube films. However, the photon mechanism's absence in 2D systems results in the establishment of a filling factor threshold below which conductivity begins to decline as carrier concentration increases. Moreover, the photon mechanism's influence on transport in both 2D and 3D carbon nanotube films can be erased by lowering temperature. It is anticipated that the photon factor's influence on transport in carbon nanotube films can be modulated through adjustments to carrier concentration. Consequently, the photon mechanism's role in electron transport in armchair single-wall carbon nanotube film systems requires careful consideration. As such, the photon mechanism can be utilized to quantify carbon nanotube presence. In the future, the photon mechanism's influence on transport in both 2D and 3D carbon nanotube films can be manipulated by adjusting carrier concentration. Introducing fuzzy k-means clustering offers enhanced capabilities by allowing each data point to belong to multiple clusters with varying probabilities. The primary objective of this research is to improve fuzzy k-means clustering by addressing its partial liabilities through a modified objective function incorporating entropy terms. By incorporating these terms, we aim to (i) minimize the impact of outliers, (ii) reduce the effect of local data points near cluster boundaries, and (iii) enforce constraints on the membership degree variance across datasets. A comprehensive performance evaluation is conducted using synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing our approach with state-of-the-art methods in terms of theoretical robustness and practical clustering effectiveness. Results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach. Furthermore, we apply the modified fuzzy k-means clustering algorithm to a complex biomedical signal decomposition task, showcasing its practical applications. By combining robust clustering with signal decomposition, we aim to gain deeper insights into the characteristics of rare synthetic hematopoietic cells. Specifically, our method enables the detection of minimal cell populations with increased confidence. These findings are further validated by examining the statistical significance of the identified peaks using a two-sided z-test. A theoretical analysis is also performed to confirm the minimax convergence rate of the modified fuzzy k-means clustering algorithm with an outlier. This is achieved by establishing a lower bound on the minimax risk and showing that the modified objective function minimizes this risk. In addition, we examine the computational efficiency of our approach and prove that it has a polynomial time complexity. The developed approach seeks to optimize two primary objectives: (a) determining the optimal partitioning of data among multiple experts and (b) estimating corresponding parameter values. Initially, the model re-estimates expert parameters using the traditional Expectation-Maximization framework, then adjusts cluster assignments to ensure a better fit, iteratively refining these processes until the process converges. The proposed algorithm demonstrates significant performance enhancements in both speed and accuracy when compared to existing state-of-the-art methods on a range of benchmark test cases. To investigate the multi-gaussian property of star color distributions in globular clusters, we developed a novel and unbiased statistical model. This model represents varying star sub-populations within a cluster by shifting and scaling Gaussian functions in color space. We overcame previous limitations of this method by introducing Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms to facilitate the identification and parameterization of multiple Gaussian components. Employing our 3D physics-informed model, we generated simulated star color observations based on various cluster parameters and compared them to actual star color data from M22 and M22-G3 variables. Yet, despite their potential, these convolutional layers do not necessarily always produce transferable representations, with their effectiveness influenced by factors such as convolution kernel size, convolutional block composition, and the nature of the training dataset.  Convolutional layers, when analyzed side-by-side with counterparts from higher-level layers, demonstrate consistently lower variance in feature representation, suggesting a shared underpinning mechanism.  Furthermore, studies have indicated that inner-layer units tend to possess more adaptable properties than those of the final fully-connected layers, with key task information likely being encoded in the features produced by the later stages of the network.  Overall, our research indicates that variations in convolutional layers play a pivotal role in the variability of feature representations, with our findings having significant implications for the design of future CNNs.  As a practical application of our findings, we present a case study demonstrating the effective reuse of features obtained from mid-level CNN components, resulting in substantial improvements in performance for tasks involving image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. The outer disc regions of young stars contain numerous dust rings, possibly due to the influence of gravitational interactions from planets in the system. Our investigation focuses on understanding how these rings affect the evolution of solid particles and the development of planetary cores. To this end, we have developed a computational model that simulates the dynamics of a long-lasting ring at a distance from its parent disc. Our simulations demonstrate that the ring maintains its cohesion through a balance of gravitational potential energy and the particles' kinetic energy. As a result, the ring's mass distribution becomes increasingly concentrated in the centre, followed by a gradual decline in density towards the disc's edge. Our analysis of core growth in such environments reveals that the ring's structure prevents the accumulation of solids in the centre, instead favouring growth at the disc's edge. However, the ring's effects also lead to the erosion of cores by stochastic growth, resulting in the increased importance of this mechanism in comparison to the diffusion model. Our findings also show that the rapid stochastical growth of cores in rings may result in the formation of many planet candidates with masses of a few Earth masses at fixed radial intervals, in addition to a population of fewer but more massive planets near the disc's edge. Our proposed statistical methodology to identify the rapid formation of planets in such environments may ultimately enable the detection of these planets with the aid of direct imaging techniques.

A type of machine learning known as robust learning focuses on minimizing errors that are prone to disruption, using a specific set of scenarios or assumptions to achieve this. Unlike non-robust learning, which makes no such assumptions, robust learning often has to limit its considerations to a single possible disruption, resulting in a balance between the strength of this limitation and its computational demands. By combining these two concepts, researchers have been able to develop algorithms that can handle complex scenarios, draw insights from the limitations of these scenarios, and more effectively minimize errors that are easily disrupted, all while making notable improvements in terms of computational efficiency compared to non-robust learning methods. However, the efficacy of these algorithms has been questioned due to their susceptibility to unrealistic data manipulation and model selection. In this study, we have introduced a set of metrics that allow us to quantify and take into account the impact of these potential issues, drawing upon robust learning theory. Our findings have revealed that certain forms of disruption are capable of separating different data types, and that such disruptions can be used to develop targeted strategies for mitigating specific vulnerabilities, all while demonstrating the effectiveness of robust learning methods in the process. By testing these algorithms against real-world applications, we have observed notable improvements in terms of predictive accuracy and model reliability in the field of computer vision, and we have been able to quantify the adverse impact of unintended image transformations on these models, drawing valuable insights from the limitations of these algorithms. The code developed as part of this research has been made available to the public. In addition to our own findings, we have also explored existing literature on robust learning, highlighting notable improvements in terms of predictive accuracy and model reliability across a variety of applications, such as natural language processing and audio-based machine learning techniques. The enhanced version of robust learning methods presented in this study is expected to support a wide range of machine learning-based applications, and we anticipate that our proposed framework for evaluating algorithmic limitations will see significant adoption as a result of its ease of use and adaptability. The combined use of robust learning and non-robust learning has far-reaching implications and is likely to experience significant growth in terms of research interest and applicability in the future. The testing of robust learning methods against realistic disruptions has yielded mixed results, pointing to a significant need within the machine learning community for improved methods of training models that can effectively minimize errors that are easily disrupted, such as those resulting from image manipulation techniques. The enhanced version of robust learning methods presented in this study is expected to experience significant growth in terms of research interest and applicability

Optimization problem-solving time in transportation services can be significantly minimized by utilizing information about pre-designated routes. This concept is especially valuable when routes are frequently established in advance, for example, in the case of fixed public transportation schedules. We propose a novel algorithm that leverages information about fixed routes in order to expedite the computation of the fastest path in a graph where multiple paths with various travel times are available. Building on a variant of the DEPath algorithm, the proposed approach entails designing two types of paths: the first allows for travel in both directions and the incorporation of resting periods, while the second type is reserved solely for traveling in one direction and achieving higher speeds. By incorporating a binary search mechanism, the algorithm enables the efficient identification of the shortest travel time within a given bounds range. We conduct comprehensive experimental comparisons between the proposed algorithm and a modified version of the DEPath algorithm that prioritizes the construction of two-way resting paths. The results show that the latter yields superior performance in scenarios involving large graphs where edge numbers are divisible by 4 and the time ranges are relatively narrow. Conversely, when the edge numbers are not divisible by 4 or the time ranges are highly variable, the former exhibits superior performance. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating prior knowledge about fixed paths in the form of one-way designs in order to expedite the computation of the shortest travel time. The proposed algorithm establishes a high standard for computational efficiency among state-of-the-art path planning methods. Moreover, the findings highlight the versatility of the DEPath algorithm in accommodating various graph characteristics and time range specifications. Ultimately, the approach holds considerable potential for applications in traffic estimation, particularly in scenarios involving pre-designated routes. Knowledge of the environment is increasingly being recognized as crucial for multi-modal learning to adapt to challenging real-world scenarios. Unfortunately, existing knowledge frameworks assume a static knowledge base, which restricts their applicability to dynamic and uncertain learning contexts. Introducing environmental knowledge also poses a risk of compromising the learning system's integrity, making existing frameworks' robustness and adaptability subpar. To address these limitations, we develop a framework that leverages structural knowledge and incorporates environmental knowledge through a modular approach. By dividing knowledge into core and peripheral components, this framework segregates essential system functions from environmental inputs to mitigate degradation. Additionally, we propose methods to adapt environmental knowledge and study the resilience of learning in the presence of diverse environmental stimuli. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the benefits of our approach in terms of both learning efficacy and robustness, especially under uncertain or unseen environmental conditions. Furthermore, we validate its real-world applicability by adapting it to the Sim4Caps task. CapsuleNet models derived from this framework exhibit state-of-the-art performance on MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets, underscoring the significance of environmental knowledge and the modularity of our approach. By decoupling environmental knowledge from the learning system, we effectively safeguard multi-modal learning from environmental disruptions and enhance its generalizability to challenging environments. A combination of deep learning and medicine has significantly advanced the analysis of brain images, particularly in the study of Alzheimer's disease. However, accessing relevant medical history for research purposes has become a concern due to data privacy issues. This concern has led to the development of new research directions that focus on using unsupervised and semi-supervised methods for disease diagnosis and prognosis. A new study evaluates various unsupervised and semi-supervised techniques for detecting Alzheimer's disease progression by comparing their performance with a supervised convolutional neural network. The research compiled a unique dataset consisting of 1200 structural MRI scans from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative dataset, divided into three groups at different stages of the disease. The methods tested include unsupervised change detection, semi-supervised learning, and a supervised convolutional neural network. The results show that the unsupervised and semi-supervised methods are able to detect Alzheimer's disease progression at an accuracy of 76% and 84%, respectively. This is comparable to the accuracy of a supervised convolutional neural network, which reached 82%. In particular, a semi-supervised method using convolutional neural networks achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.84, indicating a high capacity for detecting Alzheimer's disease progression from early stages. This technology has the potential to be used in a predictive computation graph for an Alzheimer's disease app. The study's findings suggest that the use of unsupervised and semi-supervised deep learning methods can effectively diagnose Alzheimer's disease progression at an accuracy comparable to the supervised convolutional neural network, which may enable the development of a predictive computing graph for an Alzheimer's disease detection app. The research paves the way for implementing a predictive computing graph that can estimate an individual's risk of developing Alzheimer's disease based on unique brain features detected in MRI scans. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can effectively capture short-term patterns, yet struggle with long-term dependencies due to vanishing or exploding gradients during backpropagation. To combat this issue, various gradient normalization algorithms have been developed to mitigate the gradient explosion in RNNs. Our work introduces the Backward Dropping Algorithm, designed to address long-term dependencies in datasets by effectively normalizing gradients and accelerating model training convergence. The proposed algorithm leverages the concept of dropping techniques from dropout to effectively limit the gradient size, with experimental evaluations on multiple datasets across text, image, speech, and medicine classifications that demonstrate improved performance and faster convergence. The source code is freely available online. 

Key Contributions:
- We understand the limitations of using gradient normalization in tapping into long-term dependencies in datasets.
- We develop the Backward Dropping Algorithm, combining the principles of gradient normalization and dropout techniques.
- We experimentally evaluate the algorithm's effectiveness on multiple datasets and models.
- We demonstrate the versatility of the algorithm in multiple applications, including varying numbers of datasets, models, and dimensions, as well as differing levels of gradient dropping rates.
- We compare the algorithm's performance with multiple existing gradient normalization methods.
- We conduct thorough parameter analysis to ensure the algorithm's reliability.
- We verify the algorithm's generalizability by using inductive biases from pre-trained language models.

By considering two mock solids with perfectly crystalline structures but ambiguous spin-orbit coupling, we investigate how spin-orbit coupling influences the Hubbard model's phase diagram. As calculated using the dynamical mean-field theory, increasing spin-orbit coupling leads to two distinct metal-insulator transitions. The first occurs when strong interactions and strong spin-orbit coupling combine, transforming the metal into a topological insulator. These results suggest that the spin-orbit coupling becomes more influential than carrier doping when it surpasses a certain value relative to the interactions. It is often challenging to trust the output of a black-box model, especially when it is to be used for informing high-stakes decisions, such as those made by healthcare professionals. This study explores how the application of conformal prediction can be utilized to address the concerns associated with the reliance on such models. Specifically, this research focuses on the use of conformal prediction in the context of binary image classification, involving the analysis of lymph nodes from medical imaging. By employing conformal prediction, the predicted categories are accompanied by confidence intervals, allowing healthcare professionals to determine the likelihood that a classification result is model-dependent. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, a quantitative assessment is conducted, followed by a qualitative analysis based on expert knowledge. Furthermore, the proposed method is shown to outperform a conventional Bayesian neural network when the goal is to identify rare or unclear imaging patterns, while yielding comparable results for the more common cases. This research aims to shed light on the reliance of healthcare professionals on the predictions of black-box models by shedding light on their inherent properties. Through this analysis, the study reveals the degree to which the predictions generated by the used models are reliant on data, as well as their failure to generalize effectively to uncommon or unclear imaging patterns, thereby highlighting their potential to mislead when little domain-specific knowledge is applied. Ultimately, the proposed method is envisioned to contribute towards the reduction of adverse consequences and foster the reduction of anxiety among healthcare professionals and patients by providing a transparent and reliable estimate of the predictions generated by the used models. Concrete structures are frequently checked for degradation by using surface-mounted rebar because the dielectric properties of concrete provide essential information on its condition. To effectively assess concrete, high-resolution dielectric data is required. This study showcases a innovative approach utilizing a low-cost UWB-RF sensor embedded in rebar, which transmits power and measures the attenuation caused by the overlying concrete. By analyzing the power attenuation in depth, we can retrieve the concrete's dielectric properties. To validate our approach, we performed an experiment where we created a controlled environment with varying concrete depths and measured the dielectric properties using our sensor. The results demonstrate that our sensor can accurately determine the dielectric properties, thereby enabling concrete condition assessment with high resolution. Moreover, we develop a methodology for estimating the standard deviation of dielectric parameter estimations and employ a statistical analysis to evaluate the performance of our approach. The experimental results show that our sensor enables accurate characterization of concrete with dielectric properties, yielding mean relative errors of less than 4% for both water content and concrete age. This study presents an innovative solution for accurately and high-res assessing concrete condition. The proposed method yields a high spatial resolution, enabling rebar-attached UWB-RF sensors to effectively cover rebar with concrete depth information. The existence of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules is considered natural due to their composition of two heavy particles, but the existence of light-light hadronic molecules is considered unusual. Recent studies on $K\bar{K}$ and $\pi\bar{\pi}$ systems have made headway in understanding the rare cases of light-light hadronic molecules. This paper provides an update on the $K\bar{K}$ and $\pi\bar{\pi}$ research, specifically highlighting four distinct aspects: (1) establishing standard criteria, (2) exploring quantitative relationships, (2) investigating statistical properties, and (4) proposing a new approach. The new approach proposes that a light-light hadronic molecule can be formed by combining two meson molecules each consisting of one meson and one baryon. This idea is grounded in the observed prevalence of meson-baryon molecular states, and suggests that molecules formed through the binding of a meson and a baryon are more stable, on average, than those formed through the binding of two mesons. The idea's feasibility is demonstrated by identifying potential $K\bar{K}$ molecular states below the $K^* \bar{K}$ threshold. A new theoretical tool is developed to study the clustering of quantum fluctuations in a quantum field theory framework, and applied to the study of light-light hadronic molecules. This method views the field operators' correlation lengths as fundamental parameters, and studies their relationship with the motion energies and angular momentum properties. Building on this, a statistical analysis is performed on the light-light hadronic molecular ground states to determine their mass distribution in terms of the $D$ and $S$ hadronic molecular properties. The research is further expanded to propose a new theoretical framework, where a light-light hadronic molecular ground state is defined as the state with the longest correlation length in the set of quantum field theory parameters, and studied through a set of key properties, including the topological charge, isospin, and parity. The research under this new framework reveals intriguing patterns in the statistical properties of $K\bar{K}$ and $\pi\bar{\pi}$ light-light hadronic molecular ground states. A final aspect of the research involves using the statistical properties to develop a set of test criteria for identifying light-light hadronic molecular ground states, and applies these criteria to provide insights on the ground states of the $K\bar{K}$ and $\pi\bar{\pi}$ systems. The study concludes by connecting the research to the understanding and identification of light-light

The task of predicting pedestrian trajectories post release from congestion has
drawn significant research interests. Most studies to date have centered around
forecasting the future paths of groups of pedestrians, assuming release from
constriction occurs in a group. However, this assumption is not always valid.
Real-world congestion release points are difficult to identify, as they vary
greatly, with some individuals escaping early while others are trapped for a
while. To address this, we introduce the Trajectory Transformations (TT) method,
enabling trajectory modulation and manipulation in a structured format.
Congestion release points are considered as fixed points in a complex
topological space, and pedestrian trajectories are represented as paths with
intermediate checkpoints. The TT method pairs released pedestrians with their
originating group's trajectory up to two checkpoints, and then extrapolates their
paths in a structured format, considering multiple possible trajectories. The TT
method's effectiveness is demonstrated in a study examining the evolution of
constriction in a real-world instance, and it notably surpasses existing
techniques in a benchmark test involving the ITOP20016 and UAF datasets. The TT
method also sheds new light on the behavior of pedestrians trapped in congestion. 
The TT method, along with associated datasets and source code, can be accessed at: https://github.com/HiLT-Research/TrajectoryTransformations. The TT method has the potential to be used as a component in a control system to guide pedestrians using active incentives to expedite the process of congestion release. The active incentives are implemented as a push operation in the TT graph, and they notably yield in a significant difference in time reduction for the east-bound group when a cost-effective activation strategy is employed. The TT method can help designers develop a strategy to guide pedestrians using active incentives to expedite the process of congestion release, resulting in a significant difference in time reduction for the east-bound group. We propose a variational approach to approximate the adiabatic gauge potential based on a generalized differential form that relates to the commutator of the Hamiltonian and other kinetic components. By optimizing variational parameters, this method ensures the approximation exhibits the necessary smoothness critical properties, with its accuracy measured by the approximate gauge potential's deviation from the true physical flux. Key properties of this approximation include its relation to the nested commutators of the Hamiltonian with the wave function, as well as its connection to the squared Frobenius norms of these commutators. We further demonstrate that, during non-adiabatic situations, the approximate gauge potential exhibits an improved rate of convergence, compared to adiabatic conditions, when its accuracy is maximized through the variational procedure. To establish its applicability and effectiveness, we support the proposal with numerical simulations and analyses of a two-dimensional non-escalar SU(2) Yang-Mills theory. This paper proposes a new chromatic aberration (CA) simulation to evaluate the impact of this distortion on images and videos. Unlike previous simulations, our method employs a Catadioptric CA model, which accurately represents the refractive properties of lenses and lenses' inherent CA characteristics. As a result, our simulation yields a more precise depiction of real-world chromatic distortion. Furthermore, our method retains the inherent symmetry of chromatic aberration, thus enhancing its authenticity. Together with a perceptual experiment, our analysis demonstrates the significant effect of CA on color perception, showing that image colors undergo a $5\%$ shift in perceived warmth or coolness due to this distortion. Consequently, our findings suggest that CA correction is crucial for maintaining color's intended spectral quality in various visual applications. To facilitate further research, we release an open-source CA simulation library, enabling researchers to incorporate CA-based phenomena into their studies on human perception. The relationship between diversity in data science and model accuracy is well established, yet in the fast-paced field of natural language processing, the importance of maintaining a current edge in knowledge is often overlooked. This study examines the impact of the time gap between model training and evaluation on the speech recognition task, specifically in terms of its models' ability to adapt to changes in speaker and topic. By leveraging Amazon's S3 file service to track model development across distinct generations, we found that models trained months apart exhibit a notable decline in average performance of up to 30%. Our analysis shows that the diversity inherent in expanded training data is instrumental in enhancing model robustness. Moreover, we found that models trained in shorter intervals experience less significant degradation over time. Ultimately, we argue that incorporating a regular system update schedule analogous to that of software, alongside other techniques for mitigating knowledge drift, is crucial for maintaining the effectiveness of trained models. Incorporating these approaches can prevent the model's performance from deteriorating and allow it to sustain across distinct technological and knowledge landscapes. The time series data collected also highlights opportunities for leveraging descriptive metadata to refine resource allocation and model development strategies. The potential also exists for applying these findings to inform real-world system design and the development of the next generation of automatic speech recognition systems. Expanding on these initial results, we also present approaches for reducing knowledge drift and enhancing the long-term stability of speech models. As the majority of existing research in this space remains confined to natural language models, our analysis and the time series data generated provide valuable insights for informing system design and the development of the next generation of automatic speech recognition systems. Additionally, the methodologies discussed are universally applicable to other areas where models encounter shifting languages, topics, or knowledge. We also propose the establishment of community-driven data repositories and challenge initiatives aimed at addressing long-term stability in models and mitigating knowledge drift. The data collected through these initiatives, we suggest, will facilitate the creation of comprehensive time series data archives enabling researchers and practitioners to leverage diverse models trained on various datasets and against varying benchmarks, thus fostering shared knowledge and opportunities for across-domain analysis and the development of more robust models. To kick-start this endeavor, we also present a call for contributions to the "Long-term ASR Models" challenge, targeting the speech community. We envision a future where the collective efforts of shared initiatives and repositories enable practitioners and researchers to harness the potential of across-domain analysis and peer-to-peer knowledge transfer, thereby accelerating advancements in the field and the next generation of models capable of withstanding technological and knowledge shifts. The Hatano-Nelson chain, a model characterized by non-Hermitian behavior, is studied under the condition of nonlocal interactions that break down spatial symmetry. We analyze this model when its sites undergo slow changes, and the nearest neighbors transfer energy at a faster rate, leading to a broader range of parameters exhibiting non-Hermitian characteristics. Unlike its Hermitian counterpart, the skin effect in this non-Hermitian chain is influenced by the strength of fluctuations and correlations among elements, and we derive an expression for the skin effect based on the fluctuation-dissipation relation. We also observe that, unlike localized states, delocalized states are not immune to the effects of fluctuations in energy. Furthermore, we discover that, under specific conditions, fluctuations enhance the rate at which eigenvalues in the bulk shift towards the boundary in the complex frequency plane. This study investigated whether combining different emotional aspects of male and female voices could create a unified, androgynous voice that is perceived as being emotionally natural to listeners. To this end, we used various emotional speech synthesis techniques to produce voices that transitioned smoothly from fully male to fully female, as well as voices that combined emotional elements from both sexes. Our results revealed that, regardless of the specific emotional characteristics involved, adding male or female content made the voice more emotionally natural to listeners. Importantly, this perception held true even when a relatively large amount of only one gender was added - up to 90% of a voice could be derived from either sex alone and still be emotionally natural to listeners. These findings have implications for future research on creating emotionally natural androgynous voices, as they suggest that a seamless emotional transition between male and female can be achieved through combining their acoustic elements. Moreover, our data showed that emotional intensity level is not the only factor that influences how emotionally natural a voice is, as voices with the same level of emotional intensity but different gender content can vary significantly in their emotional appeal. This reveals that there are still other unaccounted factors at play. The aim of change detection is to identify alterations in multi-temporal satellite images. Although supervised methods are effective, they are limited by the need for extensive labeled data. In contrast, unsupervised change detection is more resilient to this constraint. A new approach, referred to as the supervised unsupervised change detection, is explored. This method leverages a fully unsupervised model to detect changes and then utilizes the outcomes to train a supervised classifier. A specific case study within the field of remote sensing compares the performance of supervised and supervised unsupervised change detection using three distinct models, including Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Convolutional Neural Network. The results reveal that the supervised unsupervised strategy yields comparable results to fully supervised methods, utilizing less labeled data in the process. A statistical analysis of three datasets demonstrates that the supervised unsupervised strategy requires 50% fewer labels from the same datasets to achieve equivalent performance. Additionally, in the majority of the dataset evaluations, the performance of the supervised unsupervised strategy surpassed that of the unsupervised model alone. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential for high-quality results with reduced requirements for labeled data. The vast potential of neural networks in learning a dynamics model from sensory data has yet to be fully realized in developing safe control strategies. Most existing methods fail to account for uncertainties when training these models, which is critical in determining the reliability of subsequent control designs. This paper showcases how utilizing the time-series analysis of noise in the learned dynamics model can enhance the robustness of learning-based controllers. By imposing a minimum likelihood threshold on model output predictions, we can ensure simulation trajectories align with real-world data, thus, ensuring a controller designed on the model will also operate effectively in the actual system. Our approach is supported by our experimental outcomes where we observe a notable improvement in the learned controller's performance using our proposed model modification method. This development holds promising implications for applying learned dynamics models in the design of safe control strategies. To facilitate widespread use, we have made our code openly accessible via this link: https://github.com/advance-robotics-research/likelihood-trained-neural-dynamics. By applying the Generalized Viscosity Solution framework, we analyze the upper and lower solutions, and derive an accurate solution independent of parameters. We further provide a concrete example illustrating precise solution recovery for Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, and explore its connection with various differential games including Stackelberg and probabilistic games. Additionally, the paper examines the relationship between viscosity solutions and Gordan-Trocheck solutions for Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. Finally, by leveraging the visitation format, we establish an exact formula for the value function of probabilistic games with Ambiguous coefficients; this formula holds even when the probability density function is not explicitly defined. We recognize this formula as a type of Level Set equation. Moreover, we analyze the sensitivity of this formula with respect to small perturbations in the probability density function, and demonstrate its utility for recovering the ambiguous probability density function from the viscosity solution. We conclude by establishing the connection between our viscosity solution formulation and recent research on differential games with ambiguity focusing on Stackelberg and probabilistic games. By employing our level-set formulation, we derive upper and lower bounds for the value functions in these games. We recognize the Stackelberg game bound as a generalization of the Black-Scholes formula when ambiguity is absent, and the probabilistic game bound satisfies the Level Set equation. We analyze the well-posedness of the stochastic verification principle for the Stackelberg game bound. The pion-nucleon sigma term is a key parameter in various areas of nuclear physics research, including nuclear structure, neutron stars, and nucleosynthesis. It is also crucial for investigating the nucleus as a quantum liquid and understanding quark matter in high-energy collisions. However, determining the sigma term precisely is challenging due to the uncertainties associated with nucleon mass and the pion mass. Modern lattice simulations have the potential to overcome these limitations, and we utilize results from lattice calculations to derive an upper and lower bound for the sigma term, taking into account the variability of the nucleon mass between 800 and 1200 MeV. Furthermore, a general method is presented to interpolate bounds of the sigma term by its extremities without employing the pion-nucleon sigma term as a function. This approach enables us to explore the feasibility of extracting the sigma term from lattice simulations of nucleonic matter with non-zero pion density. We find that the upper and lower limits for the sigma term range between -93 and -82 MeV and -87 and -74 MeV at zero pion density, and between -92 and -81 MeV and -87 and -76 MeV at the pion density of the nucleonic phase transition. It is worth noting that the nucleus as a quantum liquid and the nuclear structure in general may face a crisis when considering quark mass derived from the above calculations. We also discuss the implications of the nucleus as a quantum liquid and the nuclear structure in general, and explore the mystery of neutron stars, particularly the neutron radii of the solar-type material, the instability of long-lived supernovae stars, and the nuclear flow, all under the uncertainty of the sigma term and the nucleus as a quantum liquid. Additionally, we utilize the nucleus as a quantum liquid and the nuclear structure in general, and the lattice simulations of long-lived supernovae to derive an upper and lower bound for their baryonic mass. We find that the upper and lower limits for the baryonic mass range between 2.49 and 2.67 times the sun's mass, respectively. Recent studies have shown that nuclear short-range correlations affect the distribution of charge within the nucleus, thereby accounting for its thickness. High-order correlations play a crucial role in this phenomenon, and by analyzing the nucleus $^{208}$Pt at varying orders, researchers found that the distribution of quarks across space is consistent with experimental data when considering up to fourth-order correlations. However, when only the lowest-order correlations are factored in, the nucleus appears more compact than indicated by experimental measurements. The significance of this finding lies in the fact that while it is well-established that short-range correlations have a minor impact on the energy of monopole resonances, they remarkably influence the neutron skin thickness. Furthermore, this discovery has implications for understanding the properties of meson-nucleon and meson-nucleus interactions within the nucleus. In order to verify these findings, researchers plan to analyze the quadrupole form factor of the $^{208}$Pt nucleus via hadron experiments. The results of this research are expected to contribute to improvements in meson-nucleus potential, thereby enhancing the precision of chromo-electric form factor calculations. Ultimately, this technique may be expanded for use in investigating exotic nuclei with reduced stability. The development of this research technique may, in the future, facilitate the investigation of phase transitions between normal and quark matter within dense materials. The theoretical model employed in this research can also be applied to understanding the structure of meson-nucleus interactions at the quantum fluid dynamics level, particularly in the context of relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The results of this research are expected to facilitate the development of more accurate theoretical models for simulating heavy-ion collisions and studying QCD phase transitions. To better understand geometrical scaling, researchers compared the momentum spectrum of gluons in nucleons and photons, where the spectrum of the photon can be described by a simple formula. This knowledge informs our discussion on how to apply geometrical scaling when analyzing the momentum spectrum of gluons in p+p collisions, where the gluon momentum spectrum is typically represented by a function called xg. Notably, this spectrum can be expressed as the product of two individual gluon spectra, one belonging to a single nucleon and the other describing how nucleons interact. To compare these spectra, researchers normalized them so that their average values are 1/3 and 1, respectively. This comparison enabled researchers to reevaluate previously published data on geoscaling in order to establish a relationship between the momentum spectrum of photons and those of gluons within p+p collisions. Each core-collapse event is randomly selected from a modelled distribution of 10$^5$ progenitor masses, sampling from a power-law distribution (M$\propto M^{-\alpha}$) for $\alpha$ in the interval [0.5,3.0] as derived from studies of CC SNe in the Milky Way. We find that low-mass progenitors (M$\lesssim 10 M_\odot$) lose a portion of their mass to the surrounding gas before exploding, but the amount of material returned to the interstellar medium is primarily determined by more massive progenitors (M$\lesssim 20 M_\odot$). However, due to the dense gas environment, the effect of pre-explosion mass loss significantly impacts the final outcome, even for more massive CC SNe. Our paper introduces a framework for variational quantum models based on
polynomial circuits, allowing us to develop a variational quantum classifier
and explore the scalability of a specific optimization technique in various model
outputs. The effectiveness of such an optimization technique in small clusters of
superconducting qubits relies on whether the technique optimizes circuit parameters
for predicting class labels or, alternatively, output measurement probabilities.
Through analysis and numerical investigations, we find that in near-term quantum
computing, the efficiency of a specific optimization technique strongly depends on the
output of interest, specifically in the case of superconducting qubits. The experiments
also reveal that in near-term quantum computing, the technique is more efficient when
optimizing circuit outputs than measurement outputs. The latter, however, is more
efficient in noisy mid-term quantum computing. The proposed framework is valuable
for studying the efficiency of variational quantum models in various outputs. The
implementation of such models based on polynomial circuits provides a foundation for
understanding their performance and enabling their practical applications in quantum
machine learning. The source code for the model, based on polynomial circuits, is
available on https://github.com/quadcat/poly_circuit_model. The research was
supported by grants from the Australian Research Council and the NSW data science
initiative.

The study of active particles near a deadlock proves particularly significant, given its direct relevance to macroscopic systems where a similar scenario can be induced by a driven particle or a controlled steering wheel. Building upon previous findings that an active trimer positioned over a passively Brownian dimer creates a force imbalance leading to dimer motion, we investigated whether this effect could be achieved using two uniformly propelled trimer particles. Surprisingly, our results indicate that a specific arrangement of actively moving particle pairs generates a force dynamic that induces significant movement in the companion passively rotating dimer, which in turn can be equated to the effect of a steering wheel on a larger scale. Notably, this finding holds promising implications for the development of miniature engines that could potentially power tiny devices in the future.

Using both numerical simulations and real Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) maps, our research compares the error characteristics of biased and unbiased estimators in the presence of intense point sources. The instruction of tasks via natural language offers a potentially convenient method for teaching tasks, yet commonly utilized approaches based solely on language have shown limitations in effectively learning task objectives. This paper presents a novel framework that incorporates teacher guidance to learn task objectives. The framework assumes teacher feedback in the form of corrections on actual task system operation, drawing inspiration from the educational theories of pedagogy and pragmatism. Pedagogical instruction simulates a teacher's direct instruction of a student, whereas pragmatic feedback simulates a teacher's feedback to a already skilled student. We capture the teacher's intent through unsupervisedly defined abstract task objectives and store them as a graph. This allows the teacher to provide feedback in the form of modified graph nodes or edges following system performance errors, which the agent uses to update its policy. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach using a simple robotic arm task and compare its performance to traditional reward-based methods. Results indicate our approach successfully resolves the task with efficiency and adaptability. Additionally, performance analysis demonstrates the distinction between pedagogical and pragmatic guidance. We discuss various future research opportunities inspired by the findings. The code for our approach has been made publicly available. \href{https}{https://github.com/asharakeh/TeacherGuidedLearning}

We introduce a novel method of quantum state tomography, dubbed shadow tomography, which relies on performing a series of projective measurements to obtain probabilistic estimates of a quantum state's expectation values. This approach allows for state reconstruction without accessing the quantum state directly. It is feasible to use shadow tomography with quantum states accessible through quantum reading, a process that respects quantum privacy. We demonstrate that shadow tomography can successfully reconstruct arbitrary quantum states, including those that are pure or mixed, using any set of measurement operators. However, the amount of data needed for accuracy grows exponentially with the number of qubits in the state. A modified version of the method, incorporating data efficiency, is also presented, along with an initial exploration of its practical applications. Applying the principle of shadow tomography to the quantum circuit model reveals an intriguing connection between state reconstruction and circuit inversion. We show that using shadow tomography to reconstruct a circuit's output state after performing a specific task allows for the approximate calculation of the circuit's input state. This concept provides a new perspective on quantum circuit privacy. Further research is necessary to optimize the method, particularly concerning the optimal selection of measurement operators to facilitate more efficient reconstructions. The problem of minimizing the product of the inradius and circumradius for planar shapes was investigated, with specific conditions on their convexity and the constraint that they contain a given line segment. Extending this, a general formula was found for the minimum product of the inradius and a particular radius when a line segment's position is variable. This was done by transforming the problem into a one-dimensional optimization issue, involving a specific type of convex body area minimization, which was then related to another type of convex body height minimization. These optimizations were solved, allowing the resulting formula to be applied to the original problem. Additionally, the measures of convexity of the shapes were also considered, yielding new results. Conversely, a different approach involving convexification of the line segment was used to tackle another version of the original problem, focusing specifically on the case where the shapes are contained within a circle and all touch the same circle. This approach involved transforming the extremal shapes' geometries and touching conditions using a specific transformation of the midcircle of the original segment. The resulting applications of this approach included formulas for the extremal product of inradius and circumradius involving powers of the tangent points of the shapes, as well as relationships between the eikosasteroons and other type of convex bodies called zonoids. Furthermore, the other type of convex body height minimization that appeared in the first part of the paper was also related to the convexification of the line segment, yielding new results. Finally, several issues and questions raised in the text have been compiled into the appendix of the document. These issues include questions such as identifying the most convex shape given certain conditions or finding specific types of convex bodies height minimization formulas. They have been left as open problems for potential future optimization research. In designing experiments, especially those utilizing low-fidelity Ramsey measurements, there are essentially two approaches - either employ a Bayesian strategy, leveraging prior knowledge to inform decisions, or adapt to changes through heuristics or random methods. Our analysis, however, suggests that the Bayesian approach excels in scenarios requiring precise measurements, while in situations requiring rapid results, a heuristic or random protocol might be more suitable. Our work aims to further explore the distinction between experimental designs, specifically those improved through adaptation, in low-fidelity Ramsey measurements. Additionally, we introduce a novel Bayesian experiment design, incorporating both quantum process noise models and performance metrics, to achieve this goal. Our simulation data indicate that the Bayesian strategy, combined with an informative prior, leads to a significant reduction in the number of measurements needed to reach a defined level of accuracy - approximately three times fewer on average. Our results also reveal that, in this Bayesian design, uncertainty primarily lies in the distribution of estimation errors, rather than the quantum state itself. Our approach may serve as a foundation for developing tailored designs for quantum process estimation, with applications in validating quantum nodes for distributed quantum information systems. Our code is publicly accessible via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/quantumchannelrepresentation/BayesianProcessEstimation. Our research, although primarily based on low-fidelity Ramsey measurements, can potentially be extended to various other noise models and algorithms in quantum process estimation. Our forthcoming study will delve into the implications of our findings on quantum process estimation using high-fidelity algorithms. That work can be accessed under the repository https://github.com/quantumchannelrepresentation/BayesianProcessEstimationFollowup. We explore the properties of continuous-trace algebras in R-duals of type II string theory, focusing on the mathematical framework of localisation and its implications for classical T-duality in non-geometric cases. Our results demonstrate that R-duals with continuous-trace algebras have classical T-duals described by specific 3-categories. The construction of these categories relies on group-cohomology and associated classes that encode key geometric data. Additionally, we establish a condition ensuring that the quantum BPS spectrum of an R-dual is finite, related to elements of the algebra with the highest trace. Our findings include a broader analysis of the algebraic structure in non-geometric contexts, such as torsion elements in cohomology triples, and offer a natural generalisation of the Picard category to higher cohomology degrees. Moreover, we show that our categories fit within a broader theoretical framework known as non-Abelian Drinfeld-Sokolov formalism. Importantly, our work identifies certain obstacles to quantisation and classical T-duality that arise from the failure of the quantum BPS spectrum to be finite, as well as limitations stemming from the presence of torsion elements. Interestingly, our results for geometric R-duals classical T-duality yield a connection with the branch-cut melonic 3-categories constructed by Weis and Bennett-Baker, suggesting a potential equivalence of corresponding non-geometric and melonic geometric aspects. Notably, the 3-categories corresponding to algebraic generalisations of Picard bundles provide a natural interpretation of the recently proposed non-Abelian string net formalism. Furthermore, the R-duals classical T-duality procedure might be realised through a non-Abelian version of the Toda lithium process, an analogue of the Toda quantum recursion relation. The paper includes detailed explanations and illustrative examples, as well as an appendix discussing generalised geometric aspects and potential generalisations. It is submitted to Journal of Mathematical Physics. Explicit, ready-to-use code for computing cohomology triples associated with specific group-cohomology degrees is provided at this repository. We develop a novel method for compressing large graphs lacking minor pairs, a characteristic associated with Baker's metric problems. This compression technique has a polynomial information density and can be achieved in polynomial time. It exhibits two beneficial applications, enabling us to solve specific algorithms twice as fast and extend the results to more complex graph types, although the time complexity in this case is increased to Super Polynomial. Moreover, our Compression technique facilitates a deeper understanding of the NP-hardness of the metric Closest Pair problem in certain graph structures. It turns out the Hard-Instances are characterized by specific restrictions, and these instances correspond to graph configurations where the distance between pairs of nodes is constant. Our research builds upon recent works by Marion and Thomas, as well as those by Blum, Evans, Hartline, and Yao. A reduced version of the Compression technique was presented at the FOCS 2020 conference by Demaine et al., however, the current research extends its applications in two distinct directions. Furthermore, the Results are extended to more complex Baker's problems such as Gap Closest Pair and Directed Closest Pair that were proven to be NP-complete by Marion and Thomas. We establish sufficient conditions for the asymptotic stability of periodic solutions in a general class of nonlinear, spatially homogeneous time-periodic parabolic equations. These conditions are based on the prevalence of specific initial conditions that lead to periodic trajectories and on the continuity of solution trajectories in their initial conditions, with respect to the topological norm. Furthermore, we prove that the existence of periodic solutions and the associated stability results are linked to the properties of the equation's homogeneous steady-state solution and its small amplitude oscillations. As specific instances, we consider the Brusselator model and the models proposed by Kelemen and Weidmann and Szekely. We also provide numerical evidence supporting our findings. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that the prevalence of initial conditions plays a crucial role in the models' convergence to periodic trajectories, in direct contrast to the usual small-amplitude approximation, which may yield non-converging sequences of initial conditions or trajectories. The study concludes by highlighting several open questions related to the models' behavior. Kelemen and Weidmann's model and the Szekely model turn out to exhibit different patterns of solution convergence, which are related to the models' singular invariant sets. Finally, our analysis indicates that the models' behavior in the scenarios of global or local convergence of solution sequences depend on the models' representation as ordinary differential equations or degenerate parabolic equations, with the latter showing a higher degree of complexity. The recently proposed ADAPT-VQA framework aims to optimize the variational quantum algorithm by strategically combining classical and quantum computations. In this research, we have developed a fermionic adaptation, qubit adaptation, and quantum electronic structure protocol based on the ADAPT-VQA concept, which utilizes a mixed basis of spin orbitals and qubit operators to approximate the electronic wave function. The qubit adaptation protocol achieves higher efficiency by using a reduced number of amplitudes compared to fermionic adaptation, while fermionic adaptation exhibits faster convergence in some instances. The qubit adaptation protocol was also combined with the quadratic group-variational principle to account for errors in the wave function, thereby facilitating the determination of energetic minimum. Both the fermionic and qubit adaptation protocols were evaluated using hydrogen molecule and lithium hydride models. The results suggest that qubit adaptation achieves greater efficiency than fermionic adaptation, with an average reduction of around 85\% in the number of required amplitudes. Furthermore, fermionic adaptation exhibited faster convergence than qubit adaptation when treating hydrogen molecule, but qubit adaptation showed better performance in treating lithium hydride. The application of the quadratic group-variational principle to qubit adaptation yielded a more accurate energetic minimum than fermionic adaptation without such a principle. The overall success of these protocols bodes well for their utilization in quantum chemical calculations employing mixed-basis representations. In particular, they may facilitate the efficient simulation of molecules comprising multiple fermions, thereby paving the way for faster wave-function optimization and error mitigation in variational quantum chemistry. A recent paper proposes a new framework, the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), as an alternative to traditional generative deep networks. The DGD's main distinction lies in its ability to map data into a structured representation space where its latent variables adhere to specific statistical properties. Specifically, the work utilizes a multivariate normal distribution with varying means and covariances across data points. Implementing the DGD in an unsupervised manner proves challenging due to the need to optimize both the data distribution and the decoder's parameters. To address this limitation, the study focuses on incorporating the DGD into a semi-supervised learning framework by leveraging the prior knowledge of class labels. Similar to traditional generative models, the DGD achieves class separation in the representation space when labeled data is utilized. Consequently, supervised classifiers can now be applied to the representation space, producing improved performance in semi-supervised datasets. Moreover, the DGD's inherent structure allows it to incorporate additional prior knowledge through its normal distribution parameters, representing the data's inherent variability between classes. By factorizing the covariance matrix, the representation space can be decomposed into inter- and intraclass variabilities, which can be minimized, thereby enhancing the DGD's ability to capture interclass variabilities and, in turn, the performance of downstream classifiers. To validate the proposed approach, the study compares the results with those from traditional semi-supervised learning methodologies on diverse, visual datasets. The experimental findings demonstrate that the DGD's capability to capture complex interclass patterns and minimize intraclass variabilities can lead to superior classification accuracy, especially when the diversity between classes is primarily attributed to their covariances. However, the DGD's reliance on the quality of the classifier used in the forward pass might impede the method's robustness, which warrants further exploration. Additionally, the study reveals that the DGD's potential to capture the data's inherent variability can be overly aggressive and result in overfitting when the diversity between classes is relatively low. To address this limitation, the research proposes an edited version of the DGD's loss function, which can help rectify the model's overfitting tendency while preserving its ability to capture the data's variability. The study's results show that the edited approach can indeed achieve an optimal balance between the DGD's potential and the risk of overfitting. The findings suggest that the DGD's ability to capture the data's variability can be leveraged to enhance the model's robustness, which can be validated through experiments conducted across multiple adversarial robustness datasets

Recent breakthroughs in neural speech synthesis from raw audio using sequence-to-sequence models have revealed an intriguing observation - these models converge to a understandable solution without any supervision, which typically requires transcription data. This study takes it a step further by asking whether unsupervised systems can produce speech that sounds natural. We enhance the existing sequence-to-sequence model with an automatic speech recognition component and propose a training objective that relies on raw audio features and transcription probabilities. The model is then trained on a large corpus of speech and text data without any speaker identity labels. As expected, even though the model is unsupervised, our results show that it produces speech that is easily understandable and sounds natural, outperforming a supervised baseline system. Furthermore, our results indicate that the model learns distinct acoustic characteristics for individual speakers within the training corpus, both in terms of speaker identity and sentence-level context. This study proves that unsupervised neural speech synthesis can produce high-quality output and suggests that the naturalness of the speech is linked to its understandability. The model's ability to generalize to new speakers also implies that its source of naturalness is fundamentally different from that of supervised models, which rely on idiosyncratic aspects of speaker voice. The model's training recipe and code are publicly available, and we hope that these results will pave the way for future speech synthesis applications without requiring transcription data. We also believe that the insights gained from the experimental findings will aid researchers working in the domain of automatic speech recognition and speech synthesis. The model's potential applications in scenarios where data is scarce or annotated speech is expensive to obtain, such as in low-resource languages or for individuals with laryngopharyngeal reflux, are considerable. We discuss the practical implications and challenges associated with voice cloning in these scenarios.
