This study utilizes Reinforcement Learning techniques to teach a robotic system how to combat adversarial attacks autonomously, comparing its outcomes with direct gradient optimization methods. Reinforcement Learning methods, particularly Gradient Episodic Reinforcement Learning, are based on an adversary-loss gradient optimization without requiring a direct computation of the gradient of the loss function, making them more resilient to adversarial attacks compared to traditional methods. However, the stability of the reinforcement learning training process is a concern, particularly during the initial phase. To address this issue, we developed a simulation-based reward function design that improves stability, enabling the model to learn effectively. Our experimental outcomes indicate that the Genetic Gradient Reinforcement Learning method achieves higher adversarial accuracy (73.53%) compared to the traditional Evolutionary Neural Network technique (on average, 73.03% vs. 73.03%). Furthermore, we evaluated both techniques under varying levels of adversarial noise and found that the Genetic Gradient Reinforcement Learning method demonstrates greater robustness, achieving a 10.54% higher accuracy at the highest noise level (32/255). These findings suggest that Reinforcement Learning methods offer an effective solution to adversarial machine learning attacks, and our proposed Genetic Gradient Reinforcement Learning method may serve as an alternative to traditional gradient optimization methods. To facilitate future research, we are making our code and data sets available to the public. Please visit our repository at https://github.com/asharakeh GenGRRL for the implementation. Our contribution is significant, as it provides a novel framework for Robust Reinforcement Learning that can be applied to real-world scenarios. Our findings indicate that robust training is feasible but poses a greater challenge than non-robust training. To address this issue, we developed a novel framework that splits RL training into robust and non-robust phases, making it possible to achieve state-of-the-art adversarial accuracy using fewer resources. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, achieving an 11.64% higher accuracy (from 73.03% to 84.67%) with reduced training samples (by 1.64% decrease). These results suggest a potential trade-off between achieving robustness and computational efficiency through the isolation of robust training phases. Our findings provide valuable insights into RL training methods, shedding light on their instability under adversarial attacks. To facilitate future research, we are making our code and data sets available to the public. Our contribution is significant, as it offers a novel solution to the robustness issue in RL, providing an alternative path for future research.

We have developed a method to identify matching sources among widely separated optical and gamma-ray counterparts of the same blazar. Utilizing gamma-ray data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope and incorporating new information about the associated optical variations aids in resolving potential source confusions. Our methodology integrates the entire probability distribution and yields reduced matching errors by 65% compared to a previously employed method and increases the overall success rate to 91%. Application of this method to 56 optical-gamma-ray associations results in 50 confirmed matches, addressing earlier doubts in 46 cases. Additionally, we present the initial results of matching 13 years' data from the Fermi telescope, which reveals that 24 sources exhibit incompatibility with single-meeting associations and possibly have two separate counterparts. We discuss three of these complex cases in more detail. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive list of 105 blazar associations, resolving 82 uncertainties and leaving 23 ambiguous cases unresolved that require further investigation. As a separate entity, we demonstrate a simplified alternative to our primary method, which demonstrates matching errors and success rates of 8.4% and 91%, respectively. Finally, we address potential future applications of our approach, such as its usefulness in multi-messenger astronomy, particularly in associating gamma-ray sources with neutrino and fast radio burst investigations. Although primarily designed for blazar research, our method can potentially be applied to other astronomical studies involving extra-galactic sources. Similarly, the incorporated model of optical variations might also be useful for analyzing the behaviors of individual blazars and facilitate broad understanding of their long-term variations. Although we relied on a simple linear model, we believe that leveraging machine learning could lead to substantial improvements and reduced uncertainties. As an additional resource, we make our code available for others to use.

All forms of deep learning generative models are based on an assumption that real-world data is consistent and can be represented in a relatively consistent manner. However, this assumption is challenging to implement using the latest deep learning techniques, especially when dealing with diverse, globally unsensory data. As a result, deep learning generative models may struggle to produce samples that accurately represent real-world scenarios, limiting their capabilities despite continuous improvements.

Real-world data is often irregular and can be consistently described only in a general sense. For instance, images of the same object can exhibit significant variations due to factors like lighting, pose, or composition, and may not share any similarities beyond the obvious. To address this complexity, cutting-edge deep learning generative models can learn to capture the inherent inconsistencies and irregularities of real-world data, enabling them to generate realistic images that resemble a wide range of scenarios.

A comprehensive understanding of the subject requires an in-depth examination of the most effective techniques in image synthesis, which encompasses various generative models like Autoencoders, Markov Chains, Variational Autoencoders, Autoencoders, GANs, and Normalizing Flows. Each type of model is distinguished by its capabilities, advantages, and limitations in terms of performance and resource requirements, as well as the ease of training and the ability to learn complex patterns in data. The research explores the relationship between the thermal diffusion properties and molecular flexibility in binary mixtures, demonstrating that flexibility significantly impacts the thermal diffusion factor under temperature gradients. Through molecular dynamics simulation, the thermal diffusion factor in an ethylene oxide and water mixture was investigated, revealing that molecular flexibility causes non-ideal behavior and affects the temperature dependence of the thermal diffusion factor. The study further indicates that flexibility can lead to non-Debye behavior and influences the temperature dependence of the thermal diffusion factor in mixtures, which can be attributed to differences in nuclear spin restriction and electron/nuclear interactions between molecules. Nonetheless, quantum effects primarily influence the thermal diffusion factor at high temperatures, with flexibility having a greater impact at lower temperatures. The simulation results show that molecular flexibility plays a crucial role in the thermal diffusion properties, with flexibility-related variations in the thermal diffusion factor reaching up to 100% at room temperature. The study emphasizes the necessity of considering molecular flexibility in the analysis of thermal diffusion. The research also reveals that molecular flexibility can manifest as frequency-specific fluctuations, with molecules exhibiting greater flexibility at lower frequencies. The study further indicates that internal degree of freedom affects flexibility at lower frequencies, with frequency-specific flexibility being much lower than that of the entire molecule. The analysis of frequency-specific flexibility shows a quadratic relationship with molecular interactivity, with greater interactions corresponding to greater flexibility at lower frequencies. The study provides a clearer understanding of the frequency-specific flexibility of molecules, with internal degree of freedom playing a pivotal role, especially in situations where energy requirements are low. The research demonstrates that molecular flexibility can be utilized to tailor the functions of biomolecules and surfaces by manipulating intermolecular interactions. The study further enables simulation of gas-liquid interactions to develop strategies for enhancing surface functionalities. The research also enables simulation of cellular processes at the nanoscale, allowing for a deeper understanding of transport phenomena in living organisms. The study further paves the way for the modeling of wide-ranging phenomena, such as atmospheric interactions, through the utilization of molecular flexibility. The study further enables simulation of molecular interactions in liquids and solids, allowing for a deeper understanding of mass transport at the nanoscale, leading to significant advancements in various fields, including materials science, chemical engineering, biology, geology, and climate studies. The study further provides insights into the molecular interactions in aerosol particles, enabling better management of atmospheric processes and impacts. However, the ongoing growth in the size and capabilities of these models has raised concerns about their practical feasibility due to increased costs, resource requirements, and difficulty in model interpretability.  To address these issues, we investigated the potential of smaller, finely-tuned models to perform as well as larger pre-trained transformer models in the task of essay grading.  Our study compared the performance of a range of pre-trained models and our proposed BERT-based model, trained with fewer than 3 million parameters, which we found to be comparable to the performance of larger pre-trained models on the TOEFL test dataset, consisting of extensive human-generated text.  Overall, our results demonstrate that by using a modular, multi-layer architecture and leveraging task-specific data augmentation, it's possible for smaller models to surpass the performance of larger pre-trained models used for the task of essay scoring.  Our approach may also provide insights for the improvement of other fine-tuned transformer models. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly enhanced the restoration of degraded music recordings. These advancements have improved the quality of low-quality music recordings significantly. However, a key challenge persists: applying deep learning techniques to diverse types of music which up to now have been underrepresented in databases used for training. To address this limitation, this paper introduces an innovative method for increasing the training data available for deep learning by utilizing a broader definition of music that includes unnotated, non-audio formats such as sheet music and lyrics. We extract audio from these sources using suitable pre-processing techniques, which are then used in a deep learning framework to support the restoration of degraded music. This pioneering approach opens up new possibilities for applying deep learning to a wide range of music genres, including those with limited availability of high-quality training data. Experimental results confirm that this extended training data leads to improved audio restoration. These findings indicate that increasing the diversity of sources used in training can lead to better outcomes. Furthermore, this approach encourages the collaboration of multiple disciplines including musicologists, engineers, and data pre-processors to gather and expand training data effectively. The research also includes a new method for converting sheet-music to audio in real-time, which has applications in its own right. These contributions include the development of an audio generation system for generating drum tracks, and an extended definition of Music Information Retrieval that includes non-audio formats. The research outcomes indicate that it is feasible to produce high-quality drum tracks automatically, which could be employed successfully in video games and film production, for instance. Creating realistic throwing animations can be challenging for character animation designers. Although researchers have made significant progress in generating stochastic motion trajectories based on human demonstration, the lack of a comprehensive framework for evaluating throwing motions has limited the incorporation of local realism constraints in generative models. This study proposes a subjective evaluation method to assess the realism of throwing animations and identifies key factors that affect users' perceptions. We found that both the type of object thrown and the viewer's knowledge of the task influence how realistic the animations are perceived to be. Building on these discoveries, we conducted a series of experiments utilizing a GPPM-based generative model and discovered that constraining the energy of the throwing motion can enhance the perceived realism of the resulting animations. The findings from our research provide valuable insights for the design of realistic throwing animations and serve as a basis for further research in the field. The evaluation tools, demonstration videos, and evaluation results mentioned in the paper can be accessed via the website http://kangzfu.github.io/Throwing. Additionally, the code for generating the trajectories using the GPPM algorithm is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/JoonmingY/PPM-G. A third-party license for the CMA-ES has been uploaded to https://github.com/audrianoc/CMA-ES. The research was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea under grant No. 2019R1A2B2032002. A pre-print paper with the distinct identifier https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.13253 is hosted on arXiv. A video introducing the research, including the abstract, can be found at https://youtu.be/UMfzOoQXQkM. The research demonstrates an improvement in applying human-knowledge in computer animation systems. The evaluation method contributes to motion design by showing how motion quality can be enhanced through subjective evaluation. The research applies a multidisciplinary framework, combining human psychology, signal processing, and physics, to the field of computer animation. The evaluation results pinpoint specific factors that affect the quality of animation and suggest ways to enhance them. The research explores the limitations of current AI-based motion generation technology. The research adjusts a motion generation algorithm, taking into account the specific tasks it is used for, and discovers the effects on generated motions. The research introduces a new evaluation method to assess the quality of animations by humans. The research moves the field towards more applied, data-efficient algorithms. The research provides necessary data to train a deep neural network to perform the same task

To improve the fluency and coherence of machine translations, particularly in cases where source and target sentences differ in length, researchers are developing new methods of sentence rearrangement. This research introduces a syntax-aware attention model, incorporated into a novel Reranking approach, to steer the attention mechanism towards more syntactically aligned areas of interest within sentences. By incorporating this new model, researchers observed a notable enhancement in the fluency and semantic coherence of translations. Notably, the elevated syntax awareness in the attention mechanism tended to increase the extent of sentence reordering. This study further investigates the connections between sentence length, syntax-aware attention, and sentence reordering. The benefits of the syntax-based attention model are variably affected by the amount of sentence reordering, with benefits most pronounced in cases involving moderate to substantial reordering when shortening sentences, or lengthening them. Conversely, the extent of syntax-based attention in cases involving minor reordering tends to be less significant. This research indicates that the application of syntax in the attention model is a practical means of increasing the coherence of the target sentence, particularly in cases involving changes in sentence length. The elevated syntax in the attention model is seen to predominantly favor rightward attention in cases involving minor reordering, or lengthening sentences, and leftward attention in cases involving shortening sentences. However, the extent of syntax in the attention model is observed to exhibit a uniform increase in the presence of sentence reordering. The proposed approach is a straightforward means of improving the efficacy of sentence reordering techniques in the post-NMT era. This research is grounded in experiments conducted using the WMT14 English to German dataset, incorporating the top-performing models from the WMT14 English to German competition, employing various forms of sentence reordering. The experiments further reveal an increase in the syntax-based attention in the presence of certain reordering techniques, such as decreasing the blockage of reordering, and increasing the extent of sentence lengthening in the target sentence. The proposed approach is shown to enhance the coherence of the target sentence across all reordering techniques, and datasets, leading to an overall decrease in the number of incorrect words, and an increase in the number of correct words. The elevation of the syntax-based attention in the presence of reordering tends to increase the number of incorrect words, but this trend is seen to be inconsistent in the case of increasing the blockage of reordering. The proposed approach is seen to improve the efficacy of sentence reordering in the post-NMT era, leading to an overall decrease in the number of incorrect words

Planets in their childhood are heavily influenced by ice condensation in the outer reaches of the disc, which sets aside material for planet formation. The snow line is of particular significance in this process, and recent studies employing the MIGRATION AND MIXING model have allowed for simultaneous simulation of the migration and development of the planet. In these studies, the movement of the planet is determined by a second-order Runge-Kutta method, with a time step set by the planet's distance from equilibrium. However, previous research has demonstrated that this approach is flawed, as it results in an unrealistic increase in computation error when the planet's initial binding energy is high or low, which must be corrected in the analysis. A revised approach has been developed to allow the planet to escape from its initial position, which is consistent with the findings of the previous research. The revised method also ensures that the planet's initial binding energy has little to no effect on computation error. By employing the revised approach, it has been found that varying ice condensation binding energy values by a factor of two or ten leads to variations in the snow line of about 50% and 100%, which is as substantial as the changes brought about through differing opacities by a factor of one hundred. The significant impact of binding energy on the planet's migration and snow line is matched by its substantial influence on gas and dust development. Ultimately, further research is needed to clarify the uncertainty in the snow line resulting from the varied planet binding energy. Based on the MIGRATION AND MIXING model, it is anticipated that this uncertainty may be as high as two, which is consistent with the changes brought about through differing gas and dust development. The revised approach has been made available at: https://github.com/astrokkt/planet-migration. This work offers a straightforward way to match a theoretical distribution, B, to an observed dataset, A, by shifting and scaling it, resulting in a transformed distribution, T(B), that closely approximates the dataset. This approach involves using cumulative probability to compare observed data to T(B) and adjusting parameters in an iterative process to match them. A specific formula is provided that allows for numerical computation of a unique transformation that closely aligns T(B) with the dataset A. This method is described in the context of fitting Gaussian and Cauchy distributions, but has broader applicability to other theoretical distributions, including those related to partial differential equations. Additionally, the formulation provides insights into optimizing parameter values by shifting and scaling a distribution to minimize distance to a dataset, as well as offers a potential tool for interpolating between different datasets. Finally, the formulation is explored in the context of physical systems, including in the case of shallow water waves, for potential applications in adaptive filtering and active control. In the process, errors in standard filtering methods are corrected, and recommendations are offered for applying this technique to other domains of science and engineering. Furthermore, the formulation provides insights into optimal threshold values for signal detection in various domains. The quantum-state detection process is represented by a collection of non-selective measurements. Theoretical foundations are developed to address probability distributions of measurement results and associated standard deviations. An algorithm is proposed for estimating the expectation values of Pauli operators, with convergence rates and expected values of estimation errors being calculated. The viability of this approach is explored through simulation and practical application with real photonic-qubit data. The results demonstrate that the quantum-state parity is recoverable through estimation of the expectation value of the Clifford observables, thus suggesting the potential for parity-beam-splitter-based quantum-state learning. Quantum-state learning of Fock-state qubits is also possible if the number of photons in each circuit can be determined. Additionally, we discovered that the quantum-state learning of Fock-state qubits can be viewed as a specific instance of quantum teleportation, with associated rates of convergence and error probabilities being investigatable. This work develops enhanced asymptotic relationships for a function that represents high-frequency wave solutions in geometrical optics, with an emphasis on scenarios with rapidly changing coefficients in three-dimensional space. Specifically, we consider a particular class of functions defined by $\psi(x,\xi)$ that describe waves oscillating according to $e^{i\phi(x)}$, where $\phi(x)$ is a real, convex function at a given frequency $\omega$. By drawing parallels to short-wave asymptotics in Helmholtz theory, we derive improved estimates for $\psi(x,\xi)$ that accommodate algebraic decay in the phase $\phi(x)$ and its derivative, thereby expanding the scope of previous estimates significantly. Moreover, we demonstrate the robustness of these estimates in the presence of smooth potentials with compact support, offering a new estimate that aligns closely with the behavior observed in the Dirichlet problem. This research also explores the application of these estimates in the context of electromagnetic wave scattering from chiral particles. In the case of zero boundary conditions, we observe that the far-field representation remains valid even for unsmooth chiral shapes, provided that the surface of the chiral shape can be parameterized smoothly. Additionally, we derive an explicit representation of the far-field pattern, denoted as $E^{0}(\hat{\vartheta},\xi)$, in terms of the phase function $\phi(x)$ and a function $w(x,\xi)$ that, for smooth cases, reduces to an expression involving the chiral shape's geometric properties, including the orientation, size, and orientation-dependent vector ${\mathbf n}_c$, where ${\mathbf n}_c$ represents the chiral axis vector. This explicit representation serves as a valuable tool for analyzing and predicting the scattering behavior in various electromagnetic and wave scattering problems in the high-frequency limit. By observing the absence of frequency-dependent modulation in the phase component of $E^{0}(\hat{\vartheta},\xi)$, we can conclude that no diffraction effects occur, thereby validating and extending known results from the smooth case. Furthermore, we also establish an explicit representation of the far-field pattern for magnetic dipole radiation from a chiral sphere in the presence of a harmonic terahertz field. By exploring the connection between the phase component of the far-field representation and the time dependence of the field, we can determine the sign of the chirality parameter $\epsilon$, thereby providing a feasible method for measuring the chiral parameter. We explore how algorithms become sample-efficient by utilizing techniques like feature smoothing, leverage score optimization, and pseudo-labeling, which all struggle with overcoming a key obstacle in these algorithms: curvature vanishing. By identifying the most effective methods to mitigate curvature, we establish a unified framework that compares these algorithms and determines their optimal performance based on a limited number of samples. We also identify specific conditions that separate tasks must meet to achieve efficiency in these algorithms. We demonstrate through numerical experiments that our analysis accurately predicts performance, providing valuable guidance for choosing the most suitable method among those examined. The knowledge gained from these findings can be applied beyond multi-task linear regression to other classification tasks, such as multi-task logistic regression and the multi-task generalized linear model. Our analysis reveals that existing algorithms may fail or become less effective when the number of tasks increases, encouraging the development of more efficient methods to tackle more complex problems. Baber and Talbot recently proved a central result in graph theory, establishing an optimal limit for the Turán density of r-uniform graphs. Building upon their work, we investigate whether this density determines the maximum possible number of $K_r$-free subgraphs within r-uniform graphs, effectively acting as a sharp threshold for their emergence. Our research reveals that this density lacks this threshold characteristic for all values of r exceeding 3. In addition, we show that while the structure of r-uniform graphs exhibiting the maximum number of $K_r$-free subgraphs may be highly complex, its Turán density-like value, expressed as a limit involving the maximum subgraph density and a specific function, equals the density of the complete graph $K_r$. We also explore an alternative form of this value, referring to it as the "greatest tangent density" to $K_r$, and prove that it has a meaningful interpretation for large graphs of 3 uniformity. Consequently, although the optimal large-constant behavior of r-uniform graphs differs significantly from their complete graph counterpart, the two share a connection through their "greatest tangent density" values. We also use our approach to reprove a result previously established by Talbot and Vena, stating that for r = 3, the maximum possible number of $K_r$-free subgraphs within r-uniform graphs occurs exactly at its complete graph $K_r$. We further derive an extension of this finding to graphs defined by small monochromatic freebase patterns and obtain similar results for their "greatest tangent density" values. Our study ultimately leads to an understanding of how to construct diverse and highly structured r-uniform graphs of various types, including those free of specific subgraphs or defined by specific patterns, while achieving the maximum possible density of their respective structures. We also present two challenging open problems aimed at clarifying our main research question. By employing cutmix and mixup techniques on chest x-ray images, the necessity for a large set of labeled training data significantly decreases, enabling the model to achieve comparable performance with less than 10% of original data. We use the metrics of precision, recall, F1 score, AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, and top-1 accuracy for evaluation. Notably, using 10% of original data results in F1 and recall scores of 0.814 and 0.877, respectively, compared to their counterparts on fully labeled data. We also adopt the mixup technique from the perspective of features and weights to improve model generalizability. These image enhancements, specifically cutmix and mixup, demonstrate effectiveness in reducing the needed labeled data by roughly spreading out the pixels uniformly, thus minimizing overfitting and allowing the model to effectively utilize less data. Moreover, the unsupervised nature of these image enhancements does not necessitate additional annotation for generating pseudo-labels. We intend to contribute to the field of medical image classification by introducing an innovative method for reducing required labeled data, thereby minimizing the burden on clinicians during the annotation process. We believe healthcare professionals should focus their valuable time and resources on diagnosing and treating patients rather than data preparation. We further intend to contribute to the field of active learning by presenting a pioneering approach for selecting samples to annotate, specifically cutmix pseudo-labeling. We compare our proposed method with three active learning techniques, specifically entropy, uncertainty, and uncertainty-engaged on the reduced dataset with cutmix and mixup. The results show the cutmix approach results in top-1 accuracy of 0.916 and F1 score of 0.814 on 10% of original data, thus implying the need for careful selection of the dataset to annotate. We compare the performance of the dense labeling of original data with the sparse selection of cutmix pseudo-labeling, top-1 accuracy of 0.916 and F1 score of 0.814, respectively. This research builds upon the convergence of vision and language studies by embedding prompt learning within the image captioning framework. We present PPLC, a novel approach that uses a two-stage process: first, it leverages prompts to constrain the description of an image to a fixed length, thereby automatically selecting relevant visual and semantic components from a vast set of possible descriptions. Then, the output is refined through a series of copy and generation operations guided by prompts. To further enhance the process, we incorporate a protocol enabling the use of a shared encoder for multiple tasks, thereby significantly reducing the amount of parameters to learn. We demonstrate PPLC to be a highly effective method, achieving exceptional results on the Image Captioning 2015 dataset. Notably, we also show that PPLC is adaptable to existing image captioning architectures, making it a versatile tool. The code and prompts used to achieve these results are publicly available on the repository https://github.com/AmiiLab/pplc.

Concepts like contrastive causation, equifinality, and interaction play crucial roles in causal reasoning, particularly in assessing the negative consequences of actions. Developing an effective definition of harm requires incorporating these concepts, enabling a more nuanced understanding of its relationship with desired outcomes and overall utility. Building upon Cariou and Hadfield's work, we extend their notion of contrastive causation to capture the negative impact, where the same causal processes can produce both beneficial and detrimental effects simultaneously. This approach enables more precise assessments of harm by focusing on interventions causing undesirable consequences, whereas the previous definition was too broad, encompassing even beneficial outcomes. We demonstrate the usefulness of this refined definition by applying it to existing utility formalisms and evaluating its properties. Moreover, we establish a connection between our work and concepts like tipping points and amplifying the good and the evil. Finally, we showcase the potential of this definition by using it to specify community criteria for beneficial artificial intelligence.

We introduce an approach for creating speech-to-text models that don't require training on specific domains or languages, leveraging speech-to-text models fine-tuned on text data for the same language. This method achieves this in a few steps: first, identifying similar text data to use as a proxy; second, transferring knowledge from this proxy text data to the model; and third, using the model for speech-to-text without further training. We show that this technique leads to better results, especially in few-shot scenarios, and significantly outperces current top methods when translating to a new domain or language not encountered during model fine-tuning. For example, when translating from different domains within the same language, our fully speech-based approach yields a 14% increase in word accuracy. Furthermore, our approach also yields improvements for zero-shot and few-shot translation across various languages, including up to a 9% increase in word accuracy. We also present a more effective variant of this technique that incorporates a neural alignment between the original and proxy text data, and show that this model achieves higher word accuracy and domain adaptation metrics. All the code and models used in this research are available at https://github.com/jamiejp6/speech2text_zero_shot. This research was supported by a Google Fellowship. The traditional Fourier heat conduction equation is valid for an infinite number of timescales, which is not always the case in real systems. Introducing the concept of fading memory leads to the Carnahan-Fornier-Lorenz (CFL) heat conduction equation, which can be modeled using a constitutive relation. However, the integration of the relaxation spectrum is often difficult to determine. In this study, the spectrum's integration was simplified using the minimum dynamic variability theorem, which is supported by the spectral width. Utilizing the theorem's properties, the integration was transformed into a straightforward geometric task, resulting in the substitution of the integration of the relaxation spectrum with the integration of the spectral width. A method for dynamically determining the width was also developed, which can be used to identify the number of relaxation times. Using the width, the distribution of relaxation times can be identified as a combination of primary and secondary processes. For verification purposes, the direct and inverse problems were numerically simulated using the finite element method. The ability to model additional heat conduction phenomena using the minimum dynamic width makes the CFL equation a versatile tool for a variety of applications. It is essential to note that the width's minimum value is not necessarily zero and that the primary and secondary relaxation processes may or may not be overlapping. For direct problem simulations, the width was determined from the material's dispersion relation, while for inverse problems, the width was calculated from the second derivative of the displacement field. The width's ability to identify the number of relaxation times was visually verified through 2D direct problem simulations using the material parameter dispersion relation. Inverse problem simulations using the second-order of the displacement field showed the identification of the minimum dynamic width and the number of relaxation times. The width's ability to identify the material's time constants was achieved through 2D inverse problem simulations using the second-order of the displacement field. Consequently, the minimum dynamic width offers a straightforward geometric task for the integration of the relaxation spectrum and provides insight into the material's dynamic behavior by identifying the primary and secondary relaxation processes as well as the number of relaxation times. Additionally, the width allows for the estimation of the material's dispersion relation and its first and second-order displacement fields. In conclusion, the use of the minimum dynamic width in the integration of the relaxation spectrum is simple and easy to implement and represents an important advancement in the field of heat conduction research. The study compares the predictive capabilities of conventional forecast methods, peak forecast methods, and combined approaches, revealing that blending these techniques yields superior results during peak hours. The paper presents a novel multi-scale neural network architecture, dubbed MS-FFCN, for integrating insights from different scales and using feature fusion to further enhance prediction accuracy. The proposed approach exhibits competitive performance while requiring fewer model parameters than alternative neural network techniques, such as MS-CNN and Pi-SparseNet, especially when predicting energy consumption under varying weather and load conditions. The study utilizes real-world data on energy consumption and weather from over 310,000 households in Germany and repeats the analysis using data from over 200,000 Australian households, producing consistent results across both datasets. The proposed MS-FFCN approach outperforms the benchmark neural networks in terms of predictive accuracy and efficiency, making it a suitable choice for energy retailers seeking to minimize costs and optimize services. The research also explores the potential benefits of using peak forecast fusion to improve a self-charging Wireless Power Transfer system using kinetic energy. The idea is to harness orbital, vibrational, and movement energies from satellites, drones, and electronic devices. The results indicate a significant reduction of up to 50% in costs associated with keeping devices charged, as well as the potential for MS-FFCN to contribute to the advancement of smart grid systems, improving energy efficiency, and consumer experience. The novel multi-scale neural network architecture, dubbed MS-FFCN, demonstrates its potential across diverse applications, achieving optimal performance and efficiency. The rapid growth in machine learning research over recent years has created immense interest in applying these models to various real-world problems, and as a result, the field has achieved remarkable success in achieving state-of-the-art results for a range of important tasks. Nonetheless, most machine learning models continue to overlook essential information and rely on flawed data that is often marred by biases and inconsistencies. Utilizing prior knowledge can help address these limitations, and incorporating diverse data sources can enhance the accuracy and robustness of machine learning models. This knowledge diversity often leads to improved model performance, higher parsimony, and greater resilience when dealing with unexpected data deficiencies or aberrant data patterns. We present a thorough survey of ensemble methods that leverage multiple data sources, offering in-depth examinations of various techniques, a detailed discussion on challenges, and a range of topics for potential future research investigation. The survey delves into decision tree ensembles, neural networks, stochastic gradient descent, semi-supervised learning, clustering, outlier detection, feature selection, and active learning areas. To facilitate further research, we have categorized several complex issues that might be of interest to researchers in the field. This document aims to provide an informative overview for researchers who are familiar with ensemble learning as well as those seeking an introduction to the topic. The survey has derived many of its insights and recommendations from a comprehensive program, including a thorough literature review and interviews with leading machine learning experts, as part of the Machine Learning for Science initiative. We introduce a data-driven approach that learns to localize lesions without image annotations, relying solely on meta-data labels, in this case, for the MSKCC Challenge 2022. By leveraging a attention-based autoencoder, we bypass the need for manual segmentation masks. The method involves training a multi-task autoencoder that minimizes density map reconstruction errors while simultaneously regression tasks that identify pixel indices of lesions. To enhance lesion localization precision, we employ a progressive co-training strategy. We also investigate the effects of oversampling on dense regions containing lesions. The proposed method demonstrates its potential by achieving a high area under the curve score of 0.96 on the training set and 0.94 on the validation set, resulting in a 0.91 AUC score on the testing set. The method also achieves a high Q* of 0.78 on the validation set. Our final model ranks 8th in the MSKCC Challenge 2022. The code for the proposed method is available on this repository. Furthermore, we suggest that the performance of the proposed method can be further enhanced by utilizing additional data from public domains to mitigate the limitations imposed by small datasets. The proposed method's performance is evaluated based on the density map quality and the density energy perspective. The density map quality is evaluated by the ratio of the density map area to the density map maximum value, whereas the density energy perspective is calculated as the sum of the gradient of the density map across the entire density map. The method's performance is compared with the baseline MSKCC Challenge 2022 solution that utilizes a fully convolutional network. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves better results compared to the baseline solution with a density map quality of 0.73 versus 0.54 and a density energy perspective of 1.00 versus 1.43. The method's performance suggests that a significant improvement in lesion localization accuracy is achievable when transitioning from dense to sparse representation of the density map. The method's performance also indicates that a progressive co-training strategy outperforms the simple oversampling strategy. The findings of the density energy perspective suggest that the density map needs to be refined to remove the noise and ensure smooth transitions across the entire density map. The method's performance further reveals that the attention-based autoencoder re-learns the identity function as a convolutional layer and relearns the oversampling operation and the attention strategy, thereby enhancing the lesion localization accuracy. We introduce an innovative end-to-end neural network, 'Equivalent Ledge Representation and Translation Tornado Network' (ELRTNet), specifically designed for lumbar vertebra localization and identification. This approach utilizes a novel training technique, 'Equivalent Ledge Translation', that mimics the effects of orthogonal transformations to efficiently detect symmetrical features in vertebraas. As a result, the algorithm generates an 'Equivalent Ledge Representation' (ELR) from 2D input images, facilitating automatic identification of vertebral level, position, and number through a coarse-fine learning strategy. To further enhance performance, we integrated a powerful localization module, 'Tornado Localization Network' (TLN), to locate lumbar vertebra L1 to L5 in lumbar spine CT scans with an improved localization rate of 99.73%, a significant increase of 5.16% and 13.47% compared to DeepLearnBP, ELNN, and CASL respectively. The method also achieved a high identification rate of 100%, a significant improvement of 16.67% and 13.06% compared to DeepLearnBP and CASL respectively. On the 'Location and Identification of Lumbar Vertebra' challenge of the 2019 Medical Image Understanding and Analysis (MIUA) conference, the method demonstrated exceptional performance with an average across-training lumbar spine dataset of 97% L5 identification rate and 99% localization accuracy. The method also achieved 100% identification and 99.73% localization rate on the training dataset of the challenge. The code is available at https://github.com/Ayazudas/ELRTNet. Recent research on cavity polaritons has gained significant attention due to its promising potential for generating non-classical light and implementing novel quantum information technologies.  To explore this potential, we investigated the stability of an N-nested cavity system hosting polaritons, employing a linearized Einstein-Podolsky-Russell-Born-Oppenheimer model.  Our findings presented in a previous study indicated a complex phase structure resulting from the interplay between polariton dissipation and vacuum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field.  When the electromagnetic mode experiences zero-point fluctuations, polariton dissipation is minimized, but this leads to instability in polariton energy, while maximizing polariton dissipation via electromagnetic field occupation enhances stability in this regard.  Conversely, vacuum fluctuations have a negative effect on the polariton's coherence properties, although this can be compensated for through electromagnetic field occupation.  Our analysis sheds new light on previous research, clarifying the relationship between electromagnetic field occupation and polariton dissipation, a relationship previously understood only qualitatively.  Our findings also highlight the practical utility of electromagnetic field occupation in stabilizing the electromagnetic field, a capability previously unrecognized.  Our work offers a foundation for exploring electromagnetic field influences on polaritons, uncovering novel phenomena resulting from electromagnetic field occupation, and leveraging cavity polaritons to control and generate non-classical light.  Furthermore, we anticipate our research to contribute to the advancement of cavity polaritons as foundational elements in quantum information technologies.  Our analysis, although primarily applicable to semiconductor microcavities, offers insights with far-reaching implications for other cavity polariton systems, including those based on quantum dots and atoms.  Our work has broader implications, as electromagnetic field influences on polaritons remain an understudied area of research.  Our research may inspire the development of novel methods for enhancing electromagnetic field occupation times and controlling the coherent properties of polaritons at the level of individual quanta.  Our study offers a starting point for exploring the intersection of vacuum fluctuations and dissipative effects on polaritons, enabling a deeper understanding and potentially groundbreaking applications of cavity polaritons.  Our analysis provides the groundwork for leveraging cavity polaritons to control and generate non-classical light, an area of ongoing research with the potential to revolutionize the field.  Our research identifies electromagnetic field occupation as a versatile tool for stabilizing the electromagnetic field, leveraging cavity polaritons to control and generate non-classical light, an area of ongoing research with the potential to revolutionize the field. This paper showcases a spring-based actuator used in a jumping robot that requires only rechargeable electricity to launch itself to a sustained flight phase. Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices can help solve the full separability problem in quantum states, offering an advantage over classical methods for small state dimensions. We highlight the benefits of employing unitary transformations, then provide an example based on a three-qubit GHZ state, demonstrating that a NISQ device can efficiently determine its entanglement. This example serves as a model for future experiments and potential applications of NISQ technology. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of extending our approach to larger, partially entangled states. Finally, we suggest future research directions for scaling up the method, including potential applications to identify bell-diagonal states and handle multi-partite quantum states. We also address the potential use of this method in quantum key distribution to detect entangled bells. We found that this approach can easily be extended to any number of parties, making it a versatile tool for the field. We also compare our method with other existing ones, highlighting its unique capabilities and weaknesses. We conclude that NISQ devices, although imperfect, can utilize quantum characteristics to solve the separability problem, paving the way for new applications and experiments. We also envision future applications of this method, including the ability to identify bell-diagonal states and handle multi-partite quantum states. We conclude by suggesting that NISQ devices offer a valuable platform for the quantum information processing community to explore new and exciting applications and experiments. We hope that our work contributes to the ongoing effort to bridge the quantum-acoustic divide by investigating novel approaches that can easily be implemented with QIO devices. These notes cover the implementation and analysis of a method for addressing ill-posed problems via the gradient flow algorithm. Due to its unfeasibility, most problems require modification of the gradient flow into a discrete algorithm. A widely used method involves utilizing an energy functional that incorporates data-driven terms to regulate solutions, but this approach still necessitates the selection of stoppage time, which significantly influences the approximation accuracy. Consequently, we center our discussion on stopping time choices, examining their impact on convergence rates in combination with discrete dissipation schemes. A potential solution to mitigate this issue arises from dynamic regularization techniques and their representation through bundled energies. Therefore, we explore applying a discrete bundle gradient flow. A crucial element of this approach involves defining a finite-dimensional characteristic energy space that, in combination with the temperature parameter, determines the path stability and connection to standard discrete bundle methods for local minimization. Furthermore, we prove that the discrete bundle gradient flow produces a convergent sequence as the temperature tends to zero. Importantly, the resulting limit depends on the choice of energy functional and discrete time scheme. Consequently, we examine the continuous limits of standard discrete bundle methods, such as backtracking and one projection schemes, and analyze their convergence rates. Additionally, we establish that stopping times based on limited oscillation or prediction-correction strategies converge to optimal solutions, while the bundle gradient flow enables the efficient computation of optimal oscillation limits with minimal computational burden at equilibrium. This paper presents a novel cost function for monocular depth estimation, aimed at enhancing the state-of-the-art in depth and volumetric methods. The created cost constructor partitions the scene into fixed 2D shapes, and assigns an index to each point based on the shape with the closest center point. This index constructor surpasses prior methods in several aspects: it disregards occlusions by using geometric proximity as the criterion for point assignment, and thereby maintains more accurate depth estimates. Moreover, it generates compact and uniformly distributed tetrahedra across the scene, and facilitates the development of a cost constructor that operates in high-dimensional point clouds with minimal memory consumption. Additionally, the index constructor enables the computation of a cost vector that indicates the reliability of depth estimates based on spatial variations in nearby shapes. Results show that our approach yields superior monocular depth and volumetric reconstruction performance on real-world datasets, and its training data can be freely applied to volumetric reconstruction tasks, resulting in significant improvements over the current state-of-the-art. Code and model weights are available on the repository at https://github.com/asharakeh/ tetra-monodepth. This work also yields substantial improvements on the NYU-V2 dataset with only training on the tetra-monodepth objective, and achieves top-ranked performance on the ScanNet dataset after retraining on the dataset with the index constructor. Moreover, the paper presents a cost vector that indicates the reliability of depth estimates and volume occupancy, and shows that it correlates with common metrics used in computer vision. The constructed cost vector yields insights on the local reliability of depth estimates and volume occupancy, and can be employed in future research to develop more effective metrics for monocular and volumetric tasks. The paper also demonstrates the applicability of the cost vector in assessing the local reliability of other vision metrics through publicly available visual analytics tools at https://dash.dc.tu-berlin.de/monodepth. In summary, the research presents a novel cost function for monodepth and volumetric reconstruction that boasts superior performance, and develops a cost vector with reliability information for further research. The research additionally enables the development of a visual analytics interface to study the local reliability of other computer vision metrics. The research was carried out at TU Berlin, and the associated code and model weights can be accessed at https://github.com/asharakeh/tetra-monodepth. Home WiFi networks can significantly suffer from poor user experience due to poor design, poor installation, limited access point capabilities, badly conflicting signal frequencies and speeds, etc.  Most current devices associate with access points primarily using RSSI metrics, which isn't effective in managing conflict and load.  We propose a new method that takes into consideration minute variations in signal intensity and load when selecting access points.  We implement load detection through active measurement, while associate with access points also being controlled by the same active measurement, allowing devices make informed decisions about frequency and load.  We evaluated this method in a laboratory setting versus traditional RSSI-based association methods and our results indicate that it's capable of improving throughput and reducing delay.  We further studied how this method impacts energy efficiency and fairness.  Despite its benefits, we found that it's difficult to improve energy efficiency while improving throughput and reducing delay may even decrease user experience for some users.  We further analyzed this method and found its benefits diminishing as more users are online.  We conclude that our new method is capable of improving performance, but its practical implementation is still a challenge.  We suggest further exploration of methods to improve user experience, energy efficiency and fairness.  Public domains can be an ideal testing ground to investigate these issues and we hope our work can serve as a basis for future research.
